28 The Or, 〈◊〉 . suburbs The lesser Cities on Terra Firma, alarmed with summons of their Governours to put themselves in a posture of defence. Or, the Waves, an elegant Hyperbole thus read, the very Waves which roar, and terrifie shall hear, and tremble at a stranger, and more doleful cry, then their own. Or, as our Version, the Suburbs, which are nearest the Sea shall first hear the outcries of Pilots, and Mariners despairing of escape, when, their Ship broken to pieces, all at once shreik out. So shall thy Citizens cry and fall. shall shake at the sound of the cry of thy pilots.

29 And all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea; shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land.In the Allegory of a miserable shipwrack, the Prophet sets forth Tyrus fall, and in this verse he represents them all shifting out of the shattered sinking Ship, in great confusion, and greater fear, the Slaves quit the Oars, the mariners throw up the Tacklings, Pilots leave the Helm, a • l make for the long Boat, and the Land, where they bewail their undone condition. Or, it may be more literally understood thus, all Seafaring men, who got their living by service done for Tyrus at Sea, seeing her utterly broken, shall leave the Ships, get to Land, that elsewhere they may get employment, or by a timely flight save themselves, and bewail their old Masters fall.

30 And shall cause With greatest cries they shall make the Countrey eccho forth their sorrows. their voice to be heard against Either standing on higher ground over-against the shipwrackt City, Or rather, for thee, those Eastern People did use to lift up their voice in mourning, Iob 2.12. Ier. 2.18, 19. and 31.15. Zech. 11.3. thee, and shall cry bitterly Their weeping shall be from a deep sense of the misery of t •• ir Friends, and this exprest by bitter cryes, so such sorrow is exprest, Zeph. 1.14. Isaiah 22.4. and 33.7., and shall cast up dust Another expression of great distress, and sorrow proper to those Countreys, Iosh. 7.6. Iob. 2.12. Lam. 2.10. and Ier. 6.26. upon their heads, they shall wallow Rowl themselves in ashes, which they used to do in their greatest mournings, as Mic. 1.10. and Ier. 6.26. as every Countrey hath its peculiar manners, and customs in mourning, so had these customs, that exprest most vehement sorrows in gestures, which we are not accustomed unto. themselves in ashes.

31 And they shall make themselves utterly bald It was the custom of the Heathen, to either pull off with their hands, or cut off the hair of their heads in great mournings, which God forbad to his people, Lev. 18.28. Deut. 14.1.1. thus do Tyrus mourners in baldness express their sorrow, and despair. for thee, and gird them with sackcloth Another usual Ceremony of mourners well known to all., and they shall weep for thee with bitterness of heart It shall be a hearty mourning, not a counterfeit one, this referring to the inward grief, the next bitter wailing refers to the outward expressing it., and bitter wailing.

32 And in their wailing In their sorrowful speeches of Tyrus. they shall take up Into their mouths, or with a composed, significant, and comprehensive form of speech to shew much grief in few words. a lamentation for thee, and lament over thee, saying, What city is like A few years since no city like her in beauty, riches, glory, and joy, now none like her in all the contraries. Tyrus, like the destroyed Now no more Tyrus the flourishing, the renowned, the Mart of Nations, and the stately built; but now the destroyed, the silent overwhelmed with grief, which was full of Songs. in the midst of the sea Alas! what was once her safeguard, is now her grave, what enricht her once hath now swallowed all up at once.?

33 When thy wares Brought home from all Coasts. went forth out Were Landed, brought on shoar for the Mart. of the seas thou filledst There was enough to supply to the full. many people Numerous, stately, sumptuous Nations, though their prodigality was great, thou furnishedst them, hadst wares rich, and stately enough for all of them.; thou didst enrich the kings Such influence had thy vast Trade, that not only meaner men and subjects, but Kings themselves were made more wealthy by it. of the earth i. e. All Kings of the known World, or Kings of Nations far off, as well as neighbouring Kings. with the multitude of thy riches The greatness of thy Trade, the variety of thy wares brought from all parts, were thy own riches, and enricht all thou didst Trade with; Kings were enricht by Customs, and Tolls paid to them by the enriching their subjects, who thereby were fitter to pay Taxes, or by furnishing their treasuries with all the peculiar Treasures of Kings, the rare, and precious Jewels, which they esteem; and since we know some Kings did Trade too, by this Tyrus increast their Wealth., and of thy merchandise.

34 In the time So soon as, or ever after the unhappy day. when thou shalt be broken Shattered to pieces. by the seas The Powers of the Babylonians that like Seas shall swell, roar, and break in upon thee. in the depths of the waters In the deepest afflictions, and by sorest oppressions, and violence., thy merchandise All thy Trade., and all thy company The multitude of thy Citizens, of thy hired Souldiers, of thy Allies abroad, and of those, that came into thy Markets for Trade shall cease, wither, and perish too. in the midst of thee shall fall.

35 All the inhabitants of the isles Strictly and in a larger sense the Sea-Coasts. shall be astonished Wondering, it ever should be effected, that Tyrus should fall. at thee, and their kings shall be sore afraid Knowing how they are much less able to resist, and defend themselves▪ and not knowing where that mighty Conqueror would next trie his Arms, and Fortune., they shall be troubled They shall not be able to conceal the discomposure of their mind, but in their countenance a trouble made up of grief, fear, and indignation, grief for their Friends, fear for themselves, against that cruelty, and inhumanity, which without respect to any thing dear to mankind, ruined the glory of the World, destroyed, what could not be repaired by all the riches, and wisdom, and bounty of the Babylonish Kingdom. in their countenance.

36 The merchants among the people shall hisse This usually is an expression of scorn, and contempt poured forth on the Person hist at, if thus understood the meaning is there should be some among Tyrus Customers that would rejoice at her fall, and flout at her, either, perhaps wronged by her in their Trade, chap. 28.16. or else with envy, and expectation of her Trade to turn to them, return to her the wicked carriage she shewed to Ierusalem fallen, and sacked; if it be a sign of ought else, 'tis of wonder as, 1 King. 9.8. at thee:
• hap. 26.21. thou shalt be
• eb. terrors. a Matter of many fears, and to many People, who do, or shall hear how terribly thine Enemies have raged against thee and prevailed. terrour,
• eb. shall not for ever. and never shalt be any more Vid. c. 26.14, let. o. .

div.head: CHAP. XXVIII.
div.p: 1 THE word of the LORD came again unto me, saying,

2 Son of man, say unto Of. the prince King, whose name was either Ethbaal, or Ithoba •• . of Tyrus, thus saith the Lord GOD; because thine heart is lifted Thou art waxen proud, and aspirest above all reason, and boastest extravagantly in thy self, state, policy and power. up, and thou hast said Thought, imagined, or flattered thy self. I am a god Or the mighty and strong one, for so the Heb. is, and perhaps were better so rendred, he gloried in his strength, as if he were a God, the like you have, Isai. 14.14., I sit in the seat of GOD As a Magistrate he did bear the name, and authority of God, but he thought not of this, he dreams of the stateliness strength, convenience, safety, and inaccessibleness of his seat, as if he were safe and impregnable as heaven it self., in the Heb. heart. midst of the seas, Isa. 31.3. yet thou art a man Subject to all the casualties, sorrows, and distresses of mans state and life, thou art Adam of Earth, not El, nor like unto the mighty one in Heaven., and not GOD, though thou set thine heart Thou hast entertained thoughts, which become none but God, thou hast projected things, which none but God can effect, thou hast promised thy self perpetual peace, safety, riches, and happiness in thy self, and from thy self. as the heart of GOD:

3 Behold, Zech. 9. • . thou art In thy own thoughts of thy self. wiser then Who was then famous for his wisdom, which was imparted to him from Heaven, chap. 14.20. Dan. 1.20. and 2.20, 48. Daniel, there is no secret that they That any sort of men can conceal, that thine adversaries shall contrive against thee to thy danger, or hurt; all this Ironically said. can hide from thee:

4 With thy wisdom By thy policy in Government, and by thy skill in Trading, for he speaks of that kind of prudence, to which these names are given. and with thine understanding thou hast gotten Or made, so the word. thee riches Power, and might, so the Heb. as well as wealth, and riches, and so the Gall. Version reads puissance, the Princes of Tyrus had been prudent, and so increast their power, and interest., and hast gotten Or made, procured. gold and silver into thy treasures.Into both his own private purse, and into the publick Treasuries too.

5 Heb. by the greatness of thy wisdom. By thy great Here the eminent degree of this Princes Wisdom is owned. wisdom, and
And, might as well be spared, for, as 'tis not in the Heb. so it rather obscures, then clears the Text, let it be read by thy great Wisdom in thy Traffick, and 'tis very plain, and so the French reads it. by thy traffick hast thou increased Made great or enlarged. thy riches Thy Power, as ver. 4. let. n. , and thine heart is lifted Exalts it self, carrieth it loftily, and proudly above thy Neighbours, which is not good, above thy self, which is worse, and above God too, which is worst of all, as ver. 2. up because of thy riches Thy puissance at home, and abroad by Nature and Art..

6 Therefore, thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou hast set thine heart Vide ver. 2. let. b. as the heart of God Who doth, as justly he may, design himself, his own glory in all he designeth and worketh, and take the glory to himself, thou hast done so too, designed thy own greatness, and gloried in it.;

7 Behold therefore, I will bring Cause to come. strangers upon thee, chap. 30.11. and 31.12. and 32.12. the terrible of the nations A forreign People, called strangers for their multitude in the plural, and to intimate how little regard they would have to the Tyrian glory; these strangers were the Babylonian Forces. A fierce, violent, and cruel Nation, Hab. 1.7, 8.: and they shall draw their swords against the beauty Those beautiful things, in which thy wisdom appeared; either thy noble regular, and strong buildings, or thy beautiful well stored Arsenal, and Army, or the unparallel'd rarities, which all but rudest Souldiers, would esteem, and spare these Monuments of thy Wisdom. of thy wisdom, and they shall defile Pour contempt and stain. thy brightness.Thy Royal dignity, depose thee from thy Throne, and kill thy Autority and thy Person.

8 They These strangers shall s • ay thee, which is a blemish to the honour of a King thus to be brought to the Pit. shall bring thee down to the pit A usual periphrasis of Death and the Grave., and thou shalt die the deaths In the plural, because of the many Terrors, Dangers, and Wounds such mee • with, the successive deaths s • ain, drowned, eat of fish, cast upon shoar, and become meat to Sea Fowl. of them that are slain in the midst If literally understood, Thou shalt dye as other common Marriners, and be cast overboard, if figuratively; Seas for great distresses, then amidst multitude of deep distresses thou shalt meet with more than one death, be often dying. of the seas.

9 Wilt A cutting taunt, or sarcasm, what will become of thy Godship then? thou yet say Wilt thou then dream of Immortality, and Almighty power, when thine Enemy is cutting thy Throat? before him that slayeth thee I am God: but thou shalt be Appear then to thy self, and others to be a mortal, weak, conquered man, who dieth a Sacrifice to the Conquerors pride and c • uelty. a man, and no God, in the hand of him that slayeth Or, woundeth. thee.

10 Thou shalt die the deaths Ver, 8. let, h. A Twofold Death, Temporal, and Eternal. of the uncircumcised Of the wicked, or an accursed Death, the Iews do express a vile, and miserable Death thus, or the uncircumcised; i. e. Heathens, cruel, and merciless men shall slay thee, and this suits with what follows in the verse, and this was ignominious with the Iews, 1 Sam. 31.4., by the hand of strangers; for I have spoken it, saith the Lord GOD O thou proud, self-admiring Prince! Slight not what is threatned, for God, the God of truth hath spoken it..
11 Moreover, the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

12 Son of man, take up a lamentation See chap. 27. ver. 2. let. a, b. upon the King Called Prince, ver. 2. let. b. of Tyrus, and say unto him: Thus saith the Lord GOD; Thou sealest up the sum In the search into the frame of thy Government, the manage of it, the prosperity thereof, and its Glory, Power, Riches, and Confederacies thou doest think thy self but just to thy Kingdom to account it the perfect Idea of a good Government, that in the Tyrian State nothing is wanting that might be required in a good Government, in the best Government, and so sealest to the premisses; thus vainly puft up thou wilt have it, that fulness of Wisdom, and perfection of Beauty are in thee, but neither thy Wisdom shall prevent, or defeat the attempts of thine Enemies, nor thy Beauty charme their rage, thou shalt fall by them., full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty.

13 Thou hast been Thou hast dwelt and reigned. in Eden In the midst of all delights, and though nature made thy lot a very barren Rock; thy Art and Industry added to that of thy Progenitors have made it as Pleasant, Rich, and Beautiful, as Eden, that place of all desirable enjoyments. the garden of GOD This is explicative of the former, a Garden is a place of delight, and men have made some delightful to a wonder, but none ever like that God planted: This of Tyre came as near as any, and yet ungrateful, and Atheistical Tyre dreams of Divine Power, and Stability, forgetting Humane frailty, and uncertainty.: every Every • ort of Rich Stones. precious stone was thy covering Bought to adorn thy Crown, thy Robes, thy Bed, &.c. , Or, ruby. the Sardius Of a R • d, and by some said to be the Ruby., Topas Of a yellowish Green., and the Of clear, waterish, sparkling colour. diamond, Of a Sea-Green colour, the best. the Or, chrysolite. beryl, Resembles the whiteness of the nail of a mans hand. the onyx Of divers colours, but the best Green., and the jasper Of Sky colour, or blue., the sapphire, Green interspersed with Golden spots. the Or, chrysoprase. emrald, Of flame colour. and the carbuncle, Beside the abundance, of which in their publick Treasures much was used about the Clothes, and Robes of this proud Prince, 'tis like these precious stones were set in Gold, that they might the safer be put upon his Garments. This was the acco • trement of Solemnities, especially of the Coronation, as appears in close of the verse. and gold: The Now the Prophet notes their Joys, Musick, and Songs, both to Wind, or Loud Musick, and to softer Musick, as the Lute, and Tabret in the day of their Kings Coronation, and all this Musick on Instruments of most exquisite make, and of their own Artists work too, in this they exceeded as in the other. workmanship of thy tabrets, and of thy pipes, was prepared in thee in the day that thou Either born, for birth of Princes hath been celebrated with great Joys, or rather in the day of this Kings Coronation, or investiture in the Kingdom and Royal Dignity. wast created.

14 Thou art the I would rather keep the order of the words in Hebr. which the French also keep, thou art a Cherub, Anointed, a Protector, or one, who covereth for defence. For thy Wisdom, Power, and Excellency like a cherub, or Angel, for the Sacredness of thy Person, and Office, as the Anointed of God, for the exercise of thy Power and Office, as a Shield, as a Protector of the weak; thus thou art, or thinkest thy self to be, and pridest thy self herein. anointed cherub that covereth: and I have set I, whom thou forgettest, I have made thee so, set thee above others, this should have been matter of thanks and humility, not of pride, and Atheism. Thus the sarcasm is continued, and he is upbraided for his insolence. thee so: thou Or thus, in the Holy Mountain a God thou hast been, so 'tis an Ironie. and suits the rest; or else, in pursuance of our version, thou wast advanced to Kingly Dignity, (which David calls a Mountain, Psa. 30.7. Ier. 51.25 Dan. 2.35.) a Sacred Office, and of Divine Institution, and Consecration, and thou hast in pride exalted thy self above me, as well as above men. wast upon the holy mountain of God: thou hast walked up and down In proud, and stately manner. in the midst of the stones Surrounded every way in thy Chambers, and Beds, and Clothes with stones, that sparkle like fire, thy Crown, thy Throne, thy Chariots, thy Umbrellas, or Canopies glistering, and dazling Beholders; as if thus also thou wouldest contend with God, who is clothed with light. of fire.

15 Thou wast perfect I think the Prophet continues his Ironie: The Prince of Tyrus would be a God, yes. Now God is perfect in all his wayes, or works: And thou, O Prince, wert so too; wert thou, and from thy Original? in thy waies But remember what a God is he, that hath a beginning that was created, that at last was found full of Iniquity? And this reproof, and taunt leads us to look with the Prophet from the proud claim of this Prince to his great miscarriages. If any else will think all these things in the 14th and 15th verses to be asserters of God's bounty to this Prince, and of his great magnificence and state in Hyperboles and allusions: Nothing I have said shall contradict them, for they have their Liberty as I have mine, to think what seems most like the truth. from the day thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee.

16 By the multitude By, or in, or according to (as the Gall. version) the multitude, or greatness of thy Trading, in Tyrus were Merchants, that Traded in very great Adventures, with vast Stocks, and in mighty Cargoes. of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned Either as one Trading among them, thou hast violated Justice to promote thine own, and their gain, or hast connived at thy Merchants, when they opprest all they could, or hast contrary to Justice, and Equity supported them in their violence, and judged for them against oppressed Strangers: Thou who wert a King, and wouldest be thought a God, is this like to God, who hates violence, loves Justice, and relieveth the Stranger, and righteth the oppressed?: therefore I will cast thee as profane out of the mountain Either of thy Throne, and Kingly Dignity, vid. ver. 14. let. o, p. or thy fancied and imagined Heaven where thou wouldest be a God, for such Gods of violence, and injustice deserve to be cast out with the aspirng Angels. of God: and I will destroy Utterly destroy. thee, O covering cherub Vid. ver. 14. let. n, o., from the midst of the stones See ver. 14. let. r. of fire.Thy Merchants have by crafts, where that would, and by violence where craft would not, compassed their unjust designs, as noted chap. 27. ver. 36. This injustice and violence grew, as their Trade did, and filled the City with guilt as fast, as that did with wealth. These abominable things hast thou done, and now, as an abominable thing, I will throw thee out.

17 Thine heart was lifted See ver. 2. let. c. d. e. and ver. 5. let. u. up because of thy beauty See ver. 12. let. s., thou hast corrupted thy wisdom Depraved, or lost thy Wisdom. by reason of thy brightness By reflecting and gazing on thy own Glory, State, Wealth, and Magnificence, and hast forgotten thou art a man; thou exaltest thy self above Man, above thy Neighbour Kings.: I will cast thee to the ground, I will lay thee before Kings, that they may behold thee.I will bring down thy pride, dethrone thee, and make thee fit in the dust, fully▪ and darken all thy brightness. Or set thee before men of thy quality, who are, as thou, apt to forget men, themselves, and God as he, who, though he said not I am God, yet Atheist like askt, who is God that I should obey him.
Or that thou mayest be a spectacle, an example, and warning to them, or, that they see thee in chains, or an abused Captive, and despise thee.

18 Thou Thou who shouldest have kept all pure in Religion, as thou art King, pretending to Divinity, hast polluted it. hast defiled thy sanctuaries Still there is, as all along from the 14th verse I think there hath been, much of an Irony deriding this proud Prince, an allusion to his pretended Godship. A God hath his Sanctuaries, and thou thine, but they nasty polluted ones. by the multitude By the greatness, as as well as number. of thine iniquities Impieties, Irreligion, and Atheism of thy Merchants, as well as by their injustice, falsehood, and oppressions, by their perjuries, breaking Covenants confirmed in the Temples at the Altars, or in the name of their Gods, when thy Trade thrived by these, thou, and they have thought there was nothing Sacred, nor any God above thee., by the iniquity
of thy traffick Impieties, Irreligion, and Atheism of thy Merchants, as well as by their injustice, falsehood, and oppressions, by their perjuries, breaking Covenants confirmed in the Temples at the Altars, or in the name of their Gods, when thy Trade thrived by these, thou, and they have thought there was nothing Sacred, nor any God above thee.: therefore will I bring forth a fire Some civil dissension or occasion of thy injustice shall, like a fire, rise. from the midst Among thy injured malecontents. of thee, it shall devour Which, like fire in the house, shall burn all up, and waste all, thou shalt never quench it; thy discontented Subjects applying themselves to Nebuchadnezzar with addresses for his Favour, Power, and Royal Justice to relieve them, and to right his own Subjects opprest by Tyre in their Trade, shall enkindle Nebuchadnezzar's rage, and he shall never be appeased, but in thy ruine. thee, and I will bring thee to ashes Thou shalt be burnt to Ashes, these cast on the Earth to be scattered abroad, and trampled under feet. upon earth in the sight All this done, that all about thee may see, fear; and reverence the Justice, Power, and Holiness of the God of Heaven, who ruleth among men, and knows how to abase proud Atheists. of all them that behold thee.

19 All they that know All, that have heard, seen, or formerly known, thy Riches, Power, Allies, Wisdom, and Vigilance. thee among the people, shall be astonished Be amazed at the certain news of thy great fall from greatest Glory to greatest reproach. at thee: chap. 27.36. thou shalt be Heb. terrors. a terrour To all, that hear the bruit hereof, though thou hast been a terror, so the Hebr. to others by thy puissance, and Arms, thou shalt never be so again for ever, and this word hath been made good; Tyre never rose to that greatness, as to be feared by her Neighbours., and never shalt thou be any more.
20 ¶ Again the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

21 Son of man, set thy face Vid. chap. 21.2. let. i. and chap. 20. ver. 46. let. o.
• sa. 23.4, 12. 〈◊〉 . 25.22. 〈◊〉 27.3. against Zidon Neighbour, and Confederate of Tyrus. , and prophesie Declare her sins, approaching sorrows, and my Judgments against her. against it.

22 And say, Thus saith the Lord God To these Heathen, yet Neighbours of the Jews the Prophet might well suppose the name and greatness of the God of Israel was so known, as to command their attention, when he speaketh.; behold, I am against thee Provoked by thy sins, I am an adversary to thee, and as such, determine to proceed with thee., O Zidon A City in the Northwestfrom Canaan, at the foot of Mount Liban • s, a Kings Seat of old, and from which Tyrus descended, as a swarm cast out of that Hive. Isa. 23.2. for 'twas a great City in Ioshua's time, Iosh. 11.8. and 19.28. and built by Sidon Canaan's Son, Gen. 10.15. and 1 Chron. 1.13. a famous Mart full of Merchants like Tyre, and as full of sin as riches.; and I will be glorified When my Judgments make my Justice, Power, Holiness, Sovereignty, and Truth appear, both you Sidonians, and others about shall confess my Glory, and ascribe Honour to me. I will vindicate my Honour, and Glory, which by thy sins thou hast eclipsed, and I by judgments will illustrate, as Exod. 14.4, 17. in the midst of thee: and they That dwell in thee, and round about thee, all that are concerned for thee. shall know See chap. 6. ver. 10. that I am the LORD, when So late do sinners come to any due sense of God's Power, Justice, and Majesty. I shall have executed judgments The hardned Sinners learn not by any other way, but this, and by this too in the rigours, and repeated executions of it. in her, and shall be sanctified Own'd as Holy, Reverenced as just, obeyed as Sovereign, and submitted to as Wise, and Mighty, and a hater of Violence. in her.

23 For I will send The Pestilence is one of God's Arrows, and he sends it wheresoever it walks, 'tis one of his sore Judgments, and wasteth where it cometh. into her pestilence The most dreadful of Diseases, because most deadly, swift, and comes so immediately from the Wrath of God offended with men, this Pestilence attends o • War, and seldom faileth to make havock in besieged Towns, or Cities., and blood Bloody War by an Enemy, that shall bring the War to the Gates, nay into the Streets of Zidon. into her streets; and the wounded shall be judged Fall, be cast down, punisht in the midst of the City. in the midst of her by the sword By her Enemies Sword prevailing, and conquering. upon her on every side A Description either of the Siege that Sidon should suffer by, or pointing out the multitude of her Enemies on every side agreeing against her.; and they shall know that I am the LORD.

24 ¶ And there shall be no more The time intended here is, when after 70 years Captivity, loathing themselves for their Iniquities, and repenting, they return and settle in their own Land. a Num. 33.5 •
▪ Josh. 23.13. pricking briar By these two Metaphors the Prophet points out the troublesom Neighbours of the Jews. unto the house of Israel, nor any grieving thorn of all that are round about Such as Moab, Ammon, Edom, Tyre, and this Sidon, which on all occasions did grieve, wound, and reproach the Jews, and triumph in the fall of the Jews, and were ever ready, being near. them, that despised them Contemning both in word and carriage, the Jews, their Religion, Manners, Laws, and their God.; and they shall know See ver. 22. let. k. that I am the Lord GOD.

25 Thus saith the Lord GOD; When Seventy years is expired, which is the term of their Captive State▪ I shall have gathered Move the hearts of my people to come together upon Cyrus Proclamation, and from all parts of that vast Kingdom, prepare for a return to the Country most of them never saw, it was God, who moved Cyrus to give them leave; 'twas as much God's work to stir up the people to return. the house The generality of them, those that were Israelites indeed. of Israel from the people Several Nations subjects to the King of Babylon. among whom they are scattered By the Babylonish King at first, and afterward, by incident necessity, or their own choice., and shall be sanctified Have vindicated my Name, which by them was blasphemed. in them in the sight I was dishonoured by the Jews in the sight of the Heathen, and I will be honoured by the Jews in their sight, they shall be witnesses of my vindication. of the heathen, then shall they dwell Settle in peace, and for continuance. in their land In a Land that is theirs, their own, as 'tis often called., that I have given Their Title is of me by deed of Gift, not of late, But to my servant to one that was long since my Servant Jacob To Iacob, Father to these returning Captives. The Heb. repeats the Praeposition, to my Servant, To Iacob, with an Emphasis to mind them of God's faithfulness..

26 And they shall dwell Or, with confidence. safely Which is to be understood comparatively, safer than before, it must be accommodated to the circumstances of Humane condition, in such safety, as excludes continual inward cares, and fears, and perplexities, as 'tis said of Laish, Iudg 18.7. or as in the dayes of Solomon, 1 King. 4.25. or as Iob 11.18, 19. therein, and shall build houses, and Jer. 31.5. plant vineyards; yea, they shall dwell with confidence, when That seems to intimate, that there might be some attempts as by Sanballat, and Tobias, but God blasted these, or it may refer more properly to the destruction of Babylon, and the Nations Confederate with them, who ruined, and despised the Iews. I have executed judgments upon all those that Or, spoil. despised them round about them; and they Returned Captives. shall know that I am the Lord their Shall own, and know by experience, that I am not only the Lord, but their God too. GOD.

div.head: CHAP. XXIX.
div.p: 1 IN the tenth year Of Ieconiah's Captivity., in the tenth month Which answers to part of our December, and part of Ianuary. , in the twelfth day of the month, the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

2 Son of man, set thy face Vide chap. 20. ver. 46. let. o. and chap. 21. ver. 2 let. i against Pharaoh Hophra, as the Scripture stiles him, Ier. 44.30. the Greek Authors call him Aprees, and Vaphres, most like he was Grandson to Necho, who slew Iosiah in Fight, 2 Chron. 35.23, 24. king of Egypt, and prophesie In Prophetick stile, and Authority declare what shall be done to him in his person. against him, and Isa. 19.1. Jer. 25.19. and 46.2. against all The whole multitude of Egyptians, for 'tis the place, for the people dwelling in it. Egypt.

3 Speak, and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD That God that drowned one of thy Predecessors with his Army, Horsemen, and Horses in the Red Sea, at whose Name thou shouldest tremble, who ever fulfilled his word, and is the same, 'tis he foretells thee by my mouth what is to be.; Behold I am against thee See chap. 28. ver. 22. let. f., Pharaoh See ver. 2. let. d. king of Egypt, the great It may refer, either to the Grandeur of this King, as if he had been Pharaoh the great, or to the largeness of this Creature, to which he is by this Hieroglyphick compared. Psal. 74.13, 14. Isa. 27.1. &c. dragon Some would have it the Whale, but that lies not in Rivers, as in his own place, 'tis surely the Crocodile, of which Nilus hath many; and chap.
• 2.2. our Prophet doth, and so Isa. 51.9. compare the Egyptian King to that devouring Serpent, or Dragon. that lieth Not only at rest, but waiting for a prey, which never scapes, if this devourer lay any considerable hold of it. in the midst of his rivers Nilus was the chief River of Egypt, but, either there were some less Rivers, that run into Nilus, or some divisions of it, where it made some Islands, or the seven mouths of it, where it falls into the Sea, which may give the Name of Rivers to it, or those Channels that were cut large, and deep, to convey water into the Country, in all which these Crocodiles bred, and rested, and waited for their prey., which hath said Which hath thought, accounted, and boasted, by which it appears, the Prophet speaks of a Dragon in a figurative sense., my river Kingdom, Power, Riches, and Forces signified here by a River: All the strength and glory of Egypt are mine, saith this proud King. is mine own At my dispose, and will; 'tis probable, that this King of Egypt was an aspiring King, who aimed at absolute power, and thought he had secured it to himself, for the River, the Emblem of the Kingdom is mine, saith he., and I have made it This seems to give some credit to the conjecture, that this King had raised the Prerogative Royal, and done what others before him would, but could not, and therefore assumes it to himself, as his own work, forgetting God who gives Kingdoms, and whose they are. for my self Somewhat like the proud boast, I have built for the Glory of my Name. Dan. 4.30. and like to meet as sad an end..

4 But Isa. 37.29. chap. 38.4. I Thou art secure against all, but God will draw thee out of thy River to thy ruine. will put hooks The Allegorie is continued; Fish are drawn out with hooks and lines, and God hath Hooks for this proud Dragon, first Amasis, and next the Babylonian King: The expedition of Amasis in the head of the Cynen • eans and Graecians, and the event of it is exactly represented in▪ this Hieroglyphick in the Text. Amasis with those Forces mastered Libya, the King thereof applys for help to this Pharaoh, he gathers all the Power of Egypt out of Egypt with him into Cyrene, where he was defeated, lost all, but a few that fled with him, and on this occasion the Egyptians rebelled against him; now this short history opens the parable. The first Hook you see in the chaws of this Dragon, this drew him out of his River, i. e. his Kingdom. into thy chaws, and I will cause the fish These are the people of Egypt, the subjects of this Kingdom. of thy rivers to stick To adhere to their King in this War. unto thy scales, and I will bring thee up out of the midst of thy rivers Both the King, and his Subjects, which made up his Army go out of the Rivers, leave Egypt, and march into Cyrene (which was part of that Kingdom now called Barca) with their King, as if they had been litt • e Fishes on the back of a mighty one. Thus far the Emblem, the rest follows., and all the fish of thy rivers shall stick unto thy scales.

5 And I will leave When thus brought out, as a Fish out of the water, I will leave thee▪ God le • t this King. thee thrown into the wilderness The Deserts of Libya and Cyrene. , thee and all the fish The whole Army of Egyptia • s. of thy rivers: thou shalt fall upon the Heb. face of the field. open fields There was this King and his Army ruin'd.; thou shalt not be brought together, or gathered As usually the slain are to be buried, these were not buried, but le • t in the Wilderness, where they fell to be a prey to wild Beasts, and Birds of prey which haunted the Wilderness, and would soon gather to their prey.; I have given thee for meat to the beasts of the fields, and to the fowls of the heaven.

6 And all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I am the LORD; because they Both King, Princes, Councellors, and people of Egypt. have been a 2 King 18.21. Isa. 36.6. staff of reed Treacherously, as next verse, dealt with the Iews, whom they seduced to trust, and depend on them, and then perfidiously broke promise with them; It was the sin of the Iews to trust Egypt, it was Egypts great sin to falsifie promise with the Iew, and for this God now punisheth Egypt. to the house of Israel.This mighty overthrow shall be known through all Egypt, and as it shall fill them with fears and troubles, so it should be a convincing argument to them, that God had done this, and punisht them, and their proud King, who used to say as Herodote reports, That God could not turn him out of his Kingdom.

7 When they The Iews unable to stand on their own legs, as men ready to fall. took hold of thee by thy hand Catch thine hand to lean on, as when besieged by the Chaldaeans. thou didst break It includes a designed, and voluntary faileur: Egypt would not support., and rent Didst tear, and pierce, and wound Arm and Shoulder, didst them much mischief instead of benefitting them, as thou hadst promised. Ier. 37.7. and 42.17. all their shoulder: and when they leaned The same thing in words little different. upon thee, thou brakest, and madest all their loins These are the strength of a man, thou hast put them to use all their strength to repel the Enemy, thou h • st been chief occasion of their engaging against. to be at a stand.

8 ¶ Therefore, For thy Atheistical Pride, and thy perfidious mischief to the House of Israel, and other thy sins. thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will bring a sword War, and the effects of it. First, a Civil war arose against this King Hophra, who weak, and contemned, and fallen under the jealousies, and disgusts of his Subjects after his overthrow in the De • erts of Libya, and Cyrene was again overthrown by his Rebel Subjects in a bloody Battel at Memphis, was taken in his • light towards Sain his Royal Seat, and sometime after strangled by the enraged rout. The next Sword brought on Hophra's Successor, and on the Land of Egypt was the Sword of Nebuchadnezzar in the same year after the overthrow of Tyrus, the Civil War of Egypt inviting him to take the occasion, and some few requests, 'tis likely from the Rebellious to assist them. upon thee, and cut off man By the Sword in Battle, and Sieges, and by Famine. and beast Eaten up by a numerous Army invading, and prevailing, and which will drive away what they eat not. The same phrase you have chap. 14. ver. 12. let. z. and ver. 17. let. r. out of thee.

9 And the land That part here intended, say some, and in the 10th verse bounded from Syene to the Borders of Aethiopia, nor is this inconsistent with that ver. 2. against all Egypt, for all Egypt suffered much, though all were not equally wasted, and turned into a desolation, as these parts shall be of Egypt shall be desolate A Desolation, i. e. most desolate, and wastness by the Sword of the Enemie, and by drought, as the word imports both, and this latter part of the Judgment was executed by the folly of the 12 Egyptian • oitelets, who made a mighty Lake Maeris, to fill which they much drained and weakned Nilus that it could not as before it did, water, and fertilize the Land sutable to Isa 19.5.
〈1 paragraph〉
and waste, and they shall know that I am the LORD; because See ver. 3. let. n. o. p. q. r. he hath said, The river is mine, and I have made it.

10 Behold therefore, I am against Chap. 28. verse 22. let. f. thee, and against thy rivers Verse 4. let. y. , and I will make the land of Egypt Heb.
〈◊〉 of 〈◊〉 . utterly waste Verse 9. let. t. , and desolate, chap. 3. •
from the tower Thus as a common name, we, and the French, and others read it, but some account it a proper name of a Town or City, called Magdalum, for ought I know, the old Migdol. Exod. 14.2. and Num. 33.7, 8. 'twas on the Red Sea side, North-East of Egypt, from this part unto Syene. of Heb. 〈◊〉
Syene A City on the East of Nilus over against Arabia, saith one, a City that is just below the great chataract or fall of Nilus toward Aethiopia, and such a boundary between Aethiopia, and Egypt, as admits dispute, to which it belongs. even unto the border of Aethiopia Now, to dispute nothing of this Geography, it seems likely to me, that what we render Aethiopia is not so well, and plainly rendred, for Syene being so near to Aethiopia, we must look some place of Egypt at some greater distance from Syene, than this Aethiopia is, if then 'twere translated the border of Cush, to whom Moses assigns Arabia, Gen. 10.7. Let us suppose then Magdalum instead of the Tower, as one term; Syene on the edge of Aethiopia, as another, and the opposite point on the Red Sea towards Arabia, and then almost all Egypt is comprised herein from North-east to South-east down the Red Sea, thence to the Westward, as far as Aethiopia, and thence up the Nile, as high Northward as Magdalum. .

11 chap. ••
No Not strictly to be taken, but in an accommodated sense, or comparatively to what once was, or so little Traffick and passing to, and fro, that no footsteps, or tracts of men found. It's a Scripture Hyperbole, as Luk. 19.44. Isa. 14.33. and Ezek. 26.14. and 21. foot of man shall pass through it, nor foot of beast Of profitable, useful, and tractable, as Sheep, Oxen, and Horses, but wild beasts, too many are in the desolate places of that part of the World. shall pass through it, neither shall it be inhabited Accounting these years from the first wastings of Egypt by their civil Dissensions and Wars some 9 or 10 years before Neb • chadnezzar subdued, and wasted it which he did in the 35th, 36th, and 37th years of his Reign, or thereabout. So that these Forty years will fall in about the 30th year of Ieconiah's Captivity, and end with the 70th year of the Captivity, which was the first of Cyrus. forty years.

12 chap. 30.7. And I will make the land of Egypt desolate in the midst of the countreys that are desolate, and her cities among the cities that are laid waste shall be desolate forty years, and I will scatter the Egyptians among the Nations Some into Captivity, others by a timely retirement disperst themselves, and got among their Neighbours, who escapt, and where they kept, till the forty years expired., and will disperse them through the countreys.This verse is a farther repeated confirmation of what was said before, and needs no new explication, every thing in it being already spoken to in the former verses.

13 ¶ Yet thus saith the Lord GOD; At the Isa. 19.23. Jer. 46.26. end of forty See ver. 11. let. f. years will I By some eminent acts of Providence toward them, perhaps inclining the generous mind of Cyrus to favour them, and proclaim liberty to them, and under the Government of old Amasis, that Reigned 55 years saith Diodorus, some 10 or 12 of which might be under Cyrus, who had a kindness for the old man, and he, to repair the wastes; obtain'd and publisht great priviledges for the new replanters. gather the Egyptians from the people Babylon, Aethiopia, Libya, and other Countreys, that can be but conjectured to have been receptacles for them. whither they were scattered.

14 And I will bring again the captivity Which Nebuchadnezzar led away into Babylon, of Egypt, and will cause them to return into the land of Pathros One Province, or Country of Egypt, it was a Southern part of Egypt, in which was the famous City Thebae, or Thebais known for its hundred Gates., into the land of their Or, birth. habitation The Antient Habitation of the Fathers of the most of those that did return, forty years having eaten up almost all that had lived there before., and they shall be there a Heb. low. base A low, tributary, dependent Kingdom subject to the Persian Kingdom as Amasis was to Cyrus, and though it did at length grow great, yet was it alwaies dependent on Greeks or Romans. kingdom.

15 It shall be the basest The most abject, debased, and most underling, 'tis likely the Kings, to whom Egypt was Tributary, kept them lowest, as knowing how dangerous that Kingdom might be, as it recovered its antient greatness, and the word seems to intimate this, for 'tis more than the Kingdoms, it shall be depressed. of the kingdoms; neither shall it exalt it self Its Masters would so watch and check it. any more above the nations: for I will diminish Beside the hard and cruel usages of the Persian Kings, which might be unjust enough, God's most just Judgment should follow them to lessen their Numbers, Power, Wealth, and Honour. them, that they shall no more rule Though once they had subdued, and ruled, yet should they not any more, in the times of the Ptolomey's though 'twas considerable, yet then 'twas not a Kingdom, tha • ruled the Nations about her, though she made war upon them. over the nations.

16 And it shall be no more the confidence On every occasion the Iews were wont, against express prohibition, to renew friendship with Egypt, and make Leagues for defence by them, and her • they sinfully rested, as Isa. 30.2. and 31.1. and 36.6, 9. vid. v. 7. of the house of Israel, which Which sinful reliance on the arm of flesh provok't God to call to mind other their iniquities, which accompa • ied this, viz. their Idolatry, and going a Whoring with these their Confederates. bringeth their iniquity to remembrance God never forgets, but when he visits, punisheth, and judgeth a Nation for their sin, then their sin is come up into remembrance., when they shall look Or in their, i. e. the house of Israel's looking after, i. e. with desire that the Egyptians would, with hope they will, and with confidence, that they c • n relieve, rescue; and save them; when they forgot God, and respected Egypt. after them: but they The House of Israel shall know, that I am the Lord, and whoso know him, will put their trust in him. Psal. 9.10. shall know that I am the Lord GOD.

17 ¶ And it came to pass in the seven and twentieth Of Ieconiah's Captivity, the year after the Conquest of Tyrus, and the 35th of Nebuchadnezzar. year, in the first moneth Part of our March, and April. , in the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

18 Son of man, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon caused The Army, the inferiour Officers, and principal Commanders 'tis like were weary of the siege, and might advise the raising it, but the Authority, Presence, and immoveable Resolution of the King kept them on still, and made them hold 〈◊〉
▪ his army to serve a great 'Twas service to the justice of God in punishing the Tyrians by the Ambition of Nebuchadnezzar, who would not endure any thing to stand against him. 'Twas great Service both for hardness of work, heaviness of burthens, and unreasonable length of the siege, thirteen years together. service against Tyrus: every head was made bald Either age, or sicknesses, (which often make men bald) or continued wearing of the Helmets, spoiled the best heads of hair amongst them, or perhaps it noteth the weeping bargain they had, though they mastered Tyre, where they got no booty, and both Nebuchadnezzar and his Army might shave their heads in token of mourning for their loss, rather than crown their heads with Garlands of joy for gaining of the City., and every shoulder was peeled Either clothes wore out, they had scarce any to their backs in so long a siege, or galled and blistered with carrying Burthens, Stones, Timber, Iron and Earth for Fortifications, and to make a passage from the Continent to Tyre, which sores, when healed, left Scabs, or dead skin that peeled off.: yet had he no wages For though Tyrus was very rich, when first besieged, no doubt very much wealth was carryed away by shipping at beginning, and during the siege, which none could prevent, very much spent and wasted in the Siege, and what was left preserved by Articles of surrender; for most conclude that it was delivered on composition, and the Conqueror had only victory for his pains, and charge. for his army for Tyrus, for the service that he had served against it:

19 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will give Yet 'tis certain that the Discontents of Egypt gave occasion, and the revolts of some of the Subjects from Hophra, or Apries, and their inviting Nebuchadnezzar gave him Egypt, but these were the irregularities of men, which God did wisely, and justly manage to effect what he design'd, and God gave, and men gave too; as the Ten Tribes gave, so God gave the Kingdom to Ieroboam, so the first cause, and second causes produce the same effect. the land of Egypt to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall take her multitude Common people, who shall be made Captives by the power of the Conqueror, and Servants, or Slaves next by the will of those that buy them of the Souldier., and Heb. spoil her spoil, and prey her prey. take her Much of the Egyptian Riches were the spoil of other Nations, or the spoiles of one another in the late civil Wars between Pharaoh, Hophra, and Amasis, and now their dishonest gains shall be a prey to Babylonians. spoil, and take her prey That, which was once anothers possession, whilest right prevailed, but became a prey when Egypts power mastered the possessors.; and it shall be the wages His Army could not have plunder of Tyre, because it was surrendred on terms, but now they shall, and this shall be their prey. for his army.

20 I have given 'Tis as sure as in his possession; though he must fight for it, and it will cost blood, yet he shall surely have success. him the land of Egypt Or, for his hire.
for his labour wherewith he served against it Tyre. , because they The proud, revengeful, covetous, and cruel Babylonians. wrought for me They designed themselves, and did work for themselves, but God had farther, higher, and more excellent ends, his work was doing by them, who thought nothing less., saith the Lord GOD.

21 ¶ In that day About that time, when Egypt was spoiled, Nebuchadnezzar returned to Babylon, his Wars first, and soon after his life ended, about four or five years after his return out of Egypt into Babylon; for about the 37th, or 38th of his Reign, he finisht his conquest of Egypt, and in the 43 year he dyed at Babylon. will I cause the horn Iehoiakim by Evil Merodack was advanced Ier. 52.31, 32, 33▪ beside dignities given to Daniel, the three Children, and many others, under whose Authority, and favour the Affairs of the Iews began, as a root that had life in it, to spring and flourish, and whatever was the more immediate visible cause, that prevailed with Evil Merodach we are sure the principal cause was this, God's mercy, and veracity, who had promised he would do it, and foretold the time when he would begin to do it. of the house of Israel to bud forth, and I will give thee the opening of the mouth Thou shalt with greater Authority be heard speaking, when the sorrows thou foretoldest, and the joyes thou promisedst both come to pass; and both Iews, and Babylonians shall see, and own it, or thou shalt have liberty, and freedom as well, as will and cause to speak, to open thy mouth in comforting the good among them, and to give praise to God, who revived their hopes, and made them know him, as the Lord their God. in the midst of them: and they shall know that I am the LORD.

div.head: CHAP. XXX.
div.p: 1 THE word of the LORD came again unto me, saying,

2 Son of man, prophesie and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Howl ye Inhabitants of Egypt, and who so are near enough in Friendship and Alliances to fall under the like calamities., wo Ah the day! Oh sad and miserable times. worth the day.

3 For the day The time of such distresses, as never the like known by you. is near It will begin in your overthrow in the Cyreniac, and Libyc deserts in very little time, next 'twill continue in your Civil war, and finally end in the Babylonish Conquest some two years, and you shall be miserably routed in the deserts of Libya, immediately after the Civil War for eleven years together shall waste you, and then Nebuchadnezzar's Forces will be upon you, so that, whereas there may be about 16 or 18 years between the Prophesie, and its fulfilling, here is 13 or 14 of them taken up with sorrows, and afflictions, fore-runners of the last., even the day of the LORD Of the Lords sore displeasure against Egypt, and its Allies. is near Within two years, as is said., a cloudy A dark day, so times of trouble are called, whereas prosperity is a day of light. Troubles like storms, violent storms are black. day; it shall be the time of the heathen Of the Egyptians to be wasted, and of the Babylonians to waste them, the day of the pride, cruelty, and revenges to the one, the day of falling, spoil, and destruction to the other..

4 And the sword See chap. 29. ver. 8. let. p. shall come upon Egypt, and great Or, fear. pain shall be in Aethiopia Next Neighbour, and Allie to Egypt, they shall tremble at so great danger, so near, and they uncertain whether 'twill come on them, but very certain to be ruin'd, if it does come, and as certain, that they have cause to suspect it will come on them., when the slain shall fall in Egypt, and they shall take away her multitude, and her foundations shall be broken down.When the Egyptians, under the eye of the Aethiopians shall fall in Battle, and at the taking of their Towns. In miserable Captivity carry them to Babylon, by whole droves, Their Government, Laws, Councellors, strong holds, which are to a Nation, as Foundations to a house, are destroyed.

5 Aethiopia Heb. Cusch, which are commonly thought to be the Aethiopians in Africa, but some more inquisitive Geographers have found them originally, and chiefly in Arabia, which was either Subject, or Allie to Egypt in its prosperity; and these were as ver. 4. in a panick fear, least the Babylonian should pass the Sea, and take them in his way home., and Heb. Phut. Libya Heb. Phut hence the Puteans or Phutaans, who afterwards were better known by Libyans, a part of whose Country was near to Egypt. , and Lydia Lydians, not the Asiatick, but the Africans placed between some part of Cyrene, and Egypt. , and all the mingled The hired Souldiers from all parts, a confused mixture of Nations, such as the Libyans had got together; or all Arabia, so the word 2 Chr. 9.14. Isai. 13.20. or all that ravenous sort of people, that like Crows fly to slaughters, so Souldiers of Fortune follow the Wars, and the word Heb. is Crow, Lev. 11.15. Deut. 14.14. Ps. 147.9. as well as mixt. people, and Chub Aethiopians beyond Egypt south, the Inhabitants of the inmost Libya ▪ which reached to the Nigritae Negro's; perhaps they may be the Nubians at this day, a Letter easily changed., and the Heb. children. men of the land that is in league The Sons of the Land of the Covenant; some refer to the Iews Children of the Covenant, but this is forced, 'tis all the people of Egypts League; all the Allies of the Egyptian Kingdom., shall fall with them With the Egyptians. by the sword In War by the Sword of Babylon. .

6 Thus saith the LORD; They also that uphold Either the Princes, Councellors, and Martial men in Egypt, or those abroad, that favour her▪ and help her. Egypt shall fall, and the pride The Glory of all her strength, of which she was proud. of her power shall come down Be trodden under foot.: from the tower From Magdalum in the North-East part of Egypt toward the Red Sea, to Syene in the most South-west part of Egypt. See chap. 29. ver. 10. let. a. b. c. of Syene shall they fall in it by the sword, saith the Lord GOD.

7 chap. 2 •
▪ And they All those before mentioned. shall be desolate As much wasted, as any of them, that are most wasted, in the midst of the countreys that are desolate, and her Cities Of Egypt equally wasted with other Cities, that have been sack't, as Ierusalem, Tyre, Sidon, Rabbath. &c. shall be in the midst of the cities that are wasted.

8 And they All that Act, and all that suffer in this Tragedy, shall by the evidence of the things be enforced to own God's hand, and ascribe Justice, and Truth, and Glory to him. shall know that I am the LORD, when I have set a fire That War, which like increasing fire, consumeth all. in Egypt, and when all her helpers shall be Heb. 〈…〉
destroyed The destruction of so many, and powerful aides shall prove, that 'twas God's hand did it..

9 In that day The day of Gods severe, but just Judgments, and Egypts fatal Desolation. shall messengers Such, as having seen, and scaped the Sword, shall tell the dismal news. go forth from me By my permission, and providence they shall go, as if sent by me. in ships Ships, that either carried them over into Pentapolis crossing the River Nilus, or rather going down the River into the Mediterranean, and so to any part of those North parts of Africa, and others by Ship through the Red Sea to Arabia Faelix, which is that Aethiopia, which is here meant, though 'tis possible, in those dayes the African Aethiopia might, as once it did, extend quite to the mouth of the Red Sea, on whose shore their Ancestors must needs first land out of Arabia, whence the Habessines, who are our present Aethiopians, do own their descent. So Messengers by Ships might carry the news to both the Aethiopian, Asian, and African, by the Red Sea. to make the careless Aethiopians In much security they had hitherto lived, the most potent, and formidable Neighbour having been their Antient Allie, till the news of so mighty an Enemy at their very Doors. afraid, and great pain Apprehensions of Danger, that puzzles their Wisdom, weakens their Courage, makes them in perplexity, both sick, and astonished. shall come upon them, as in the day Either like that, which, when their Host was drowned in the Red Sea, seiz'd all Egypt, or rather like this latter fear, which arose from the Mighty havock made by the Chaldaean. of Egypt: for lo it A storm like that certainly cometh against you. cometh.

10 Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also make the multitude The numerous Families, and Tribes. of Egypt to cease To dwindle, and decrease. by the hand By the Army, Power, and Conduct of Nebuchadnezzar. of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.

11 He Nebuchadnezzar. and his His own Subjects, not hired Souldiers. people with him, chap. 28.5. the terrible This is the description of them. Hab. 1.7. a fierce, and cruel people, as Psal. 147.8, 9. of the nations shall be brought By the hand of God using means for that end, as before noted, chap. 29. ver. 4. to destroy the land: and they shall draw their swords Readily, and with Resolution not to sheath them, till Egypt be filled with slain. against Egypt, and fill the land with the slain.

12 And Isa. 19.9▪ I will make the rivers Heb. 〈◊〉 . dry Either by some extraordinary drought, or rather, by means of that mighty Lake, that, which drew so much water from Nilus, that all their Canals were ever after shallow, and the Lake, as the Oracle foretold, helpt their Enemy, and hurt their Friends: or the Chaldaeans might divert them, and so their Fortified Towns would want one great defence., and sell God gave it, here he sells; the one is proper, the other a borrowed expression, indeed God seems to pay wages with it. chap. 29. ver. 19, 20. but hereby is intimated, that as Sellers deliver into the hand of the Buyer, so God would deliver Egypt into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar as surely, as if he had bought it, and we may conclude, the Chaldaean as a Buyer, will make the most of all he buyes. the land into the hand of the wicked Not of just, and compassionate, but of injurious, and merciless men.; and I will make the land waste, and Heb. the f ••
ness thereof. all that is therein, by the hand of strangers Who leave nothing, they can carry away, eat up, or spoil.: I the LORD have spoken it.'Tis the Decree, and Edict of Heaven, which can't be broken.

13 Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also Jer. 43.12. 〈◊〉 46.25. • ech. 13.2. destroy God did it by the Babylonians; those proud, and impious Nations did triumph over the Gods of the conquered, and out of contempt of them, burnt them, or broke them, as is well known, so Sennacherib threatned, 2 Chr. 32.19. Isaiah. 37.19, 24. against the true God, as he did to Idol Gods. the Idols Dunghil Gods, as the words, fitter to be trod under foot, then to be deck't, and respected., and I will cause their images These nothings, as the word imports, whoever destroyed the Image, destroyed the God, for 'twas nothing but an Image. to cease out of Noph Memphis now grand Cair, the chief City of the Country, the seat of their Kings first, of their Priests by consequence, and of all their several Gods too; But the Chaldeans destroyed the nest, and birds too.; and there shall be no more a prince Either an Egyptian born, or, independent, or over all Egypt, or that shall have the Power, Wealth, or Honour like a former brave Egyptian King. of the land of Egypt: and I will put a fear Of consternation, and cowardise that should disable them for counsel, and action in their most urgent Affairs. in the land of Egypt.

14 And I will make Pathros See cap. 29. ver. 14. let. m. desolate, and will set fire It may be literally understood that Zoan, Tanis, for that is its name, should be burnt down to Ashes; or Metaphorically of War, and civil Dissensions. in Or, Tanis. Zoan, and will execute judgments in No A very great and populous City, scituate on one of the mouths of Nilus, and on the Sea, Nahum. 3.8. Now Alexandria stands, where that did, but 'twas greater in sin than in people, and it was visited with very great, and dreadful judgments. Nahum. 3.8, 9, 10, 11. which see..

15 And I will pour See chap. 21. ver. 31. let. d. my fury upon Or, Pelusium. Sin Either Sain, or more likely Pelusium, which was a Frontier, and secured the entrance of Egypt fromward the Desert of Sin, was the key of Egypt, and therefore alwaies well fortified, and strongly garrisoned, it was called Damiata. , the strength One of the principal munitions of Egypt; for 'twas a good, and large Haven, and was strengthned with all needful Fortifications. of Egypt, and
〈◊〉
when I have 〈◊〉 off. I will cut off the Or the Riches, and Tumultuous noise, which the multitudes thereof made. multitude of No If we read, as the Margin, 'tis plain, God does threaten Pel • sium after No is cut off; if we retain our own Translation, we must think of another City of that name, which God threatens with Sin: Now this may be Thebae Egyptiacae, or this City may be Hamon No called Diospolis, the City of Iupiter, possibly it may be the same mentioned already, and the threat repeated to confirm it.,

16 And I will set fire See ver. 14. let. o. and chap. 20. ver. 47. l. u. x. and v. 8. let. y. in Egypt: Sin Ver. 15. let. r. shall have great pain See ver. 9. let. o., and No See ver. 14. let. p. and ver. 15. let. x. shall be rent asunder Her Walls, and Towers, and Fortresses battered, torn, and broken through by the continued violence of Engines, and by the assaults of the Souldiers., and Noph See ver. 13. let. k. shall have distresses Being the chief City where King and Councels sate, whence Orders should be given, whither all intelligences were brought, all should be so bad abroad, that nothing, but fears, and distresses fill their Ears, Mouths, and Hearts, beside the wants, that would increase dayly on them. daily.

17 The young men 'Tis probable these might be a select Army of valiant youths in one body, collected out of these two Cities, that resolved to break the Chaldaean Army, or fall in the Enterprise, or else that they did to the utmost, defend the Walls, and were put to the Sword when the City was taken by assault. of Or, Heliopolis. Aven Bethshemesh, and Heliopolis an Idolatrous City, that Worshipt the Sun, and in which was a stately Temple built to the Sun; Its greatness was 150 Furlongs, 6 miles, and 3 quarters in compass, a very vain and sinful City, as its name Aven intimates. and of Or, Bubastum. Pibeseth Bubastus, and sometime called Haephestus, no inconsiderable place, and, I believe not far from Aven, it should seem to be some convenient pass, as I conjecture. shall fall by the sword: and these cities The Citizens, Cities put for Citizens. shall go into captivity Some of the first, it may be the very first, which put Memphis, at report of it into a sick fit, with great pain; this being the first fruits of the sad coming harvest..

18 At Tehaphnehes A great, and goodly City of Egypt, Tachapanes, Tachpanes, Tahapanes, Tahpanes, Chanes, and Hanes, Isai. 30.4. are Name • given it, and this from a Queen of Egypt of that name in Solomon's time, 1 King. 11.19, 20. it stood not far from Sin or Pelusium, and by the Greeks a little softening the Name, call'd Daphne Pelusiaca. 'twas a Royal City, in it Pharaoh had a house, to it many Iews fled, when forbidden of the Lord by the Prophet Ieremy, chap. 44. 'twas one of the first Cities you come to out of the Desert of Sin, and was one of the keys of Egypt. also the day shall be Or, darkness • the day. Or, restrained. darkned A night shall come upon it, and such a night of sorrow, as shall grow darker, and darker, till the day, i. e. their day be darkness, or else word for word, Darkness shall be the day, and may bear this sense, shall be more welcome, more useful, more desired, then the day, whose light would discover their flight, which the night concealed., when I shall break As into shivers. there the yokes The Scepters; for there was one of Pharaoh's houses, and probably, some Scepter, and other Regal Ornaments; or the Bars, which kept Enemies out, and secured the Citizens, and Country, such was this Frontier Town, or, when by giving this strong place into Nebuchadnezzars hand, I shall break the Kingdom of Egypt, that it no more oppress with yokes, i. e. burthens▪ of Egypt: and the pomp The Beauty, and Goodliness, with which the strength of this City was set out in her Buildings, Towers, Forts. of her strength shall cease in her Shall be buried in her own ruines.: as for her, a cloud Sorrow by the success of the Chaldaeans against her, compared often to a cloud. shall cover her, and her daughters Either Metaphorically, i. e. the Towns, and Villages about her, or literally, her Children, her Daughters only mentioned, because her Sons were destroyed, and slain. shall go into captivity.
19 Thus will I execute judgments in Egypt: and they shall know that I am the LORD.

20 And it came to pass in the eleventh year Of Ieconiah's Captivity three Moneths, and two Days before Ier • salem was taken, Ier. 52.4., in the first moneth The fourth day of our April. , in the seventh day of the moneth, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

21 Son of man, I have broken I have often told thee, I would break, now I tell thee I have broken, partly by the victory of the Chaldaean over Pharaoh Necho, partly by the victory the Cyrenaeans got over Pharaoh Hophra, to raise the siege, from which attempt he fell with shame and loss, but more by Civil Wars. the arm of Pharaoh Hophra or Apries. king of Egypt, and lo, Jer. 46.1 • . it shall not be bound up to be healed And this wound is incurable, it shall never be bound up to be healed, his Arm shall never be strong and fit to encounter a potent Enemy, as once it was. to put a roller to bind it, to make it strong to hold the sword.

22 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and will break his arms In the former verse God had broken the arm, in this he will break the Arms of Pharaoh, he will shew, he is still against Pharaoh, and will break him more, and more., the strong That part of his Kingdom which remains intire., and that which was broken That, which was shattered before, That part of his Kingdom in Syria, taken from him from Euphrates, to the River of Egypt, that once was a strong arm, but now broken, and useless to him: And Egypt, whatever strength it now hath, shall be as weak, and useless too, thus all his power, and strength shall be destroyed.: and I will cause the sword to fall out of his hand.
23 And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countreys. Vid. chap. 29. ver. 12. let. g. and chap. 20. ver. 23. let. o. where the same expressions are.

24 And I will strengthen Give the first strength, and continue it with new supplys, so that with strength from God, he shall proceed. the arms of the king of Babylon, and put my sword His strength shall have a weapon suited, and proportion'd to it, and what will be hard, where God's Sword and his strength are engaged to effect it? in his hand: but I will break Pharaohs arms, and he Hophra. shall groan Not only, as the stoutest must, when nature breaks, but cry out, and sigh, or howl not becoming a brave man. before him King of Babylon. with the groanings of a deadly wounded Who hath given him his deadly wound, under which he roars, while he hath any strength, and groans, when his voice sails him. It speaks sore griefs, and deep sense of them; as Exod. 2.24. Iudg. 2.18. Iob 24.12. man.

25 But I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and the arms of Pharaoh shall fall
down, and they shall know, that I am the LORD, when I shall put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall stretch it out upon the land of Egypt.These two forgoing verses are a repetition of God's threats against Pharaoh, and of his promises to assist Nebuchadnezzar in the War, and every thing plain in them.
26 And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them among the countreys; and they shall know that I am the LORD. Vide ver. 23.

div.head: CHAP. XXXI.
div.p: 1 AND it came to pass in the eleventh As chap. 30. ver. 20. let. t. year, in the third moneth Our Iune 26th day old stile, the 16th day new stile; Calvisi • s. Vsserius. just one moneth, and eight dayes be • fore the taking of the City on the 27th of Iuly, vet. stil. but 17th of Iuly, new stile. , in the first day of the moneth Tam • z. , that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

2 Son of man, speak unto Pharaoh Apries, or Hophra. king of Egypt, and to his multitude His numerous Subjects, with the power, and Riches they Glory in.; ver. 18. whom art thou like in thy greatness Bethink thy self, what King of all before thee, art thou equal with, or else greater? On what surer, and more immoveable Foundation doth thy greatness stand? That thou dreamest of a perpetual quiet, and flourishing state in the midst of all thy sins, and wickednesses??

3 Behold the Assyrian Kingdom, and its Kings were the greatest, the world ere knew before thee, they had longest time of growth through 1340, or 1360 years from Belus, who was Nimrod, or Belus Assyrius, to Sardanapalus, from 1719, or 1717, or 1718 to 3059. of the World. And they had as fair advantages, as reaching a foresight, and as unwearied diligence to advance the Kingdom; yet I brought it down. was a cedar Like a Cedar; Kings and Kingdoms oft compared to Trees, both in profane, and sacred Emblems, or like the most Goodly Cedar for Strength and Beauty. in Lebanon A great Mountainous tract from East to West, 125 mile in length, encloseth Canaan on the North. Heb. fair of branches. with fair branches Which are the Beauty, Greatness, Strength of the Tree, so had this mighty Kingdom fair Provinces, as Branches springing from it., and with a shadowing What we render shadowing in the Hebr. may signifie, either silent, and quiet, or framing, and modelling, intimating, that this Kingdom, like a shady Tree, gave shelter to the weak, as if fram'd artificially to this, and 'twas a silent, quiet repose its Subjects had; as weak Creatures find shelter in a mighty wood, so these. shroud, and of an high stature This Kingdom grew to great height, while its branches were so beneficial.; and his top was among the thick Or Clouds, for so the word will without violence bear; Cloud being called so from their thickness; however, the Head among the thick boughs speaks the magnificence, and greatness of this King compassed about with Tributary Kings, and Princes, and Mighty men. boughs.

4 The waters As Cedars grow great by the water courses, so this Kingdom by multitudes of people, convenience of Trade, by the plenty of the Country, if no Trade, for 'twas first planted in the fruitful fields among the sweet Rivers, Euphrates, Tigris, Lycus, Diava, and others. Or, nourished. made him great, the deep The Sea sent out her Waters, which gave being to the Rivers, that water'd him, and improved him; whereas Egypt, thy Rivers arise out of a Lake, which, though great, not to be compared with the deep. Or, brought him • p. set him up on high with her rivers running round about his plants The Provinces of this mighty Kingdom, that are like plants about a great Tree., and sent out her Or, conduits. little rivers Beneficence, Justice, Protection, encouragements, that Subjects need, and good Princes disperse among them, so the deep filled this King, and he sent out his streams. unto all the trees To all his Subjects in his Kingdom. of the field.

5 Therefore his height was exalted His Power, Glory, and his Pride too, run up on high, a just administration of Laws for benefit of the publick, and a kind usage of the Subject, while 'twas here, made the King great, and his Kingdom famous. above all the trees of Above all his Neighbour Kings, among whom oppressed weaklings still came to this Kingdom, while just, for shelter. the field, and his boughs were multiplyed Many became his Subjects by voluntary choice, and his Native Subjects increast in numbers, and Wealth., and his branches became long The Provinces reacht far and wide by the conquest of his armes, or attractives of his kindness brought to unite with him. because of the multitude of waters The many streams of Royal Justice▪ and Beneficence sent forth from the Throne of this Kingdom, so his Throne was advanced and established. Or,
〈◊〉 sent them 〈…〉
when he shot forth.

6 Dan. 4. ••
All the Not every individual, but all sorts, and kinds of Men and People, Nobles, Merchants, Husbandmen likened to Fowles. fowls of heaven made their nests Did settle their Habitations, and Families, expecting what they found, safety, and rest, and hoping, what did ensue, an increase of their Children and Posterity as Birds do in a quiet, and safe nest. in his boughs In his Kingdom, in the Cities, or Towns of it., and under his branches The very same thing exprest by a new Hieroglyphick: Beasts here are people, the Field is the Countreys round about, their bringing forth their young includes their making their Dens, that is mens building, begetting children, and breeding them under his branches, under his Government, and Protection. did all the beasts of the field bring forth their young, and under his shadow This gives some light to the riddle. No Nation, that was great at that time in the World, but, either own'd the Dominion, or sought the Alliance, and Friendship of this King and Kingdom. dwelt all great nations.

7 Thus was he fair Beautiful, lovely, and desirable. in his greatness Not exerted in Tyranny, and oppression, but exercised in the Royal Art of imitating the greatest, and best Being, who is King over all, for he doth good to all., in the length of his branches How far soever remote, yet the Justice, and Goodness of the Government appeared, the Beauty of those Provinces as well as of the whole Kingdom.: for his root Whence he sprang, which supported, and supplyed the Kingdom, was Right, the Laws, Punishments, rewards, and encouragements, neither founded in cruelty, nor maintained by violence. was by great Not by blood, which is no proper kindly nourishment for such Cedars, but by Waters, which are kindly, and proper, and these great enough for his own growth, and to nourish others too. waters.

8 The Cedars Kings, the greatest, and most magnificent. in the Gen. 2. ••
garden of God Either in the most fruitful Gardens, or in Iudah and Israel ▪ not David, not Solomon, Iehoshaphat, or Hezekiah could top, and shade him. could not hide h him: the fir-trees A meaner sort of Trees, emblem of lesser Kings, and Kingdoms, these were but like his boughs, though they grow to great height, and bulk. were not like his boughs, and the chesnut The same in another allusion, Kings▪ like Chesnut trees, great, when by themselves, yet compared with this Assyrian, were but as branches of his boughs, all which in Isaiah's words, cap. 10.7, 8. there was some truth, though more pride in this Speech of the Assyrian, which the Prophet reports. trees were not like his branches: nor any All summed up, none like him in all the Kingdoms of the World. tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty.

9 I have made him fair All this greatness, Wealth, and Glory I have given him. by the multitude The numbers of his Provinces, and multitude of his Subjects, high, and low, great, and small. of his branches: so that all the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God envied Either did when they saw his greatness, or would have envied, if they had seen it, or, if there may be a seeming justifiableness in wondring at anothers Glory, and wishing it our own, here it might be found. him.

10 Therefore u thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou hast lifted x up thy self in height,
and he hath shot up his top among the thick boughs, and his heart is lifted up in his height;Now you shall hear the sin, and the fall of this great Kingdom of Assyria.
His mind could not longer bear so great prosperity, he lifts up himself, and in his pride forgets God, who lifted him up, and will cast him down, you have a Specimen of it in that of Isa. 10.7, 8, 9. with the rest to the 20th. verse, and Isa. 36.9.15, 18. this, as other best framed polities degenerated into pride, and violence against Neighbours, Subjects, Friends as well as against Enemies, though too much 'twas, to despise man, yet 'twas intolerably more insolent, to reproach God. It is but time to lop, nay cut down this Cedar, as Isa. 10.33. with Isa. 37.36, 38.

11 I have therefo • e delivered No Prophetick stile, as some think, I have, because I will, for most certainly God would deliver. him Proud King of Assyria, who inherited all the vices of his Progenitors more, than their Kingdoms, infamous Sardanapalus. into the hand of the mighty one Some say Cyrus, rather Arbaces, who first strook at the root of this Cedar, and cut him down, and well might this man, though no King when he attempted this, be stiled the mighty one of the Heathen, who could bring together four hundred thousand of Medes, Pe • sians, Babylonians, and Arabians a power sufficient to besiege the Assyrian King two years in his own City, and Palace. of the heathen: Heb. in doing • hall do unto 〈◊〉 . he shall surely So he did, for he held him besieged without hope of relief, till at two years end, this vicious King burnt himself with his Palace. deal with him; I have driven With disgrace, for his lewd shameless courses, as a Wife is cast out by divorce for Adultery, Lev. 21.7. him out for his wickedness So Sardanapal • s was cast out for his effeminacy, and lewdness; for 'tis reported, this gave Arbaces first encouragement to lay a des • gn against him, who was driven out, as the Prophet words it, by the breach of two mile and half wideness, made by the mighty floods from continual Rains, which the walls of Nineve could not withstand, so God rather then man did drive this beast out..

12 And strangers Forreigners, who regard neither justice, nor mercy, such were those, which made up this Army of Arbaces the Mede. , chap. 28.7. the terrible So these were for their strength, and valour much, but for their numbers, and barbarity, more to be dreaded. of the nations, have cut him off Not shall, for 'twas down before Ezekiels time, about the time Ezekiah was born, and about 240 years before the destruction of Ierusalem, and the Babylonish Captivity., and have left him Revolted or forsaken Sardanapalus.
upon the mountains As a Tree, that growing on the Mountains, which hang over the Valleys, when it falls, breaks, and its branches are scattered in the lower ground, on the banks of Rivers, that run in the bottom, so is this mighty Cedar, this King, and Kingdom fallen from highest power, and honour into deepest contempt and impotence, not able to repell his Adversaries, or escape out of their hands. and in all the vallies his branches are fallen, and his boughs are broken by all the rivers of the land: and all the people of the earth are gone down from his shadow, and have left him.All, that were Tributary to him, have withdrawn their Tribute, and rejected his Dominion, and such as were his Allies, and depended on his Patronage, have quit their Leagues, and dependences, and left his shadow.

13 Upon his ruin His broken state. shall all the fowls Which built, and bred there, shall now despise the Tree, and triumph over it. of the heaven remain, and all the beasts The same in another emblem, as ver. 6.
