28 Saying, Did not we straitly As indeed they had, Acts 4.18. hence they aggravated the Apostles crime as done out of malice, and not out of ignorance. command you, that you should not teach in This Name, and this mans blood, are odious reflections, full of con • umely against our blessed Saviour; as if he had not been worthy the naming by them. this name? and behold, ye have filled • erusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this They shunned not the sin of murder, but are afraid or ashamed of the imputation of it; as many scruple not to commir that wickedness, which they would be loath to be thought guilty of. mans The punishment of his blood-shedding. blood upon us.

29 ¶ Then Peter This they all agree in; and it is the common sense of all considering men. As Socrates in his Apology told the Athenians; I imbrace and love you, O Athenians, and yet I will obey God rather than you; this the Apostles had formerly asserted, Chap. 4.19. and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.

30 Cha. 3.13, 15. This is the rather mentioned by the Apostle, that they might not think our Saviour, or they his Ministers, Preached any other God unto them, but him whom they had worshipped from their fore-fathers. The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and Chap. 10.39. and 13.29. 1 Pet. 2.24. hanged A tree, or wood, which is rather mentioned than a Cross, that the allusion to Deut. 21.23. might be more full; where he that is hanged on a tree is accursed; and in that Christ was made a curse for us, Gal. 3.13. on a tree.

31 Heb. 2.10. See Luke 24.46, 47. Him hath God exalted with his See Chap. 2.33. right hand to be a To conquer and subdue all his enemies, to defend and protect his subjects. Prince and a To save from sin according to his name Jesus, Matth. 1.21. viz. from the condemnation that is due unto it, and the pollution that is required by it; repentance is the gift of God; and nothing does more avail with us to repent, than the loss of Christ, (his bitter suffering and death) by whom the world is crucified unto us, Gal. 6.14. and if repentance includes newness of life, (as it does) who would not walk in that way which our blessed Lord hath recommended, and in which onely we can injoy him? that doing as he did, we may come at last to be where he is, Saviour, for to e give repentance to Israel, and which never fails to accompany true repentance; and is therefore also called repentance unto life, Chap. 11.18. forgiveness of sins.

32 And Joh. •• .26, 27. we are They refuse not to • ear their testimony for Christ, who witnessed a good profession for us. his witnesses of these things, and so is also The holy Ghost does witness, 1. By the Apostles, through his grace and strength they bear their record. 2. By all the miracles that were wrought, for they were onely done by his Power. 3. By enabling any to believe these things, which belief is his work. 4. Not to say that the holy Ghost was a witness of the things concerning Christ at his Baptism, and the several attestations he gave, saying, This is my beloved So • , Matth. 3.17. holy Ghost Chap. 2.4., whom God hath given to them that i obey him.Some read, believe in him, which is to the same purpose; for there is no true repentance where there is no faith: nor no saving faith, where there is no repentance and amendment.

33¶ Chap. 7.54. When they heard that, they were They grinned with their teeth, visibly shewing the rage and fury that was within them, by which they were as sawn and divided asunder; malice and rage being a grievous torment to the cruel and malicious, 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . cut to the heart, and took counsel to slay them▪

34 Then stood there up one in the councel, a This Sect was accounted more mild than the Sadduces. Pharisee 'Tis thought that this man was the same, at whose feet Paul sate, Chap. 22.3. that he was the instructor to Barnabas and St. Stephen, with many other stories concerning him are doubtful; howsoever God made use of him, tho as yet an enemy to his Church and people, to plead for, and protect them to his Power; God can effect any thing without, or against means, and suddenly to make such as were against him, to be for him and his truth., named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people, and commanded to put the apostles That they might consult amongst themselves what to do with them: thus Chap. 4. • 5. forth a little space.

35 And said unto them, Ye men of Israel A wise and good caution; for he that injures another, brings the worse mischief upon himself; both in the sense of having done evil, and in being exposed to the revengeing hand of God, whose property vengeance is, Hebr. 10.30., take heed to your selves, what ye intend to do as touching these men.

36 For Probably under the reign of Augustus, as he whom Iosephus mentions, was another under the reign of Claudius. before these days rose up, Some suppose it a contracted name of Theodorus, as Demas is thought to be of Demetrius; tho others think it to be of an Hebrew original. Theudas boasting himself to be some body, to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joyned themselves: who was slain, and all, as many as Or, Believed. obeyed him, were scattered and brought to nought.

37 After this man rose up Whether this was the same Iudas, who was called Gaulonite, from the place of his birth, a Town in or near Galilee; and Galileus from the Province its self in which he was born, it is not so material to discuss▪ Iosephus makes mention of two of this name. Judas of Galilee, in the days of the Setting down all their names at the command of the Roman Emperor, whereby, 1 They professed themselves to be his subjects. 2. They payed him a certain rate, in token of subjection, for every head, as Poll • money. 3. By this means he knew the number of his subjects, and the strength or weakness of every Province; this was another tax than that, mentioned Luke 2.2. which is there called the first. taxing, and drew away much people after him: he also perished▪ and all, even as many as obeyed him, were dispersed.

38 And He undertakes to advise them what they should do in the present case. now I say unto you Have nothing to do with them, as Pilates wife advised him concerning our Saviour, Matth. 27.19. Gamaliel interposes, partly, out of his moderate and mild disposition; partly out of fear, lest if they slew the Apostles, they might incense the Romans, who were very jealous of their Authority▪ and had taken away the power of Capital punishments from the Iews. , Refrain from
these men, and let them alone: Prov. 21.30. Isa. 8.10. Matth. 15.13. for This Argument, or Dilemma, which Gamaliel uses for the sparing of the Apostles, is of force either way; (as that question our Saviour propounds concerning the baptism of Iohn, Matth. 21.25.) if this counsel, or this work be This first part is evident, for that building must needs fall which is built upon the sand, Matth. 7.27. of men, it will come to nought.

39 The other part of the Dilemma, Prov. 19.21. Isaiah 46.10. The counsel of the Lord, that shall stand; and it must needs be so, for all power is his, in whom we live and move, Chap. 17.28. But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found Chap. 9.5. and 23▪9. even to fight They who afflict, and contend with his people unjustly, tho they little think so, set themselves against God, who will overcome at the last, and triumph over his, and his peoples enemies. against God.

40 And to him They yielded to his reason and argument, being perswaded and convinced by it. they agreed; And when they had called the apostles, and This was what our Saviour had foretold them, Ma • th. 1 • .17. and thus the husbandmen took the housholders servants and beat them, Matth. 21.35. They had power yet left them by the Romans, to punish offenders in their Synagogues, but not capitally nor publickly. beaten them, they commanded that they should not speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.In this they left the good advice of Gamaliel, who had warned them not to fight against God.

41 ¶ And they departed from the presence of the council It argued full perswasion of the truth, and great resolution to abide by it, that they could account so frail a disgrace for Christs sake, to be an honour., Mat. 5.12. Heb. 10.34. James 1.2. 1 Pet. 4.13. rejoycing that they were 'Tis a condescension and favour, when God uses any to give testimony unto his truth, altho it be by their suffering, Phil. 1.29. Vnto you it is given, not onely to believe, but to suffer; as if to suffer for Christ, were as great, if not a greater gift than to believe in him. counted worthy to suffer Scourging being a servile and disgraceful punishment. shame for Christs name, or for Christs sake, to assert his truth, &c. some do not read the Pronoun, but the name put absolutely for God, as was usual amongst the Iews, out of reverence to Gods name, lest they should prophane it. his name.

42 And daily This is the same with what we read, Acts 20.20. publickly, and from house to house; that is, in the Temple, and publick places, they preached unto the Iews, and in more private places, (or houses) where they saw it needful; unto such they conversed with. in the temple, and in They visited their flock, and instructed, exhorted, comforted them as their condition required: See the power of the grace of God; these we • e the men who forsook Christ, when the Souldiers came to apprehend him; they durst not be seen in his company: yet now they profess his Name, and abide by their profession, though they are derided and beaten for it. every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ.

div.head: CHAP. VI.
div.p: ANd in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the These were not such, as are elsewhere called Greeks, either as being of that Nation, or more generally taken for all Gentiles at large; but they were (as to their Authority) Iews, and descended from such of them, who in several national calamities, were forced (or chose) to leave their Countrey, and fly to Alexandria, and divers other places; yet kept themselves unmixed with other Nations, retaining the knowledge of God▪ and coming to worship upon the solem Feasts; onely disusing the Hebrew Language, they were more acquainted with the Greek Tongue, (then, commonly) spoken every where) and used the holy Scripture Translated into that Language, which made them the rather called Hellenists or Grecians. Grecians against the Hebrews, because their They were not taken, as others, into the Colledge, or number of widows, who in that time had some care of the poor; or rather, because they were not so largely allowed, or carefully looked after; for those that sold their goods, being Hebrews, they might not be so tender over the Hellenists, whose estates laying farther off, could not so readily be sold for the relief of themselves or others. widows were neglected in the daily ministration.

2 Then the For such was their number now again, Matthias having supplied the place of Iudas; this is that blessed number, or the root of it, which God hath so much magnified. twelve called the multitude of the disciples unto them, and said Exod. 18.17., it is not reason that we should leave the Preaching of the word, and other duties belonging to it; either providing for the agapae and love-Feasts, or distributing to the necessities whereby they might be fed, and their tables provided. word of God, and serve tables.

3 Wherefore brethren Deut. 1.13. Chap. 1.21, 22. and 16.2. 1 Tim. 3.7. As carefully and circumspectly, as ye would in any cases of your own concerns., look ye out among you seven men of A good direction, that obbliges to this day, in all elections of any for the service of God, and his Church. honest report Of the gifts and graces of the holy Ghost, which were not bestowed on the Apostles onely., full of the holy Ghost Or prudence, and skill in the word of God, which onely is able to make a man wise unto Salvation, 2 Tim. 3.15. and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.

4 But we will We will stick close, and with perseverance, to this work. give our selves continually to The two great imploys of a Minister of Jesus Christ; to pray unto God for the people, and to speak unto the people from the Lord; these, tho great businesses, they durst not delegate from themselves unto others to perform for them. prayer, and to the ministry of the word.

5 ¶ And the saying pleased the whole multitude. And they chose All these being Greek names, 'tis likely they were all Hellenists, and descended from Hebrew Parents, but born in forreign Countries; or amongst the Iews they might have other names, which St. Luke writing this History, translated into Greek. Stephen Chap. 11.24., a man full of faith, and of the holy Ghost, and Philip Chap. 8.5, 26. and 21. • ., and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas See Chap. 2.10. a proselite of Antioch.

6 Whom they set before the apostles: And when they had Prayer is the salt, which seasoneth and sanctifieth all things. prayed Chap. 8.17. and 13.3. 1 Tim. 4.14. 2 Tim. 1.6., they A rite used in the Church of old, 1. In their Sacrifices, Exod 29.15. 2. In their blessings, Gen. 48.14. 3. In their designations unto a charge or office; thus Moses on Ioshua, Numb. 27.18. and from thence it was easilier derived unto the Gospel-Church. Our Saviour blessing thus the children which were brought unto him, Matth. 19.13. and thus also were Ministers ordained in the Primitive times, 1 Tim. 5.22. laid their hands on them.

7 And Chap. 12 and 19.20. Col. 1.6. the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly; and a great None so violent opposers of the Gospel as these were, (their interest in all likelihood, heigthning their opposition) yet great is truth, especially the spirit of truth, and did prevail; and tho in its self, the number might not be so great, as to be called a great multitude; yet considering who they were that were converted, it was very wonderful, and the fewer might pass for a many. company of the priests were obedient unto the faith.Christianity is not a bare speculation, but a practical Religion; and we believe no more than we practice, fac quod dicis & fides est. Aug.

8 And Stephen full of faith Enabled to Preach, dispute, do, and suffer all things through Christ. and power, did great wonders Of whom he cured many, or among the people, in that he did these wonders publickly. and miracles among the people.

9 ¶ Then there arose certain of the Synagogues were as Colledges in our Universities, being used for Instruction and Learning; and were distinguished according to the persons that frequented them. synagogue, which is called the synagogue of the Some think, these were natives of a certain Countrey in Africa, from whence they were so called; but more probably, they were such as were manumitted or made free, (as the word is commonly used for such) and in a middle condition between such as were free-born, and such as were bond-slaves; and might desire to frequent with those of their own rank. Libertines, and The Iews spake of no less than 480. Synagogues at Ierusalem, a vast number, and probably increased by them, tho several places are called Cyrene; this (from whence they took their name) was in Africa in all likelihood, it being joyned with that of the Alexandrians: So God pleased to sever the Hellenists, (or Iews by traduction) for the Gentiles were not yet called; that they might all hear the Gospel in the Language they understood best. Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia, and of Asia, disputing with Stephen.

10 And Exod. 4.12. Isa. 54.17. Luke 21.15. they were not able They did oppose it, but ineffectually. to resist The foolishness of God is wiser than men, 1 Cor. 1.25. What then is his wisdom, through which this holy man spake? the wisdom, and The holy Ghost directing him, and putting a Divine Power upon what he spake, according to the promise, Matth. 10.20. the spirit by which he spake.

11 What these blasphemous words were, we have verse 14. which shew, that the vail was yet over their hearts, and that they could not indure to hear, that the shadows must flee away, when the Sun is risen, and the Types be abolished, when the substance of the things Typified is exhibited; for this truth was all the blasphemy this holy Martyr was guilty of. Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous • ords against Moses, and against God.

12 And they Being overcome by reason and arguments, they betake themselves to all the evil arts imaginable; they suborn witnesses against St. Stephen, (as was done against Naboth) and (that we read of) never before; they make the people, and the number, (which is usually the worst) on their side; then they complain of him to the Priests, &c. and lest any, or all these, should fail, they lay violent hands on him themselves. Sin goes on as a Current, and never stops, unless an Almighty word be spoken unto it to go no further. stirred up the people, and the elders, and the scribes, and came upon him, and caught him, and brought him to the council,

13 And set up They mingled in their testimony, false things with truths, as they who witnessed against our Saviour had done. St. Stephen might possibly have inculcated what our Saviour had foretold, Luke 19.43. and both have been very innocent; for neither of them spake with any abhorrence of, much less blasphemy • gainst the Law or the Temple; but in that the witnesses perverted and added to their words, they are deservedly branded as false witnesses; falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus, is a granted maxime in the case of witness-bearing. false witnesses, which said, This man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law.

14 For we have heard him say, That this Jesus of Nazareth shall destroy That is the Temple; Ieremy had foretold this long ago, and did escape, tho very narrowly, Ier. 26.12, 16. Daniel had Prophesied of the destruction both of the City and Sanctuary, Dan. 9.26. and yet these were in great respect amongst them; and none could speak more plainly of the calling of the Gentiles, than Malachi, Chap. 1.11. and yet when the Apostles came to apply these very things more home, and close, they could not indure them. this place, and shall change the Or, Rites. customs which Moses delivered us.

15 And all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the With an extraordinary lustre and radiancy, above what appears in men, whereby they might be distinguished, as Matth. 28.2, 3. affecting the beholders with admiration; thus Moses his face did shine. face of an angel.

div.head: CHAP. VII.
div.p: THen said Who was resolved to condemn any, right or wrong, that should profess Christ, as appears Iohn 9.22. the high priest That he might seem just, he gives him a kind of liberty to answer for himself; not to defend his Doctrine, but to know out of his own mouth, whether he Preached it, or no., Are these things so?

2 And he said, Men To take away any prejudice they might have conceived against him; and to recommend, not his person so much, as his Doctrine to them; he calls them Brethren, 1. As hoping in the same promises with them. 2. Observing the same Law. 3. Worshipping the same God., brethren, and A word of respect (especially) the elder amongst them, or his Judges: thus the Roman Senators were called Fathers, and Magistrates ought to be reverenced as the Fathers of their Countrey. fathers hearken; The Who is also called. Psal. 24.7. The King of glory, from whom all glory descends to Angels or Men. By this and what follows, St. Stephen would shew that he honoured the true God, and thought respectfully of the Law, the Temple, and the Patriarchs, whom he was accused to contemn and disgrace. God of glory appeared unto our He names Abraham, because he was accounted the first Father, and Patriarch of the Iews, and had the first clear promise, that the Messiah should come of his Seed. father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia is sometimes taken strictly for that Countrey, which lies betwixt the two Rivers, Tigris and Euphrates, from whence it had its name; sometimes more largely, including Chalde, and so 'tis taken here. Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in A City of the Parthians, in the borders of Mesopotamia, towards the Land of Canaan. Charran,

3 And said unto him This command given unto Abraham, we read of, Gen. 12.1, 5, 6. and is here the rather spoken of by St. Stephen, to prove that Abraham was in the favour of God, and did truly serve him, before he ever saw the Land of Canaan, and before the ceremonial Law was given by Moses, and much more before the Temple was built; and therefore it could not be blasphemy in him, to hold that God might be served without those ceremonies, and worshipped elsewhere than in Ierusalem. , Get thee out of thy countrey, and from thy kindred, and come into the land which This was the glory of Abrahams faith, that it submitted absolutely to God, and enabled Abraham to go he knew not whither, Hebr. 11.8. for God did not so much as name the place he would have him go unto. I shall shew thee.

4 Abraham had as great a love to his kindred and native Countrey, as others have; but he had a greater faith, which made him yield to Gods call and command, and follow from place to place the will of God, who is said here to have removed Abraham, and does chuse the Inheritance and habitation for his people, Psal. 47.4. Then Gen. 11.31 came he out of the land of the Chaldeans, and dwelt in Charran: And from thence, when his father was dead, he removed him into this land wherein ye now dwell.

5 And he gave him 'Tis true that Abraham had a field, and the Cave of Machpelah, Gen. 23.9. but that was of no use to Abraham whilst alive, but to bury him in when dead; besides, it was not as an inheritance by Gods gift, but it was purchased with his money. none inheritance in it, no not so much as to Whereby the least parcel of ground is meant; hence St. Stephen would prove, that Abrahams happiness, and theirs too, if they rightly understood it, did not depend upon the enjoyment of that place and Countrey. set his foot on Gen. 12.7▪ and 13.15.; yet he promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and Faith met with a double difficulty, not onely Abraham must believe he should have all that Countrey given him for an inheritance, in which he had not a foot of land, but he must also believe, that it should be his seeds after him, when as he had no children; but thus faith is the evidence of things not seen, Hebr. 11.1. to his seed after him, when as yet he had no child.

6 And God spake on this wise, That his seed As men which dwell in houses that are not their own; which seem to contradict the promise mentioned in the foregoing verse; but it is onely to make Abraham the more believe against hope, in hope, as 'tis said, Rom. 4.18. tho there were never so many difficulties more, for what God hath promised, faith would overcome them all. should sojourn in a strange land, and that they should bring them into bondage, and intreat them This very space of four hundred yea •• , is also mentioned, Gen. 15.13, 16. Which is thus computed, from the birth of Isaac (the promised seed) to the birth of Iacob, sixty years; from Iacobs birth, to his going into Egypt, one hundred and thirty years, from thence to their deliverance out of Egypt, two hundred and ten years; this period is accounted, Exod. 12.40, 41. to be four hundred and thirty years; which also St. Paul reckons by, Gal. 3.17. but then thirty years is added unto the account, being the space of time betwixt the first promise made unto Abraham of this seed, and the birth of Isaac, in whom the promise was to be fulfilled: St. Stephen here reckoning onely from the birth of Isaac. evil four hundred years▪

7 And the nation to whom they shall be in bondage, will Or punish; and so the Egyptians were punished, not by humane means, but by Divine power, and with Gods own immediate hand, and that in the fulness of time, the very night in which Gods promise was to take effect: and therefore 'tis a night to be much observed, Exod. 12.42. as shewing, that the Sabbath of his people, and the destruction of his enemies slumber not, 2 Pet. 2.3. I judge, said God: And after that shall they come forth, and Exod. • .12. serve me In Mount Horeb. The reason why God delivers his people is, that they may serve him, as Luke 1.74, 75. and so long as God hath any work for them to do in this World, he will preserve and deliver them. in this place.

8 Gen. 17.9, 10. And he gave Abraham, of whom he was speaking. him the covenant of Of which Covenant, Circumcision was the sign and seal, by which on the part of Abraham and his seed, it was stipulated, that they should put off all carnal affections, circumcision: Gen. 21.2, 3, 4. and so Abraham after the promise: so that the promises were not given for Isaacs sake; but Isaac was given for the promise sake: which made these things more fit to represent Gospel grace, which St. Stephen was Preaching of. begat Isaac, and circumcisied him the eighth day: Gen. 25.26. and Isaac begat Jacob, and Gen. 29.31, &c. and 30.5. and 35.23. Jacob begat the The heads of the Tribes, from whom they were denominated. Of this Genealogy, see Matth. 1.1, 2, &c. and the History of it in Genesis. twelve patriarchs.

9 Gen. 37.4, 28. Psal. 105.17. And the patriarchs moved with Enraged; the holy Martyr accommodates his apology so, as that they may ye • have occasion to reflect on themselves: envy, for as they had sold our Saviour unto strangers, so had their Fathers sold Ioseph. sold Joseph into Egypt a: but God was with him.To favour, and bless him; for Gods presence brings all good along with it: with this he comforts himself and others; that it was not without example or precedent that God should be with such whom their persecutors could not endure.

10 The effect of Gods presence with him, which to his people is always in an especial manner, not onely as he is with all other Creatures; but as the Soul is with the Body, most effectually, so is God with them. And delivered him out of all his afflictions, and Gen. 41.37. gave him Thus God brought Daniel into favour, Dan. 1.9. and hath all hearts in his hands. favour and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and he made him governour over Egypt, and all • his house.

11 Now there came This is mentioned, Gen. 41.54, &c. a dearth over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and As seldome any mischief comes alone: Rapine, and many diseases follow Famine. great affliction; and our fathers found Any course dyet, grass or herbs. no sustenance.
12 But when The history is known, Gen 42.1. Jacob heard that there was corn in Egypt, he sent out our Our Progenitors, Iacobs Sons, from whom we are descended. fathers first.

13 And at Upon their second coming into Egypt, Gen. 45.3, 4, 16. Ioseph made himself known unto them. the second time Joseph was made known to his brethren; and Josephs kindred was made known For the continuance of their sustenance, and fulfilling of what was foretold. unto Pharaoh.

14 Then sent Joseph, and called his father Jacob to him, and Deut. 10.22. all His affinity, and not consanguinity onely, which may be the reason why, tho in Gen. 46.26. it is said, that all the souls that came with Iacob into Egypt, were sixty six. (it being then added, they were all such as came out of his loyns) yet it is said▪ they were seventy persons, Gen. 46.27. Iacob, Ioseph, and Iosephs two sons (who were also of the promised seed) being added unto the number. In this account of St. Stephen, his Sons wives might be added, which make up seventy five. • here are other accounts of this difference; but it is not of any consequence as to faith and holy living, which are onely necessary unto Salvation: the wonderful increase to so many hundred thousands of men, besides children, spoken of Exod. 12.37. notwithstanding the barbarous cruelty of the Egyptians, is to be admired. his kindred, threescore and fifteen The nobler and better part by which they are numbred, and according unto which they are esteemed by God. souls.

15 Gen. 46. ••
So Jacob went down Which St. Stephen puts them in mind of, the rather that he might insinuate, No Countrey, nor Place, nor Temple were so necessary, but that notwithstanding (they had none of them) their fore-fathers did live and die in the fear and favour of God, altho in Egypt, out of the promised Land, &c. into Egypt Gen. 49. ••
, and died, he, and our fathers.

16 And Exod. 13 • Josh. 24 3 •
That they carried Ioseph to bury him in Canaan, according to the oath he made them take, Gen 50.25. i • certain, and that this was desired to be done for him out of faith, Hebr. 11.22. but it is not so certain, (unless this pl • ce be so • nderstood) that the rest of the Patriarchs were so translated after their death: yet it is very likely; fo • first, they had as much reason to desire it, as Ioseph h • d; they believed the same promises, and had an interest in that Land as well as he. Secondly, Their posterity bare the same respect unto them, that Iosephs Family did to him. Thirdly, It seems alike reasonable, that none of those twelve Heirs to the Land of Canaan, should be left in the Land of bondage. were carried over into Sichem, and laid in the Gen. 23. •• and 33.19. sepulchre that This place is acknowledged to be most difficult, and the difficulties are better not to be mentioned, than ill solved; which the nature of these notes (not to mention other reasons) might occasion: whosoever will consider the intended shortness of the story, with the usual Idioms of the Hebrew Language, from which it was deduced, may take this as a Paraphrase upon the whole Verse: And Iacob, and our fathers died, and were removed to Sichem, and were laid in Sepulchres, in that which Abraham bought for money, and in that that was bought for the Sons of Emor, the Father of Sichem. Dr. Lightfoot, in locum. Abraham bought for a sum of money of the sons of Emor the father of Sichem.

17 But when the time of Of the fulfilling of the promise; either of the increase of his seed, or of their deliverance out of Bondage, for both were promised, Gen 22.17. tho at that very time there were the greatest endeavours to hinder either, when God accomplished both. the promise drew nigh, which God had sworn to Abraham Exo. 1.7, •• Psal. 10 • .2 •
, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt.
18 Till another King arose, which These words, are taken from the Septuagint, Exod. 1.8. knew not Joseph.

19 The same Pharaoh resolves to deal (as he thought) wisely, Exod. 1.10. and 'tis acknowledged, that the Egyptians dealt subtilly with them, Psal. 105.25. For they do not at once destroy them, which might have been hazardous, (the Israelites being so numerous) neither could Egypt well spare at once so many Inhabitants; (too great and sudden evacuations, cause swoonings) but they endeavour their ruine by degrees, 1. Wasting them by hard labours. 2. Commanding the Midwifes privately to kill their Males. 3. dealt subtilly with our kindred, and evil intreated our fathers, Exod. 1.2 •
so that Casting out, or exposing any whom they found spared. Yet this people, attempted upon by so many secret and open means to bring them to destruction, God did preserve, and so he will his Church, (which they did typifie) ma • gre all the endeavours, the most potent malice can use against it. they cast out their young children, to the end they might not live.

20 Exod. 2 •
▪
••
In which time Moses was born, and Hebr. 11. ••
was u Heb.
〈◊〉 God. exceeding fair, and nourished up in his fathers house three months:Or fair to God; which tho some understand of the inward beauty of the mind, (which is indeed the most admirable) yet in this place there is no more to be understood by it, than the wonderful beauty of his Body, which God bestowed in an extraordinary measure upon him, that it might be a means to attract the care and pity of Pharaoh's Daughter, as it afterwards came to pass; besides, that which is eminent in any kind, is by an Hebraism said to be of God; upon this account Niniveh is called a City of God, Ionah 3.3. And we read of Rachels great wrestlings, or wrestlings of God, Gen. 3.8. Iosephus says, That Moses was so beautiful, that all who passed by, left their business they were about, to gaze at him. Antiq. 2.5.

And when he Exposed and left, Exod. 2.2. &c. now was the time for God to take him up, as in Psal. 27.10. was cast out An enemy to Gods Israel; yet God did make use of her to bring up, and educate Moses who was their deliverer., Pharaohs daughter took him up, and nourished him for Adopting him for her Son, Exod. 2.10. and giving him Education accordingly. her own son.

22 And Moses was learned The Egyptians were anciently famous for Learning, especially in Astronomy, and some other parts of Philosophy. in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in He was Eloquent. words and in His deeds were equal to his words: He could do as well as say, what became him. deeds.

23
〈◊〉 . 2.11. And when he was full This Age of Moses is not set down in his History; but they might have it by tradition, which is here confirmed unto us by the Holy Pen-man: these fourty years Moses spent in Pharaohs Court. fourty years old, it came It speaks these thoughts and resolutions to have been from God, that such a great Courtier should so far debase himself; therefore this is deservedly attributed unto his Faith, Hebr. 11.25. which is the gift of God, Eph. 2 8. into his heart to visit his brethren the children of Israel.

24 And seeing one of them suffer wrong This fact of Moses some defend by the Law of Nature, which allows us to protect the innocent; but many things we know were done by an extraordinary warrant, which we are not to imitate; nor by our own Authority to avenge our selves or others., he desended him, and avenged him that was oppressed, and smote the Egyptian:

25 Or, Now. For he supposed his brethren would have This they might have inferred, 1. From his extraordinary deliverance out of the Egyptians hands, and out of the River when young. 2. From his readiness to defend them, ('twas wonderful, that such an one as he was, and might have been, should mind them.) 3. From the drawing near of the time of their deliverance, which they could not without negligence be wholly ignorant of. understood, how that God by his By his means and Ministry. hand would deliver them; but they Stupidity is frequently charged upon this people: They then did not receive Moses, as these now would not receive Christ. understood not:

26 And the next day As one appointed by God to deliver them, which he had evidenced before. he shewed himself unto them as they strove, and would have With great earnestness, and as far as words could do, he compelled them. set them at one again These words are not mentioned, Exod. 2.13. but something otherwise than here; but the sense is here and there the same., saying, Sirs, ye Brethren, not so much being all descended from Abraham and the Patriarchs; but in that they all worshipped one and the same God, which is the greatest obligation to concord and agreement that can be; and if any offence be given, or trespass committed, it obliges us as much to pass it by and pardon it: Forgive the trespass of the servants of the God of thy father, Gen. 50.17. are brethren; why do ye wrong one to another?

27 But he that The injurious are most averse from peace, and one sin makes way for another. did his neighbour wrong, thrust him away, saying
〈◊〉 Chap. 〈◊〉
▪ , Who This was a causless cavil, especially from such an one as had known what Moses had done, as an essay of his being the deliverer of Gods Israel. made thee a ruler and a judge over us?

28 He charges this great crime upon Moses, to hinder him from further reproving of him; tho recrimination do not make him, or any other more innocent; yet men ordinarily use it, as if it were some satisfaction to them, that they are not wicked alone; but that others are as bad or worse; this better befits an Egyptian than an Israelite. Wilt thou kill me as thou didst the Egyptian yesterday?

29 Then •• ed Moses Knowing that what he had done to the Egyptian, would be discovered to Pharaoh, and his life in danger. at this saying, and was a stranger in the land of Inhabited by the posterity of Madian Abrahams Son, by Keturah, Gen. 25.1, 2. Moses was fourty years in Egypt, fourty years in Madian, with Iethro or Iether, who was called also Revel, Exod. 2.18. and Hobah, Numb. 10.29. and the other fourty years in the wilderness, which make up the hundred and twenty years of his life, Deutr. 34.7. This makes to St. Stephens purpose, to prove that God is always with them that fear him, in what Countrey or place soever; as he was with Abraham in Mesopotamia, and with his people in Egypt, so with Moses in Madian. Madian, where be begat two sons.

30 And when So long it pleased God to try Moses his faith, and his peoples patience: fourty years were expired there appeared to him in the wilderness of to the Desert of Arabia, where the Law was afterwards delivered, Exod. 18.5. and 19: 3. mount Sina, an Not a Created, but the Increated Angel, the Angel of the New-Covenant, as may be seen ver. 32. and by Moses putting off his shoes because the place was holy, Exod. 3.2, 5. he is also in the four first verses of that Chapter, called the Lord. angel of the Lord in a God still appeared in such a manner as was most instructive to them he appeared to, and to us; as here in a flame of fire in a bush, to shew that he was with his people in all their sufferings, and would so provide, that they should not be consumed by them; they might be purified, but should not be destroyed. flame of fire in a bush.

31 When Moses saw it, he Seeing the bush on a flame, and not consumed; contrary to the nature of devouring flames, • hat he might be convinced of Gods presence; and made the more attentive to what God should say, and prepared to yield obedience unto it. wondred at the sight: And as he drew near to behold it, the voice of the Lord came unto him.

32 Saying Mat. 22.32. Heb. 11.16., I That he might know from whom he had his Commission, and by whom he was to be sent. am the God of thy fathers, Mention is made of these, because God had made unto them the promise of delivering their posterity, which he was now about to do, the time being fully come. the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Then Moses All great admiration hath some fear joyned with it; Gods appearing, tho in mercy, was ever full of terror and amazement; what will his appearing be, when he shall come in Judgment to render vengeance? who then shall be able to abide? trembled, and durst not behold.

33 Then said the Lord to him Either out of reverence to the Divine presence, as Iosh. 5: 15. or that thereby he might shew that he resigned himself wholly to Gods will and disposal; as in Ruth 4.7. The kinsman by pulling off his shoe and giving it to Boaz, did resign all his right he might have had to Ruth and the inheritance., Put off thy shoes from thy feet: for the place where thou standest is Whilest God manifested his presence there. holy ground.

34 Seeing I have seen, I have attentively seen and considered; It is doubled for to shew the certainty of it; if earthly parents, especially look after their Children when weak, much more our Heavenly Father. I have seen, I have seen the affliction of my people which is in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and Spoken after the manner of men, according unto which God is said to come down unto any, when he delivers them from their troubles; and to go from them, when he leaves them in them, see Exod. 3.7, 8. from which place according to the reading of the Septuagint, these words are taken. am come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send thee into Egypt.Tho but sighs, and scarce framed into words.

35 This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a Or a Redeemer; but onely as a Type of Christ, in whom alone we have redemption through his blood, Eph. 1.7. As Moses by the blood of the Paschal Lamb, brought forth, and saved the people of Israel. deliverer by the The power of the Angel; it was not Moses, but God that wrought so great Salvation. hands of the angel which appeared to him in the bush.

36 He brought them out, after that he had Exod. 7. & 8. & 9. & 10. & 11. & 14. shewed God could with the least word or motion of his Will, save his people; but he chuseth so to do his wonderful works, that they may be had in remembrance. wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the 'Tis not agreed why 'tis so called; but this name of that Sea is mentioned in prophane Authors. This whole verse, as divers others, refer to the History of it in Exodus, from the beginning to the fifteenth Chapter. Red sea, Exod. 16.1. and in the wilderness forty years.

37 ¶ This is that St. Stephen would shew, that he was so far from speaking against Moses, (as they falsly imagined) that he recommended no • e but him, whom Moses had so long before spoken of. Moses which said unto the children of Israel, Deu. 1 • .15, •• . A Christ the Messiah, and head of the Prophets, See Chap. 3.22. Prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren Or, As my self. , like unto me Mat. 17.5. him shall ye Or obey. hear.

38 Exo. 19.3, 17. This is he that was in the Or Congregation; with the rest of the people in all their difficult Journey. church in the wilderness, with Gal. 3.19. See ver. 30. of this Chap. the angel which spake to him in the mount Sina, and with our fathers: who received the Gods Law and Word is so called, as the onely rule to walk by unto Life, Deut. 32.47. It is there said to be our life, and it is the onely ordinary means of a Spiritual and holy Life, which it begets and preserves. lively oracles to give unto us.

39 To whom Their glory being in their Fathers, St. Stephen minds them, that many of them rebelled against God, and his servant Moses; as they (their posterity) now were rebellious against Christ, who came to save them, as Moses before had done; but from a greater bondage, and by more valuable means. our fathers would not obey, but thrust him from them, and in Not so much towards that Countrey, or food they had there, (Garlick and Onions) as towards their Idolatry and Superstition; a • in the following verse appears. their hearts turned back again into Egypt,

40 Exod. 32.1. Saying unto Aaron, Make us According to the Egyptians, who held that there were many Gods, and divers degrees of Gods; they therefore speak in the plural number: gods to go before us: for as for Tho they confess the great deliverance wrought by Moses his means; yet how contemptibly do they speak of him. this Moses, which brought us out of the land of Egypt, we They could not but know that Moses was gone up into the Mount unto God, at his command, and had not forgotten them; but had left Aaron and Hur to govern them; yet they soon forgot both God and Moses, notwithstanding the large and late experience they had of his wonders; this is left upon record against them, Psal 106.13, 21. wot not what is become of him.

41 And they In imitation of the Egyptians, who worshipped their God Apis in that, or the like form of an Ox. made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifice unto the The Calf which they had made, which they could not be so sottish as to terminate their worship in, knowing that they themselves had made it, and it had not made them; yet they are for this charged to have committed Idolatry, 1 Cor. 10.6, 7. idol, and Which joy they express by feasting, singing, and dancing, Exod. 32.7. rejoyced in the works of their own hands.So, this Idol and Idols, generally are called, Psal. 115.4. and 135.15. which is enough to speak their emptiness and vanity; vain man can make but vain Gods.

42 Then God From being as a Father to them, to be a Judge over them, to punish them; whereas formerly he had blessed them. turned, and This was indeed to deliver them to Satan, God withholding his grace which they had abused, Rom. 1.24, 25. and giving them up, (to fall from one sin unto another) tho not positively, yet permissively. gave them up to worship The Angels are so called, Luke 2.13. but it is rather here to be understood of the sun, moon, and stars, which are called so, Deut. 17.3. Isa. 40.26. the host of heaven; as it is written The words here referred to, are in Amos 5 25. 'Tis said to be in the Book in the singular number, because the twelve small Prophets are by the Iews mentioned but as one Book. in the book of the Prophets, O ye house of Israel This positive question does vehemently deny, that they had offered any Sacrifices unto God, whilest they were in the wilderness; but at the same time they offered Sacrifices unto Idols; for when they had corrupted Gods worship, their Sacrifices were as no Sacrifices unto him, Isaiah 1.11. and 43.23., have ye offered to me slain beasts, and sacrifices, by the space of fourty years in the wilderness?

43 Yea, ye On their shoulders, as they did the Ark. took up the tabernacle The Idol of the children of Ammon, which the Israelites were especially forbidden to worship, Lev. 18.21. and Lev. 20.2. yet they did ordinarily worship him, 2 Chron. 28.3. Ier. 7.3. And there was an high place built by Solomon for him, 1 Kings 11.7. The tabernacle of Molech, was either a chest or press in which that Idol was put, or the Chappels into which the worshippers of Molech were admitted; according to the quality of the Offering which they brought. Which of the planets they intended to honour hereby, whether the Sun, or Mars, or Saturn, it matters not so much; any of these, or any other of their Gods, might be called Molech, taking the word appellatively. of Molech, and the star of your god Remphan in the place here cited, is called by the Prophet Chiun; which is one and the same Idol in both places, the Prophet calling it by its name then in use; and St. Stephen like unto the name the Septuagint had called it by; whither Saturn was intended by this, as some think, or Hercules as others, it is not our present business to enquire. Remphan, m figures which ye made, to worship them: and I Images and representatives of the hosts of Heaven, or of the Planets. will carry you away The Prophet Amos saith, beyond Damascus, Amos 5.27. here St. Stephen does not contradict the Prophet, for they who were carryed away beyond Babylon, must needs be carryed away beyond Damascus, as the ten captive Tribes were, (unto whom this was threatned.) beyond Babylon.

44 Our fathers had Called also the Tabernacle of the congregation, Exod. 33.7. because about it on all solemn occasions the people assembled. Here 'tis called the Tabernacle of witness, because God here testified, or witnessed his glorious presence; and especially, because in it the Ark of the Covenant, the Law, and the Testimony were kept. the tabernacle of witness in the wilderness, as he had appointed Or, Who spake. speaking unto Moses that he should make it Exod. 25.40. Heb. 8.5. Moses was charged not to vary from the prescript; God being jealous of his own appointments: Now this is the rather spoken of by St. Stephen, that he might prove that the place where God was worshipped in, had varied, and therefore might also now be changed. according to the fashion that he had seen.

45 Josh. 3.14. Which also our fathers Or, Having received. that came after, brought in with Or Ioshua; it being the same name, as appears also, Heb. 4.8. onely Jesus is more according to the Greek use: Ioshua was a type of Jesus, and agreed with him in his name, and in the reason of his name; he having also saved the people, and brought them into the promised rest; yet the difference is as great between them, as betwixt the Heavenly Canaan, and the Earthly. Jesus into the possession of the Gentiles, whom God drave out before They were not able to look upon an Israelite, whilest God was for them. the face of our fathers, unto the days of David.

46 1 Sam. 16.1. Chap. 13.22. Who As Luke 1.30. found favour before God, and It was Davids earnest request, that he might any ways glorifie God, especially in his worship, and that he might know where the Ark should rest, and where the Temple was to be built, as Psalm 132. declares throughout. desired to find a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.
47 1 Chr. 17. •• . But 1 Kings 6.10. 2 Chronicles 3.1, 2. Solomon built him A fixt and stable Structure, no • moveable, as the Tabernacle was. an house.

48 Howbeit 1 Kin. 8.27. This is also St. Pauls Doctrine, Chap. 17.24. which divers amongst the wiser Heathens were perswaded of; for God cannot be comprehended in any place, no, not where he is worshipped; and therefore they did foolishly conceive, that the worship of God was so tyed to the Temple, as if he himself had been included in it. the most High dwelleth not The Primitive Christians abstained from calling the places of their assembling, by the name of Temples; and were charged by their Pagan-enemies for having no Altars, or Temples, or Images. in temples made with hands, as saith the Prophet.

49 The place referred unto, is Isaiah 66.1. Mat. 5.24. and 23.22. Heaven is my throne, and earth is my foot-stool: What That shall be big enough for one so great as God is, 1 Kings 8.27. house will ye build me? saith the Lord: or what is the place of my rest?

50 As appears in the History of the Creation, Gen. 1.1. Hath not my Spoken unto our capacity after the manner of men, and implies that God is too great to stand in need of Temples or Offerings; and that what worship he requires, is not for his own sake, for our righteousness cannot profit him; but for mans sake, that he might be exercised in the duties of Religion and devotion. hand made all these things?

51 ¶ Ye A metaphor taken from heifers that are unaccustomed unto the yoke.
Exod. 32.9. Isa. 48.4. stiff-necked, and Such as had still depraved affections, which they ought to have put away rather than the foreskin of their flesh; for they were commanded to circumcise their hearts, Deut. 10.16. which also God promised to do for his people, 〈◊〉 30.6. And St. Paul was not the first who spake of a twofold circumcision, Rom. 2.28, 29. but God looked always to the inward and Spiritual part of his own Ordinances, and mens observance of them. Lev. 26 41. Jer. 4.4. & 6.10. & 9.26. uncircumcised in heart, and Such as were not so much as willing to hear, and know their duty. ear • , ye do always resist the holy Speaking by his Prophets and Ministers, and exhorting to true and serious piety; by this St. Stephen would abate their glorying in circumcision, which they so much boasted of. Ghost: as your Thus the Prophet Ezekiel, 16.44. unto which may be here alluded, as is the mother, so is the daughter. fathers did, so do ye.

52 Which of the Prophets have not your This is the rather said to stain all their glory from succession, and their Ancestors, Matth. 5.12. and 23.31, 37. fathers persecuted? And they have slain them which shewed before of the coming of the Chap. 3.14. Our Saviour deservedly, and by way of eminence is so called; as not onely being himself Iust, and fulfilling all righteousness; but being the Lord our righteousness, Ier. 23.6. and is of God made unto us, Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification, and Redemption, 1 Cor. 1.30. This word is used in a forensick sense, and is the same with innocent, and opposite to guilty; whereby St. Stephen vindicates our Saviour, notwithstanding the unjust sentence passed here upon him. just One, of whom ye have been now In hiring Iudas. the betrayers and murderers:In that they excited Pilate to condemn him, and abetted the Soldiers and others, in executing of him.

53 Exod. 20.1. Who have received the law by the Or Ministery of Angels: The commandments were published from them Ministerially, or the Son of God, (called an Angel ver. 35.) accompanied with the Militia of Heaven, (for 'tis a Military Metaphor) did in the midst of that glorious retinue give the Law, Deut. 33.2. Psalm 68.8. Gal. 3.13, 19. disposition of angels, and have They transgressed the Law, tho so gloriously delivered by Angels, and therefore it was no wonder if they despised the Gospel, that was published by so mean and contemptible Ministers. not kept it.

54 ¶ When they heard these things, they were They were angry to madness. cut to the heart, and Gnashing of teeth is the curse of the damned, Matthew 8.12. which men by their sins do prepare for; this corrasive was applyed by a skilful hand, would they have endured the cure. they gnashed on him with their teeth.See Chap. 5.33.

55 But he being Filled with grace suitable to his present tryal and suffering. full of the holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the The glorious God, or so much of the Throne and glory of God, as Mortal eyes are capable for to see; being Iustified by God, tho condemned by Pilate: glory of God, and Jesus and standing ready to assist and comfort all that should suffer for his sake. standing on the right hand of God,

56 And said, Behold God not suffering any distance to hinder this refreshing sight., I see Mat. 3.16. the heavens opened, and So Christ is frequently called; and St. Stephen would by this inform them, how vain they were in striving against Christ or his truth. the Son of man As an Advocate, Soldier, or Captain for Stephen; or as one shewing the prize unto him, whic • he was now running for, and had need to be incouraged with the sight of: But it seems strange, that St. Stephen should tell the Iews of this Heavenly vision, being they did not see it, altho in the same place with him; but this he might do, 1. Out of his ardent love to Christ, desiring to magnifie him. 2. To invite his enemies to Repentance; now Heaven was opened, and Christs arms were stretched out to receive them. 3. To hinder any from being afraid to own Christ, and his truths. 4. To terrifie the most obdurate amongst them, by shewing them their judge, and minding them of his avenger. 5. That he might assert himself to be an eye-witness of Christs being risen again from the dead, which they made such difficulty to believe. standing on the right hand of God.

57 Then they The rabble, or multitude. cried out with a loud voice, and That they might show the great detestation of what was said, and might not contract any guilt from it. stopped their ears, and This violence and fury was both against the Law of God, and the Law of the Land; and the number of Zealots, (there were some amongst that people eminently so called) provoked the Romans to destroy both City and Temple. ran upon him with one accord.

58 And That the City might not be polluted with his blasphemy. 1 Kin. 21.13. Luke 4.29. cast him out of the city, and This punishment was appointed for such as seduced them to the worship of false Gods, Deut. 13.6, 10. and tho all power of Capital punishment was taken from them, as they themselves confess, Iohn 18.31. yet what will not popular rage attempt? stoned him: and Chap. 22.20. the Who were by the Law to cast the first stones, Deut. 17.7. whereby the witnesses, if they had not testified true, did take upon themselves the guilt of the blood that was spilt, and freed the people, who onely followed them in the Execution. witnesses laid Their upper garments, that they might carry, and cast down the heavier stones. down their clothes at a young mans feet, whose name was Saul.

59 And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying Stephen called upon him whom he saw standing, and that was our Saviour., Lord Jesus Psal. 31.5. receive my Or my Soul; Thus our Saviour commended his Spirit into his Fathers hands, Luke 23.46. and this Disciple imitates his Master; and comforts himself with this, that to be sure his Soul should be safe, whatsoever became of his body. spirit.

60 And he A posture used in most earnest Prayers; and if so, he Prayed at least as earnestly for his enemies, as for himself; he praying for them kneeling, and for himself standing. kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, Do not weigh it, reckon or impute it, that it may not remain against them, to hinder their Conversion; This our Saviour commanded, Matth. 5.44. this he practised, Luke 23.34. And whosoever can thus pray for his enemies, and do good for evil, hath a great evidence that the Spirit of Christ is in him. lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he He dyed; his Death being thus expressed in that, 1. He dyed quietly, as one fallen into a sleep. 2. Because of his certain hope of the Resurrection. 3. As easily to be raised again by Christ, as one that sleeps is to be awaked by us. 4. It is an ordinary Hebraism to express Death by sleep; which made St. Luke use it amongst them, with whom it was frequently thus expressed. fell asleep.

div.head: CHAP. VIII.
div.p: ANd Saul was Well-pleased with it, (as the word implies) and did approve it in thought, word, and deed, Acts 22.4, 20. which is here noted in the beginning of the narrative concerning this Great Apostle, that we might consider 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , what a great change the grace of God did make; which was by him, and is by us the more to be acknowledged and magnified. consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a Not as heretofore against the Apostles onely; but now it was against the whole Church. great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem, and Chap. 11.19. they were The multitude of believers, at least as many as could flee; which was allowed, or rather commanded, Mat. 10.23. when they were persecuted in one City, to flee unto another, especially such as were teachers amongst them, (besides the Apostles) were forced to remove from Ierusalem; and by this means, did publish the Gospel in all places whither they came; so that what was intended for the hinderance, God did over-rule towards the furtherance of the Gospel: as he did afterwards, Phil. 1.12. and still does, and ever will do. all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria Who were commanded to stay at Ierusalem, Chap. 1.8. there they were to make their beginning, Luke 24.47. and from thence to proceed unto other parts, Isaiah 2.3. and whilest God had any work for them to do at Ierusalem, they knew that God could and would defend and maintain them in the midst of their enemies: as he had done the bush in the fire, Exod. 3.3., except the apostles.

2 And It was an argument that they were devout (Religious) indeed, that they durst amongst such a multitude of persecutors, and furious Zealots, own their esteem for St. Stephen; It was piacular amongst the Iews, to touch the dead Corps of such an one as was put to Death for blasphemy; and these perform such Funeral rites for him, as were used for such onely as were of note and Eminency. As the Iews were wont to do at the Funeral, especially of Eminent persons; thus it was done at Iacobs Interment, Gen. 50. ult. and thus had been done more lately at Lazarus's Funeral, Iohn 11. even by our Saviour himself, ver. 3 • . Which lamentation was the greater, because of the Churches loss at such a time. devout men carried Stephen to hss burial, and Gen. 23.2. 2 Sam. 3.31. made great lamentation over him.

3 As for Saul Saul was a degree beyond the ordinary sort of persecutors, and was, as he does acknowledge of himself, eminently injurious, 1 Tim. 1.13. Chap 22.4. & 26.10, 11. 1 Cor. 15.9. Gal. 1.13., he made havock of the church, entring House after house, sparing none. into every house, and As by the hair of their heads. haling men and women This to be sure, the Iews had yet retained power from the Romans to do: All this is but as a foil, to illustrate more the riches of Gods mercy towards Saul. , committed them to prison.

4 Mat. 10.23. Chap. 11.19. Therefore they that were scattered abroad, went Now the partition-wall was about to be broken down, and the Gentiles to be taken into the pale of the Church; God provides this strange means towards it. The Disciples are forced to s • y for their lives out of Ierasalem, and have an opportunity to Preach Christ and the Gospel, wheresoever they came: thus God can make light to come out of darkness, and makes Iapheth to dwell in the Tents of S • m, Gen. 9 27. every where preaching the word.

5 Then Nor the Apostle, but the Deacon of that name; for the Apostles remained at Ierusalem, as ver. 1. Philip went down to the Samaria is a name both of a City, and a countrey, so called from the chief City, 1 Kings 16.24. here 'tis taken for that City, or at least a City in that Countrey. city of Samaria, and preached The Doctrine of Christ, his miraculous Birth, holy Life and Death, and glorious Resurrection and Ascension, together with Remission of sins, onely by faith in his name, &c. Christ unto them.

6 And the people with one accord A good preparation towards their Conversion; seeing faith cometh by hearing, Rom. 10.17. gave heed unto those things which Philip spake, hearing These Miracles were as so many evidences of the truth he spake; by which he shewed Gods Authority for what he said. and seeing the miracles which he did.

7 For unclean spirits This is frequently mentioned, as Matthew 8.29. Mark 1 26. and 3.11. and 5.8. Luke 4.41. to shew how loath these evil Spirits are to be forbid, and kept from tormenting and destroying of us; and they are called unclean Spirits, because they delight in sin, and instigate men unto it, which is Spiritual uncleanness, and de • ile the Soul;, crying with a loud voice, came out of many that were possessed with them: and many taken And other diseases and infirmities; this was promised, Mark 16.16, 17. that they which believe should cure in Christs name, or by his power. with palsies, and that were lame, were healed.

8 And there was Not onely for the cures wrought upon their bodies; but much more for the word of reconciliaton, and Salvation Preached unto their Souls; joy in the Holy Ghost, is one of the effects of the Kingdom of God, Rom. 14.17. great joy in The despised Samaria rejoyce, and the formerly beloved City of Ierusalem, repine at the Gospel; such strange alterations does the free grace of God make. that city.

9 But there was a Magical inchantments, as a wizard: certain man called Simon, which before time in the same city Chap. 13.6, 8. used sorcery, and caused them as men in an extasie to be amazed at, and afraid of him. bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was As if he had been God, or at least had some great favour with him, and had received some extraordinary power from him: Ecclesiastical Histories speak much of him, and tell us that he had a Statue set up in Rome for him, inscrib'd To Simon the holy God. some great one.

10 To whom they all gave heed Shewing how general their mis-perswasion was, and no condition is exempt from the grossest mistakes, if not prevented by the grace of God. from the least to the greatest, saying, This 'Tis said of this Simon, that he gave out himself to be that God, which any Nation held to be the chiefest; and that he was the Messias of the Iews, and the God of the Gentiles. man is the great power of God.

11 And to him They acquiesced in what he said, and yielded obedience unto it; not attending onely to his words with their ears, but with their hearts; so true is that w •• ch our Saviour says; Iohn 5.43. If any man come in his own name, him will ye receive. These Samaritans
〈◊〉 rise up in judgment against most men, who do not thus regard what was said by Christ, and such as he hath sent. they had regard, because that of long time he had Made them as out of their wits, they were not themselves, and could not act their reason. bewitched them Such wonders as by the permission of God, and Satans power he did. with sorceries.

12 But Before they were baptized, being adult and strangers from the Covenant, they must first evidence their right unto it, and profess their Faith in Christ, and testifie their Conversion. when they believed Philip, preaching the things The Kingdom of Grace, and the Kingdom of his Glory, which is one and the same, being begun here; but consummated in Heaven hereafter. concerning the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized both men and Women under the Gospel are as capable of this seal of the Covenant as men. women.

13 Then Simon himself Simon believed with an Historical faith, that it was indeed true, that our Saviour had done Miracles, and did rise from the dead, but his faith to be sure was dead all the while; neither did he believe with his heart, or purpose to live according to the Law of Christ, which is the life of Faith. believed also: and when he was baptized, he Kept him constantly company, and was amongst the forwardest of the Professors of Christs faith. continued with Philip, and wondred, beholding the Thus the Magicians of Egypt were brougth to acknowledge the finger of God, Exod. 8.19. altho their hearts were hardned. Heb. Signs and great Miracles. miracles and signs which were done.

14 Now when the apostles which were at Jerusalem, heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent unto them These were sent that they might further confirm the Doctrine which Philip had Preached amongst the Samaritans; and by Apostolical authority, constitute a Church in Samaria. Peter and John.

15 Who when Peter and Iohn: they were come down, prayed In this particular they did not pray for all that believed, amongst whom there were several women, ver. 12. Those extraordinary gifts of Tongues, of Prophesying, of working Miracles, &c. See Chap. 10.45. for them that they might o receive the holy Ghost.

16 For By which it is plain that the Holy Ghost, as the Author of saving grace, is not here meant, for so he was fallen upon all them that did believe, for faith is the gift of God; but he was not yet bestowed upon them, as the author of those extraordinary gifts mentioned, Chap. 2.38. as Chap. 19.2. yet he was fallen upon none of them: onely they were baptized 1. They were baptized by his authority and commission, Matth. 28.19. 2dly. By baptism they now belong unto, and are united with him, Rom. 6.3. They are baptized into Iesus Christ, &c. in the name of the Lord Jesus.

17 Then That this laying on of the hands of the Apostles was not intended here, as any rite whereby the Apostles did confirm some, or ordain others, seems evident from the context. Chap. 6.6. & 13.3. & 19.6. laid they their hands on them and they The power of speaking with tongues, and working of Miracles; which throughout this Book is so often spoken of in this acception. received the holy Ghost.

18 And when Simon saw that through laying on of the apostles hands, the Those extraordinary gifts before mentioned; for this appeared visibly and audibly; and by this indeed was signified the great change Gods-Spirit makes where he comes. holy Ghost was given, he This notorious Hypocrite values these outward gifts; how much more valuable are the inward and Spiritual gifts of God? offered them money,

19 Saying, Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive Such an extraordinary power of working Miracles, he did not desire, that he might glorifie God, or confirm the truths of the Gospel, (now professed by him) but out of an insatiable desire of gain, and ambition, to keep up his reputation; seeing how the Apostles had done beyond what he was able to do. the holy Ghost.

20 But Peter said unto him A formal execration of curse, not onely on his money, but also upon Simon himself; but always to be conditional, viz. unless he repented., Thy money perish with thee, because Mat. 10.8. thou hast Our hearts are to be watched over; our thoughts may be exceeding sinful, as here, which made his words or desires to be so ill taken. thought that the 〈◊〉 of God may be purchased with money.

21 Thou hast neither No Inheritance or share in such a thing as this, to wit, either in the receiving, or conferring the Holy Ghost; or in that eternal Life which we Preach, thou hast no part in it, neither art thou fit to be a Minister of it. part nor lot in this matter: for The Apostle had the gift of discerning of Spirits, which is mentioned, 1 Cor. 12.10. which might cause the execration in the foregoing verse, and in divers other places of Scripture, 2 Tim. 4.14. thy heart is not right in the sight of God.

22 The onely remedy and help in his (otherwise) desperate case: This is not spoken as if it were doubtful, whether true repentance should obtain pardon; but whether Simon Magu's repentance were true Repentance is a condition, under which God proposeth our pardon, and forgiveness; but it is far from being the cause of it. Repent therefore of this thy wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee.

23 For I perceive that thou art in the The same with gall and wormwood, Deut. 29.18. or gall and bitterness; signifying a very bad constitution, and disposition of Soul or mind▪ such as may be compared unto that meat, which the gall of any Creature hath corrupted. And for Simon Magus to be in the gall of bitterness, is yet worse than to have the gall of bitterness in him; as to be born in sin, which the Pharises upbraided the blind man with, Iohn 9.34. denotes more intended thereby, than that he had sin from his birth in him; thus David bewails, That he was shapen in iniquity, Psal. 51.5. and thus may those expressions of St. Paul be understood, of being in the flesh, and being in the spirit, Rom. 8.9. This also shews, (if any sensible or outward thing could shew it) what a bitter and poisonous thing sin is, no gall so bitter, no poison so deadly. Either the judgment St. Peter had threatned to deter him from sin, was this bond, or his sin it self might be rather so called; thus we read of the bonds of iniquity, Isaiah 58.6. One sin is twisted with another; hard to be severed or broken, and draws on judgment powerfully. gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.

24 Then Simon Magus was convinced, that he was indeed such as the Apostles had spake him to be; and knowing them to be powerful with God, he desires this of them. answered Simon, and said Numb. 21.7. He feigns himself to be a true penitent, being terrified with the threatning of St. Peter, ver. 20. and probably, fearing the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira might befall him; which 'tis likely he had heard of., Pray ye to the Lord for me, that none of these things which ye have spoken come upon me.

25 And they when they had testified and preached the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the gospel in many Not onely in the chief City, but in the smallest Villages, these great Apostles spend their pains; for so it was promised unto them that they should receive power to do, Chap. 1.8. villages of the Samaritans.

26 And the angel of the Lord spake unto Philip, saying, Arise and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza Some speak of two Gaza's, one distinguished from the other, by this epithete of desert; but rather there were two ways unto one and the same Gaza, and that it was not the City, but the way unto it, which is called desert; by which difference here mentioned, the Angel admonishes Philip, not to go the ordinary road; but the more unusual road over the Mountains, which was rarely travelled over; but was now necessary to be gone in▪ to meet with the Eunuch: God telleth our wandrings, and ordereth our steps., which is desert.

27 And he arose and went: and behold a Zeph. 3.10: The Ethiopians were the most despicable unto the Iews; and Homer calls them, 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 ; but God would now shew, that there is no difference of Nations with him; but in every Nation, he that worketh righteousness, shall be accepted, Chap 10.35▪ man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under A name common to the Queens of that Countrey; as all the Kings of Egypt were called Pharaoh's, and the Emperors of Germany are called C • sars. Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had John 12.20▪ come to Jerusalem Being a Proselite, he had been to worship God in that solemn Festival of the Passover. for to worship,In great esteem in Courts, especially to attend on Queens, to avoid all suspicion; here that prophesie was fulfilled, Isaiah 56.4, 5. Tho both in the Hebrew, and (anciently) in the Greek tongue, an Eunuch signified more largely, viz. any attendant in the Chamber.

28 Was returning, and sitting in his chariot, He had some knowledge of the true God, whom he came to worship, and he endeavours after more; and to him that thus hath, shall be given: and they that thus seek, shall find; God will rather work a Miracle, than that any that sincerely desire, and faithfully endeavour to know him, or his will, should be disappointed. read Esaias the prophet.

29 The Spirit, either by the Ministry of an Angel, as ver. 26. or by inspiration immediately by himself. Then the spirit said unto Philip, So near that you may speak with him that fits in it. Go near, and Stick close unto it, and leave it not. joyn thy self to this chariot.

30 And Philip Hastning to obey the Divine command, and cove • ing to gain a Soul: ran thither to him, and heard him with a loud voice; 'tis like, to instruct some of his attendants. read the Prophet Esaias, and said Without understanding, our reading is but as the tinkling of a cymbal., Understandest thou what thou readest?

31 And he said A wonderful modesty and humility in so great a man: he takes well Philip's interposing, and questioning with him; he acknowledges his ignorance, and desires farther instruction, and condescends to be taught by one so much his inferior., How can I, except some man should guide me? and he desired Philip that he would come up, and sit with him.

32 The Gods Providence is remarkable, that the Eunuch should be reading this very Scripture, which contains so fundamental truths, and which he had most need for to be informed of: The words referred into, are in Isaiah 53.7. whether read in the Hebrew tongue, which the Eunuch might have learned of many Iews living in Ethiopia; or whether they were read out of the Translation of the Seventy, which was then in common use, is not so necessary an inquiry; both being to the same intent and purpose. place of the scripture which was read, was this, He was led as a Christ was indeed as a sheep for his patience: sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb Not opening his mouth to defend his own case; but especially he was as a sheep, in being a Sacrifice for us; the true Paschal Lamb that causeth the destroyer to pass from us; and yet he is our Shepherd too, to supply and preserve us, Psal. 23.1. dumb before his shearer, so he opened not his mouth:

•• In his When our blessed Saviour was in his lowest condition, and the utmost degree of his exinanition; his soul being made a Sacrifice for us, and suffering that desertion for a time, we had merited for ever; and his body laid in the grave as in a prison; Then humiliat • on his his judgment, the punishment which was inflicted upon him in our stead, was taken away; for he brak the bonds of death, and opened the prison-door: this was foretold, altho in somewhat differing expressions, by the Prophet Isaiah, 53.7, 8. judgement was taken
away, and who shall declare Those that shall be brought forth by this travail of his Soul, are innumerable, or his own Eternal generation; (who could do such great things, as overcame death it self for us) is inexpressible; but by generation, others (more to the scope of this place) understand Christs duration, or abiding, notwithstanding that he died; 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , does often signifie duration; and thus 'tis an ordinary expression with the Prophet, Isa • ah 34.10, 17. from generation to generation: now none can comprehend that eternal duration of Christ who dyes no more, Rom. 6.9. and of whose Kingdom there is no end, Luke 1.33. his generation? Christ acquired his glory by his suffering; his very exceeding great weight of glory, was indeed wrought for him by his afflictions, (as for us, 2 Cor. 4.17.) his becoming obedient unto the death, was the cause why he was so highly exalted, Phil. 2.8, 9. for his li • e is taken from the earth,

34 And the eunuch answered Philip, and said, I pray thee The modestly inquisitive man, does get understanding; this question, (God so ordering it) brings in the discourse concerning our Saviour. of whom speaketh the Prophet this? This the Eunuch might well make a question, because Isaiah himself suffered much under Manasses. of himself, or some other man?

35 Then Philip So they were said to do, when they began to speak of some weighty matter. Matth. 5.2. opened his mouth, and began at the Shewing that the Prophet in that most signal Prophecy, Isaiah 53. could not mean such things of himself, nor of Ieremy, or of any other. same scripture, and preached unto him Things in that Prophecy are applicable unto our blessed Saviour; but to none else. Jesus.

36 And as they went on their way, they came unto a This water is supposed to be a Fountain in a Town called Bethsora, or a River called Eleutherus, which in that road must needs be passed over; it being otherwise very dry▪ and water very scarce there. certain water: And the eunuch said, See, here is water Chap. 10.47., what doth hinder me Altho it was not expresly mentioned, Philip had informed this Eunuch concerning baptism, its nature, and use, which made him express such desire after it; which else he had not done. to be baptized?

37 And Philip said, Is thou believest A verbal profession is not a sufficient believing, Rom. 10.10. tho we can discern no other, yet God can, and will not be mocked; Philip in Gods name requires a faith with all the heart, and not such as Simon Magus had, who is said to believe, and be baptized, ver. 13. with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said. I This was the onely thing necessary, either then or now, if rightly understood: The Eunuch was instructed concerning God out of the Law, and was one of them that waited for his Salvation; which here he acknowledgeth to be onely found in Christ, whom he owns to be the Messiah, who made his Soul an offering for sin, Isaiah 53.10. and did bear our griefs; and carried our sorrows, ver. 4. and was wounded for our transgressions, Isaiah 53. for all these things Philip had told him, were meant of our Saviour, which he did believe were so to be understood. Mat. 16.16. 〈◊〉 6.69. 〈◊〉 11.27. Chap. 9.20. 1 John 4.15. and 5.5. believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.

38 And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both In hot Countries this was usual, to baptize by dipping the body in the water; and to this the Apostle alludes, when he tells the Corinthians, 1 Cor. 6.11. that they are washed, but God will have mercy, and not sacrifice; sprinkling being as effectual as washing, and as significative also, representing the sprinkling of the blood of the Paschal Lamb, of which we read, Exod. 12.3. which pre-signified the sprinkling the blood of Jesus, that Lamb of God which taketh away the sins of the world; and our hearts must by it be sprinkled from an evil conscience, Hebr. 10.22. It is not the more or the less of the outward Element, which makes the Sacraments effectual; but they are effectual onely as they are Gods appointmenst, and attended upon according to his will. into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him.
