39 And when they were come up out of the water, the Philip was suddenly, and extraordinarily taken away from the Eunuchs sight and company, that thereby the Eunuch might be the more assured of the truth of those things which had been taught by him. Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, that the eunuch saw him no more: and he went on his way The rejoycing was the effect of his faith; being now justified, he had peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, Romans 5.1. rejoycing.

40 But Philip was Philip was set down by the Spirit at Ashdod of the Philistines, which is called by the Septuagint Azotus; names of persons and places, do in tract of time vary. This place had been famous for the Idol Dagon, 1 Sam. 5.3 and for being a chief place of the Philistines, those enemies to Gods Church; but Christ when he comes, can cast Satan out of his strongest holds: This Azotus is accounted thirty four miles from Gaza. found at Azotus: and passing through, he preached in all the cities, till he came to Cesarea.

div.head: CHAP. IX.
div.p: ANd Chap. 8.3. Gal. 1.13. 1 Tim 1.13. Saul yet St. Luke intending a narrative of the wonderful conversion of St. Paul, lets us know what manner of person he was before his conversion, that none might despond of the grace of God, who earnestly and heartily seek it. So full of rage within, that the stream was outwardly apparent, which that inward fire had sent forth; nothing less than destruction of the Church is aimed at by its enemies; whilest Saul was one of them, he hunted after their pretious life too. breathing out threatnings and slaughter against the discipl • of the Lord, went unto the c high priest,Who did usually preside in their great Council, in which they did take cognisance of such matters; the blood of Stephen did not quench their thirst, but increased it; they would spill more still.

2 And desired of him letters to Damascus This Council, tho it sate at Ierusalem, had a power (whether commanding or recommending) over all the Synagogues within or without Iudea. to the synagogues, that if he found any This was eminently so called, being the way of God, and the way of Life, and the onely right and true way; any profession, perswasion, or manner of life, is called a way frequently in Scripture, 1 Kings 15.26. Psal. 91.11. Gr. Of the way. So Chap. 19.9, 23. of this way, whether they were It speaks their extraordinary rage, that would not spare the weaker Sex, who are generally spared on that account: men or women, he might bring them Which shews that he carried many with him to the further aggravation of his sin. bound Where they had power to judge of such things, and out of which it was impossible that a Prophet should perish, Luke 13.33. unto Jerusalem.

3 And Chap. 22.6. and 26.12. 1 Cor. 15.8. as he journeyed he came He was near to Damascus before this wonderful vision, that being struck blind he might be the sooner led thither; as also, that the miracle might be more easily and publickly known, Damascus being the chief • ity of Syria; and tho about six days journey from Ierusalem, inhabited by many Iews. near Damascus: and suddenly there shined round about him This was done at noon-day, the rather that the light which Paul saw, might appear to be beyond that which the Sun gives; and this light was a symbol of that inward light, wherewith his mind was now to be inlightned; as also of the purity of the Doctrine he was to Preach, and holiness of his Life which he was to lead, and most probably it was caused by the glorified body of Christ, which appeared unto him. a light from heaven.

4 And he Saul fell to the earth, struck with the amazing light and terrible voice of Christ; as also with the sense of the presence of God, which he knew was thus reverenced by Daniel 8.17. and 10.9. fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him The name Saul is the rather mentioned, to mind him and us of his persecuting of Christ in his members; as his name-sake had persecuted David who was a type of Christ:, Saul and 'tis ingeminated or doubled, not onely to rouze and awaken Saul; but to te ••• fie the more his love to him, and commiseration of him., Saul, why persecutest thou Christ was in Heaven, beyond Sauls rage; but Christ and his Church make but one body; thus Christ says, I was hungry and thirsty, Matth. 25.35. And in all their afflictions he is afflicted, Isaiah 63.9. but me is here emphatically spoken, as if our Saviour had minded him of his great love and mercy to him, in dying and suffering for him; and why then should he persecute him? me?

5 And he said Saul was in a great consternation and doubting, whether it was God, or an Angel., Who art thou Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus Tho he did not intend this persecution against Christ; yet our Saviour looks upon the good or evil done unto his members, as done unto himself. whom thou persecutest: Chap. 5.39. It is hard for thee to This kicking against the pricks is a proverbial speech, taken either from Oxen, or Slaves, whom they used with goads to prick on to their work, which when they kicked against, or opposed themselves to, they did not hurt the goads or pricks, but themselves; so shall all persecutors find that their mischiefs recoil upon themselves; Christ and his members shall be made more glorious by it: This metaphor is common in Scripture, Deut. 32.15. 1 Sam. 2.29. kick against The pricks Saul had kicked against, were the Sermons and Miracles of St. Stephen and others. the pricks.

6 And he trembling and astonished, said, Saul being thorowly humbled, and brought to resign himself wholly to God, makes this question, giving up himself as a white paper, for Christ to write what he would upon: He had thought he had done God good service, (as 'tis said many persecutors should think so too, Iohn 16.2.) but he is now powerfully brought off from his obstinacy in that perswasion. Lord, Luke 3.10 Chap. 2.37. and 16 30. What wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go Damascus, which was near at hand; whether Christ revealed his Gospel now unto him, or in the three days in which he remained blind in Damascus, ver. 9. is not so certain; but it is certain that he was 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , taught immediately by Christ himself, as he testifies, Gal. 1.12. and in that without any farther instruction he was baptized, ver. 17, 18. yet many things might be left for Ananias to confirm him in; and God by this sending of him to Ananias, would honour his own Ordinance, and recommend the Ministry and use of means, which are the power of God unto Salvation, Rom 1.16. and thus, tho God could have instructed Cornelius by the Angel which appeared unto him, Chap. 10.3. yet he is commanded to send for Peter, and to hear from him what he ought to do, Chap. 10.6. into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do.

7 And Dan. 10.7. the men which journeyed with him In Chap. 26.14. these men are said to be fallen to the earth as well as Saul, which they might at first be, and now rose up; or rather by standing still, here, is onely meant, they being sorely amazed, they remained in the place in which they were, without going forward: Thus the Angel forbid Lot and his family, to stay or stand in the plain, Gen. 19.17. meaning that they should hasten forward., stood speechless The greater difficulty, is to reconcile these words with Chap. 22.9. where it is expresly said, that these men did not hear the voice; but it is there added of him that spake unto Saul, so that they might hear the voice of Saul, as 'tis said in this place, and wonder whom he spake unto, or what he spake about, they not hearing the voice of him that spake unto him, as in that Chap. 22.9. it is said; and it seems very likely that they should not hear the voice of Christ, for we read not that any of them were converted; and being left in their infidelity, they were in some respects the more undeniable witnesses of a great part of that Miracle: but if it be understood of the voice of Christ in both places, then they might hear it, as 'tis said here, inarticulately, or the noise which that voice made; but not hear it articulately, or so as to understand it, as in a parallel case, Iohn 12.29. The people are said to hear the voice that spake unto Christ from Heaven, yet they heard so confusedly, as that they thought it had onely been thunder: To be sure, they that are converted, and they who are not converted by the word of God, may hear the word; but after a very different manner: they that are converted by it, onely hearing it inwardly, spiritually, effectually., hearing a voice, but These Fellow-travellers with St. Paul, are said to see no man; but the expression here imports their doing their utmost for to see him that spake: thus God made a difference, Daniel 10.7. in the vision we read of there. seeing no man.

8 And Saul arose from the earth; and when When he opened his eyes as at other times, when he did rise to see, the glorious light had so dazled him, that he could see nothing; thus Saul was, and all men are before their conversion: He had the shape of a man, and of one learned in the Law, when notwithstanding he is blind, and sees or knows nothing as he ought to know. his eyes were opened, he saw no man: but they led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus.

9 And he was Some have thought that in these three days Paul had that rapture into the third Heavens, which-he speaks of, 2 Cor. 12.2. but that seems rather to have been afterwards; God would howsoever by this humble and try him, and excite his dependance wholly upon him, and that he might value his restored sight the more. three days without sight, and neither That by fasting he might be more intent in Prayer; for fasting does prepare for Prayer, and therefore fasting and Prayer is so often put together, Matth. 17.21. Chap. 13.3. In those places they could fast longer without prejudice to their health, than amongst us, as and I might add, were more willing to fast for any Spiritual advantage, than we be. did eat nor drink.

10 ¶ And there was a certain disciple at Damascus, named He was of good repute for zeal and holiness, as appears, Chap 22.12. but whether he was one of the seventy Disciples which our Saviour sent out; Luke 10.1. as some will have, is not certain. Ananias, and to him said the Lord in a vision, Ananias. And he said Thereby shewing his willingness to be sent in Gods message, and to do as God should bid him, as Samuel to Eli, 1 Sam. 3.4., Behold, I am here, Lord.

11 And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the street, which is called straight, and enquire in the God telleth our wandrings, and knoweth our abode, and mindeth his, especially in their sorrows, which was Sauls case. house of Judas for one called Saul Chap. 21.39. and 22.3. of Tarsus: for behold He spent those three days spoken of, ver. 9. in acts of great humiliation, in which he would also not taste any food; this is revealed to Ananias, that he might not fear to go unto him; a great change, is Saul also amongst them that pray? A greater wonder than that the other Saul formerly was amongst the Prophets., he prayeth,

12 If this verse be the words of St. Luke, continuing the History, then they must be included in a parenthesis, the sense being entire without them; but they seem to be the words of the Lord continued to Ananias, telling him, how he had provided for his welcome to Saul, contrary to his expectation. And hath seen in a vision a man named Ananias, coming in, and putting his hand on him, that he might receive his sight▪

13 Then Ananias answered, Lord, I have heard by His design and commission could not be noised abroad. many of this man Ver. 1., how much evil he hath done to thy The Disciples of Christ are called Saints, because 1. They are dedicated unto the Lord in their baptism. 2. They are called unto holiness. 3. They did then live holily, and exemplarily. 4. And so must all that hope for any benefit by their being Disciples of Christ, &c. saints at Jerusalem:

14 Here Ananias shews the strength of his excuse; for flesh and blood cried in him as in Moses, Exod. 4.13. send by him whom thou wilt send. And here he hath authority from the chief priests, to bind all that call on thy name.

15 But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for Chap. 13.2. and 22.21. Rom. 1.1. Eph. 3.8. 1. Tim. 2.7. he is The whole World is Gods Fabrick, and the Church especially is his house; not onely in the whole World, but in the visible Church there are all sorts of utensils, some for higher, others for meaner uses; Saul was to be a vessel unto honour, Rom 9 21. into which the treasures of Gods word was to be put, 2 Cor. 4.7. tho he was but an earthen vessel: Paul was indeed chosen by God to Preach the Gospel, Gal. 1.15. To suffer for Christs names sake, 1 Thes. 3.3. a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name This mystery of the calling of the Gentiles began now to spread abroad, and to be made more known, which was hid in those promises, Isaiah 49.6. Ier. 1.10. before Rom. 1.5. the Gentiles, and Chap. 25.22. kings, and n the children of Israel.

16 For Chap. 21.11▪ I will shew him how great things he must He shall suffer as great things as he ever did cause, or inflict; the hatred of his own Countrey-men the Iews, and the fury of the Gentiles; see the catalogue of them, 2 Cor. 11.23. And were there ever so many sufferings heaped upon one man? and yet tho all these were foretold unto him, and certainly foreknown by him; yet he would Preach the Gospel for all that; m • ch was forgiven him, and he loved much. suffer for my names sake.

17 And Chap. 22.12. Ananias went his way, and entred The house of Iudas with whom Saul lodged, as ver. 11. into the house, and Concerning this, see Chap. 6.6. besides, on what may be said of this imposition of hands elsewhere: The curing of St. Pauls blindness, was one reason of putting his hands on him here, for so it was ordinarily done towards the sick or infirm; they laid their hands upon them to heal them, as it was promised that they should do, Mark 16.18. Chap. 8.17. putting his hands on him, said Saul was become Ananias his Brother, as professing the same faith, and heir of the same promise with him., Brother Saul, the Lord even
Ananias mentions what had hapned to Paul in the way, that Paul might be assured that he was sent from God, for none else could have told him what had happened. Jesus that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be Chap. 8.15. filled with the holy Ghost.

18 And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been As scales of Fish: It was no ordinary blindness, nor from any ordinary cause, and could not have been cured by common means. scales; and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized.

19 And when he had received meat St. Paul could not but be much weakned with his journey, fear, grief, fasting, and constant praying; and now he takes a prudent care of his health, that he might be further enabled for the service of God, to what place soever he should be appointed., he was strengthened. Then was Saul certain days Saul is no sooner changed, but he changeth his company and acquaintance; he re • orts to none of the Rabbies of the Iews, but to the Disciples of Christ; he would love any, learn of any, that had Christ for their Master. with the disciples which were at Damascus.

20 And straightway he preached Christ in the The Apostles spake unto the Iews first, either that they might convert them, or at least take away all excuse from them. synagogues, that he is Which doubtless he spake largely unto, tho it be not here expressed; but he had an abundance in his heart, having tasted the power of the grace of God in Christ, and out of his heart is mouth spake. the Son of God.

21 But all that heard him were amazed, and said This great change is a most unaccountable thing, and might truly cause amazement; but ex quovis ligno fit Mercurius, cum digitu • Dei sit statuarius, Nothing is too hard for that God in whose hand Saul's heart was., Is not this he that destroyed them which called on this name in Jerusalem, and came▪ hither for that intent, that he might bring them bound unto the chief priests?

22 But Saul increased True grace thrives by exercise and opposition: The word here used, many take to be a Metaphor from builders, who in erecting their Fabricks, fit one piece or part to another, and then bring them, and joyn them together; thus St. Paul did, in bringing forth, or quoting the promises in the Old Testament, and shewing their exactly being fulfilled in the New Testament, or in the Gospel of our Saviour Jesus Christ; and he spake with such an evidence and demonstration of the Spirit, that he did as 'twere constrain men to be of his opinion: the more in strength, and confounded the Jews which dwelt at Damascus Which was the sum of the Gospel., proving that this is very Christ.

23 ¶ And after that God would not presently expose him to conflicts, but inure him to suffer by degrees; as also it pleased God to spare him so long nigh unto, that place where he had wrought so great a miracle for him; the sense of which might the • ore be upon himself and others also, for he continued here three years, as may be seen, Gal. 1.17, 18. excepting onely a journey into Arabia. many days were fulfilled, the Jews took counsel to kill him:

24 But The Iews, who stirred up Aretas the King of Damascus against Paul, 2 Cor. 11.32, 33. now began those things foretold, ver. 16. to be fulfilled. thei • laying wait was known of Saul: And they watched the gates day and night to kill him.
25 Then the disciples took him by night, and As Rahab did the spies, Iosh. 2.15. and Michal did David, 1 Sam. 19.12. let him down by the wall in a basket.

26 And Chap. 22.17. when Saul was come to Jerusalem he assayed to To be admitted to intimate fellowship and communion with the Disciples. joyn himself to the disciples: but they were Paul was sufficiently known by name and face at Ierusalem, and many had felt his rage. all afraid of him, and But how could the Disciples be ignorant of his conversion so long, if it was three years after? as it seems by Gal. 1.17. To answer which, may be considered, 1. The great distance betwixt Ierusalem and Damascus, (six days journey) 2. The little correspondence betwixt the Kings of those places, Herod and Aretas. 3. The persecution which was at Ierusalem, might hinder the Converts of Damascus from going thither. 4. Paul might have spent a great part of the three years in his journey amongst the Arabians, of which before. believed not that he was a disciple.

27 But Of Barnabas mention is made. Chap. 4.36. who is thought to have been Pauls Fellow-Disciple under Gamaliel. Barnabas took him, and brought him These Apostles, to whom Barnabas brought Paul, were Peter and Iames, as Gal. 1.18. who being the Apostles of the circumcision, or having Iudas under their charge, were abiding at Ierusalem, whilest the other Apostles probably were absent, being founding of Churches elsewhere. to the apostles, and declared unto them how Some take these things to have been related by Paul, others by Barnabas, who testified these things concerning Paul. he had seen the Lord in the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how he had preached boldly at Damascus in the name of Jesus.

28 And Gal. 1.18. he was with them Living amongst them, and freely conversing with them; that is, with Peter, and Iames, and the rest of the believers, who had now no suspition of him. coming in, and going out at Jerusalem.

29 And he spake boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and disputed Hellenists, of which Chap. 6.1. such as were born in foreign parts, but of Iewish parents; these Paul chose rather to dispute with, because these had raised the persecution against Stephen, and Paul had furthered them in it; and he was very desirous to unweave that web, and give them an Antidote unto whom he had formerly given Poison; being especially concerned for their Souls, whom he had helped to destroy. against the Grecians: but they went about to slay him.

30 Which when the brethren knew, they brought him down to q Cesarea, and sent him forth to There were two Towns of this name, one a Coast-Town spoken of Chap. 8.40. the other was called Cesarea-Philippi, nigh Mount Lebanon.
St. Pauls birth-place, where amongst his Relations and Acquaintance, they might hope he would be safe. Tarsus.

31 When Paul was sent away, against whom they had the greater spite, as having been as zealous a persecutor as any amongst them. Then had the churches rest throughout all Judea, and Galilee, and Samaria, and were The Church is frequently compared to a building, and every believer to the Temple of God, 1 Cor. 3.16. and 6.19. which God dwells in; from whence this Metaphor is taken. edified, and Walking is a progressive motion, and so is building, an adding to a Structure till it come to perfection; which signifies, that these believers increased daily in the knowledge of God, in true Piety and Charity, &c. walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the The word also signifies the exhortation of the holy Ghost, such exhortations as were given from God by the Apostles; to be sure, the comforts of the Spirit, are not 〈◊〉 our obedience to the commandments of God; and 〈…〉 to be given here as the reason why the Churches were edified, and did thus increase; because believers walked in the fear of the Lord; and nothing perswades more effectually to the embracing of Religion, than the holy living of such as make profession of it. comfort of the holy Ghost, were multiplied.

32 ¶ And it came to pass as Peter passed Where the Disciples that were dispersed had planted Churches. thorowout all quarters, he came down also to the See ver. 13. saints which dwelt at Lydda.A little Town about the west bank of I •• dan, not far from the Mediterr • nean Sea.

33 And there he found a certain man named 'Tis supposed this Eneas was a Iew, tho now living at Lydda; and that St. Luke here names him by the name the Grecians called him by; he being amongst his own Countrey-men called Hille • . Eneas, which had kept his bed To shew the difficulty of the cure, and greatness of the Miracle. eight years, and was sick of the palsie.

34 And Peter said unto him, Eneas These words are not a prayer, (tho they were not spoken without Peters lifting up his heart to Christ in prayer) but a promise to this sick man of health and recovery, declaring from whom he • hould receive it, that he might know whom to acknowledge, and thank for it., Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and Our Saviour bids the sick of the palsie to arise, and take up his bed, Mark 2.9. and so he commands the impotent man, Iohn 5 8. Here St. Peter bids this Paralytick to make his bed; which seems more strange, being he was commanded to arise, so that now he should have no need of having his bed made, but 'tis easily answered, that being it was onely intended to shew how fully that he was cured: the making of his bed, did as mch prove both to himself and others, that he was recovered, as any thing else could do. make thy bed. And he arose immediately.

35 And all that dwelt at Verse 32. Lydda, and Saron is the name of a City, 1 Chron. 5.16. but here it is rather the name of a Countrey, (which the masculine article usually shews) lying between Mount Thabor, and the Lake of Tiberias, a very-fruitful plain, 1 Chron. 27.29. Cant. 2. To the owning of his truth. Error (if in fundamentals) keeps us from God. Saron, saw him, and turned to the Lord.

36 ¶ Now there was at A post-town, see Chap. 10.5. These circumstances of places and persons, are set down to evidence the certainty of the History. Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, according to the Syriack dialect then in use amongst the Iews, and Dorcas as • he was called among the Greeks; it being common for the same person to have two names, one Hebrew and the other Greek, as Thomas who was called Didymus, and Cephas who was called Peter. Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was She was rich in good works, which are the best riches, last longest, and go farthest. full of good works, and alms deeds which she did.

37 And it came to pass in those days, that she was sick, and died: whom when they had They washed the dead, and anointed them, to fit them for their burying, and especially to shew their hope of the Resurrection; which some think St. Paul alludes unto, 1 Cor. 15.29. washed, they laid her in an upper chamber.

38 And forasmuch as Lydda was nigh to Joppa, and the disciples had heard that Peter was there, they sent They sent for Peter, that he might come to comfort those that were concerned in the great loss of so good a woman, and it may be not without some hopes of her recovery by a Miracle from St. Peter; which is the likelier, because they so much hasten his coming to them. unto him two men, desiring him that he would not She being already dead, and they preparing for her burial. Or, be grieved. delay to come to them.

39 It was strange that Peter should be sent for, or that he should go on such an account, viz. to raise one that was dead; but God, who had ordered this Miracle for the manifestation of his truth and glory, so wrought in their hearts, that they did this out of faith; tho if others should think to imitate it, it would be but presumption. Then Peter arose and went with them. When he was come, they brought him into the upper chamber: and all the widows stood by him Here needed no mourning women to be hired; the death of this good woman was a common loss: these coats were made by Dorcas in her life time, to cloath the poor and naked with all. weeping, and shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made while she was with them.

40 But Peter Peter put them out, that he might pray the more earnestly, without distraction, or interruption; thus Elisha shut the door to him, 2 Kings 4.33 when he prayed for the Shunamites Son. put them all forth, and This his kneeling is mentioned, to recommend reverence in our praying unto God. kneeled down Peter by his betaking himself unto Prayer, would shew, that he could do nothing by his own power, but it must co • e from above; and he had every mercy, as much preca • iously, and by prayer, as any other. and prayed, and turning him to the body, said, Tabitha, arise. And she opened her eyes: and when she saw Peter, she sat up.

41 And he gave her his hand, and lift her up; and when he had called Such who had sent for him, and now were gathered together, to see what effects his prayers might have. the saints and widows, presented And in perfect health, as all were that were miraculously cured; for the Lords works are perfect. Deut. 32.4. her alive.

42 And it was known throughout all Joppa; and This cure was wrought, and all the other Miracles were done, to be a means to make the Gospel to be believed, which he published, and was an undeniable proof, that this Doctrine was from Heaven; for none could do such things, unless God were with him, or rather unless God did them by him; So that this Miracle wrought by St. Peter, did more good to the Souls of many, than to the body of this relieved woman. many believed in the Lord.

43 And it came to pass, that he tarried The Miracle had onely prepared them to receive his Doctrine, which Peter tarried some time with them, to instruct them in: The Miracle had prepared the ground, and now he takes this season to sow the seed of the word into it. many days in Joppa with one Simon a tanner.

div.head: CHAP. X.
div.p: THere was a cert • in man in In Cesarea Palestine, as it was call'd in contra-distinction to Cesarea-Philippi. Cesarea, called A Roman by his name; which name was ordinarily to be found amongst the families of the Scipio's, and Sylla's. Cornelius, a centurion of the band A Band, answers either to a Regiment amongst us, or to a Legion amongst the Romans; (this latter was far greater than the former) It was called the Italian Band, as being composed of Italian Soldiers, and might be used as a guard of the Proconsul, who dwelt at Cesarea; who was that Felix we read of, Chap. 23.24. called the Italian band ▪

2 A This Cornelius was a Proselite of the gate, or such as observed the seven precepts of Noah and lived without giving any offence to the Iews. devout man, and one that feared God It was a very good sign that he feared God, in that he ingaged all his house to do the like, at least outwardly, which was as much as he could do; this was spoken by God in Abrahams commendation, Gen. 18.19. with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God He did not neglect the seasons of prayer, especially the time of offering the morning and evening Sacrifice; which by prayer they desired to partake the benefit of, by which Christ our Sacrifice, and his merits were figured unto them; Cornelius indeed prayed always, or at all times, taking time in a moral sense, for the seasons and opportunities for such a duty; (as we are commanded to give always thanks, Eph. 5.20) but he could not pray always, or at all times, taking time in a natural sense; for then he must have neglected all other duties; howsoever, his indeavour was to keep his heart always in a praying disposition. alway.

3 He saw in a Not in a dream or rapture, but sensibly and plainly. vision evidently, about Their ninth hour, was with us about three a clock in the afternoon, being the ordinary time for the evening Sacrifice; and by consequence their time of prayer, Chap. 3.1. And this devout man doth not seek Gods face in vain; Cornelius had been faithful in a little, and God would give him much, rather than he should want further instruction, who had improved what he had already; God here sends an Angel, and soon after an Apostle unto him. the ninth hour of the day, an angel of God coming in to him, and saying unto him, Cornelius.

4 And when he looked on him, he was The Angel appeared in so great splendor; all admiration hath some fear with it. afraid, and said This is equivolent to What wilt thou have me to do? And shews that Cornelius was prepared to hear the message., What is it Lord? And he said unto him, Thy prayers Prayer and alms are joyned together in our Saviours discourse concerning them, Matth. 6.1, &c. in the Apostles order about them, 1 Cor. 16.1. Alms are our Sacrifices now under the Gospel, Phil. 4.18. Hebr. 13.16. and thine alms are come up for a An allusion to the offering up of incense under the Law; the smoak of the incense did ascend, and so David desires that his prayers might ascend to Godward, Psal. 141.2. thus under the Gospel, prayers are resembled to incense, Rev. 8.3. That prayers are said to come up for a memorial, is but the pursuance of the same Metaphor; for Lev. 2.2. the frankincense, &c. was the memorial there commanded to be burned; and all this onely to represent unto us, how well-pleasing the prayers of his people are unto God through Christ, and that God keeps in remembrance all those things they thus desire of him, and in his time and measure (which are the best circumstances, bestowes all upon them; but let not prayers and alms, which God here hath put together, be put asunder, and in due time we shall reap. memorial before God.

5 And now send men to A Town that was memorable for Ionahs taking shipping there, when he would flee from God, and decline his message, Ionah 1.3. Joppa, and call for one The Angel could have declared the Gospel, and instructed Cornelius; but he sends him to Peter, God being willing for to honour the means of his own institution. Simon, whose surname is Peter:

6 He lodgeth with one These particulars, when found true by Cornelius, did very much advantage him towards his believing what Peter in the name of the Lord did tell him. Simon a tanner, whose house is by the sea-side: He shall tell thee what thou oughtest to do.

7 And when the angel which spake unto Cornelius▪ was departed, he called two of his These Servants doubtless Cornelius had instructed, as appears ver. 2. and God blesses him with faithful and successful service from them. houshold-servants, and a No condition, or temptation, too hard for the grace of God to overcome; both Centurion and Soldier, are willing to hazard all they had, rather than not to obey God, and come to the knowledge of Jesus Christ. devout souldier of them that This Soldier for his Religion's sake, and his holy life, was taken into nearer attendance on Cornelius; 'tis no small matter to have one near us, that hath power with God. waited on him continually.

8 And Thus on Cornelius's side, all things are disposed towards his receiving of the Gospel; and the same providence at the same time, disposes all things on Peters part towards his coming to publish it: for when he had declared all these things unto them, he sent them to Joppa.

9 ¶ On the morrow as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up These houses were flat on the tops, and therefore they were commanded to make battlements for them, Deut. 22.8. Peter went on the house-top to pray, that he might from thence view the Temple, which was a type of Christ, through whom onely, we and our prayers can be acceptable unto God; hence 1 Kings 8.30, &c. there is so often mention made of praying towards the City, and towards the place which God should chuse; this Daniel practised, tho upon the hazard of his life, when both City and Temple were ruined, Dan. 6.10. upon the house-top to pray, about the The sixth hour with them is high-noon, or mid-day, and is accounted one of the three times of prayer, (see Chap. 3.1.) and was as the Iews say, recommended to them by Isaac; howsoever it was the time when they might begin to prepare the evening-Sacrifice; none of these causes need to be assigned, for doubtless this blessed Apostle did watch unto prayer, 1 Pet. 4.7. and desirously laid hold upon all opportunities to pour out his Soul unto God. sixth hour.

10 And he became He might be more than ordinarily an hungred; to fit or suit the vision, which is hereafter mentioned. very hungry, and would have eaten: but while they made ready, he The most excellent way of Gods manifesting himself unto man, is by a trance: (and they reckon seven ways, in which God makes himself known unto man) but what this trance was, is diversly expressed: 'tis certain, that in it the Soul was as it were absent from the Body, drawn off from the perception of earthly and sensible things, and enabled unto the perception of Heavenly Mysteries; in such an extasie was St. Paul, 2 Cor. 12.2. and St, Iohn, Rev. 1.10. who is therefore said to be in the spirit. fell into a trance,

11 Either visibly to his corporal eyes, as to St. Stephens; or rather mentally, more suitably to the rapture mentioned in the former verse. And saw heaven Which might signifie, that Heaven that was shut to the children of men by the first Adam, was now by Christ the second Adam, opened to all believers. opened, and a certain This word is taken for any utensil, commonly used about the house; and with the sheet here spoken of, bears an Analogy to a Table, and Table-cloath amongst us: vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet So gathered up or knit, that the Vyands, verse 12. might not fall down. And this Cornelius saw to come from Heaven, to shew the liberty of taking him, and other Gentiles into the Churrh, • id come from thence onely., knit at the four corners, and let down to the earth:

12 Wherein were all manner of four-footed beasts of the earth, and As well unclean beasts, such as were forbidden by the Law; as clean, such as by the Law might be eaten. wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.

13 And there came a voice to him, Rise, Peter; Of that thou seest, without any exception, whether they be clean, or (formerly) unclean creatures: The moral of which command is, that he might now converse with Iews and Gentiles indifferently, and Preach unto these also the word of Life. kill, and eat.

14 But Peter said, Not so, Lord Lev. 11 4. Deut. 14.7.; for I have never eaten any thing that is These words may signifie one and the same thing, and the latter explain the former; shewing that those things are said to be common, which the Law by forbidding them, had made unclean: Others make some difference; and by things common, understand all sorts of creatures, which were forbidden to the Iews, but were commonly fed upon by all Nations round about them: and by things unclean, they understand such as by accident became so, as when any of the creatures permitted for use, was strangl • d. common or unclean.

15 And the voice spake unto him again the second time Mat. 15.11. Rom. 14.17, 20. 1 Tim. 4.4. Tit. 1.15., What God hath cleansed, that Do not make in thy esteem, or practice, as common: call not thou that is, polluted: The Iews did imagine, that by unclean creatures, were meant the Gentiles, (as by clean creatures they would have themselves to be understood) howsoever they opposed Common unto Holy; indeed a holy man is (as they called him) a singular man: 'twas God that cleansed Cornelius, turning him from Idolatry, to the worship of the true God, from darkness unto light. common.

16 This was done Whereby this great mystery of the conversion of the Gentiles, and taking them into the Church might be the more confirmed, and fixed in St. Peters mind. thrice: and the vessel was received up again into heaven.

17 Now while Peter Recollecting himself; for the vision had so affected him, that it had put him into a kind of extasy, out of which when he came unto himself, doubted in himself what this vision which he had seen, should mean; behold the two servants and the Soldier which Cornelius had sent,, the men which were sent from Cornelius, had made enquiry for Simons house, and stood before the gate,
18 And Being strangers, they address themselves to such of the house as came to the door. called, and asked whether Simon which was surnamed Peter, were lodged there.

19 ¶ While Peter Set himself to meditate upon that he had seen, • and heard. thought on the vision, the The holy Spirit informs him further. Thus whosoever meditates carefully upon what he hears from Gods word, God will never leave him without sufficient instruction. spirit said unto him, Behold, three men seek thee.

20 Immediately put thy self upon th • journey. Chap. 14. ••
▪ Arise therefore, and get thee down, and go with them Spend no time in disputing within thy self, because that they, unto whom thou art sent for, are not Iews. , doubting nothing: for I have sent them.

21 Then Peter went down to the men which were sent unto him from Cornelius; and said, Behold,
I am 〈◊〉 whom ye seek: Peter being in no small consternation, and not perfectly knowing whither all this tended, makes the more exact enquiry. what is the cause wherefore ye are come?

22 And they said, Cornelius the centurion That they might speed in their message, they labour to prevent all prejudice Peter might have against Cornelius, who was a Gentile by title; telling him, 1. That he was a just man, (as is said of Ioseph, Matth. 1.19.) 2. That he, a just man, and one that worshipped the true God, the same with the Iews, and not the false gods of the Gentiles. 3. That he was reputed a pious and good man, and so it would be no disparagement to the Apostles to go unto him. feareth God, and of good report among all the nation of the Jews, was This argument St. Peter could not deny, When Gods command is evident his people are determined, and resolved. warned from God by an holy angel, to send for thee into his house, and to hear words of thee.

23 Then called he them in, and lodged them. And He delays not to obey the Heavenly vision; but as Abraham took his journey the very next morning after that he had received the command, Gen. 22.3. so did Peter here, and bis dat, qui cito dat, he doubles his obedience, that obeys speedily and chearfully. on the morrow Peter went away with them, and certain These Brethren were six in number, as Chap. 11.12. who might undertake this journey, 1. Out of respect to Peter, to accompany him. 2. Being moved at the extraordinary visions that were spoken of; but especially, 3. disposed by the Providence of God to accompany St. Peter, that they might testifie the grace of God that was come unto the Gentiles, when it might be afterwards questioned. brethren from Joppa accompanied him.

24 And Ioppa was about fifteen Leagues from Cesarea, so that the next day after they set out, they might easily come from Ioppa thither. the morrow after they entred into Cesarea: And Cornelius waited for them, and had called together his His Relations. kinsmen and And such as he had the greatest love and kindness for, he thought that he could not express it better, than by giving them an oppportunity to hear the word of Life, and to gain instruction for their Souls; and probably, those here spoken of, were reckoned as friends, and near friends by Cornelius; because they were such as with him had forsaken all Pagan-Idolatry, and were worshippers of the true and Living God. near friends.

25 And as Peter Into Cornelius his house, for he hastned to meet with him. was coming in, Cornelius met him, and fell down at his feet, and Cornelius worshipped with the most humble, civil worship; but he could not think him to be God, and therefore he did give him no Divine worship, he having forsaken the Idolatry of the Gentiles; but might perhaps think him to have been an Angel, and intended to worship him accordingly, for which he is blamed in the following verse. worshipped him.

26 But Peter took him up, saying It is certain that Peter did think this worship Cornelius gave him, to have exceeded; and here he blames him for it; telling him, he Chap. 14.14. Rev. 19.10. and 22.9., Stand up; I my self also was but a man like unto him, and he needed not give any further reason of his reproof, for man must adore, but by no means may be adored; no, nor take too much honour unto hims •• f. am a man.

27 And as he They went talking together into the house; probably, of the goodness of God that they should be directed so happily unto one another; for they could not but see, and acknowledge God in it. talked with him, he went in, and found many that were come together.

28 And he said unto them, Ye know how John 4.9. and 18.28. that it is an unlawful thing for a man▪ that is a Jew God himself did erect a partition-wall betwixt his people, and other Nations, Iews and Gentiles; hence by Gods own command, the Iews might not have any familiar converse with the Gentiles, especially, they might not marry with them: The Iews themselves had made this partition-wall much larger, and they held it unlawful to eat with any of the Gentiles, or to go so much as into their houses; hence that objection made upon this occasion against St. Peter, Chap. 11.3., to keep company with, or come unto one of another nation Chap. 15.9. Eph. 3.6.: but▪ God hath shewed me, that I should not call any man common or No man is now unclean by any ceremonial uncleanness, because he is not circumcised, or because he is not sprinkled with the blood of bulls, Hebr. 9.13. yet sin hath defiled the whole mass of man kind, and they are equally by nature morally unclean. unclean.

29 Therefore came I unto you without Or delay. gain-saying, assoon as I was sent for Peter did in a great measure know the business he came about, partly by the vision, and its interpretation; partly, by what he might have heard from them, that Cornelius sent for him, unto whom Cornelius had declared the whole matter, as we find verse 8. yet Peters question is but necessary, for to give Cornelius an opportunity to acquaint his friends, who were met there, with all that had passed.: I ask therefore, for what intent ye have sent for me?

30 And Cornelius said Cornelius does not intend to declare by this, how long he had fasted; but he tells him, when he being fasting▪ saw the vision, which was four days before; at the same time of the day., Four days ago I was fasting until this hour, and at The ninth hour, which was a time of prayer, it being the time of offering the evening-Sacrifice, see Chap. 3.1. the ninth hour I prayed in my house, and behold, a A man in appear •• ce, but an Angel indeed, as in the 3. verse. man stood before me in Why Ang •• appeared in bright or white raiment. See Chap. 1.10. Mat. 28.3. Mark 16.5. Luke 24.4. bright clothing.

31 And said, Cornelius, thy prayer is heard, and thine Of which, see the 4. verse. alms are had in remembrance Unto which, not onely the outward gift, but the inward affection is visible; and this is peculiarly in the sight of God, the other may be seen also by men. in the sight of God

32 The substance of this verse, is in the fift and sixth verses before-going; Cornelius might say this to excuse his sending for Peter, being a stranger to him; as also to encourage Peter to speak in such a matter, as God had appeared in. Send therefore to Joppa, and call hither Simon whose surname is Peter; He is lodged in the house of one Simon a tanner, by the sea-side; Who, when he cometh, shall speak unto thee,

33 As an hungry Soul delays not to send for food, assoon as he knows where to have it. Immediately therefore I sent to thee; and thou hast Which does not onely approve of St. Peters coming; but thank him for it. well done that thou art come. Now therefore are we all here present We will set our selves to attend to thy words, as if we saw God looking upon us; whom we call to witness that we are ready to do whatsoever he shall require of us: Thus it becomes every one that would profit by the word of God, to attend upon it; men do not behave themselves as before God, and therefore they injoy nothing less than God in an Ordinance, and are as if God had taken no notice of them. before God, to hear all things that are commanded thee of God.

34 ¶ Then Peter An expression used (as formerly) in matters of great moment, as Matth. 5.2. opened his mouth, and said, Job 30.19. Gal. 2.6. Eph. 6.9. Col. 3.25. Of a truth I perceive that God is no God does not accept of one because he is a Iew, and respect another because he is a Gentile; tho St. Paul being prejudiced by his Education, had been carryed along with that error of the Iews; against which notwithstanding, God had declared himself even unto them, Deut. 10.17. which is also confirmed unto us in the New Testament, Rom. 2.11. 1 Pet. 1.17. so that our being of any Nation, or any condition, rich or poor, honoured or despised; as the one side recommends us not unto God; and on the other side, it will not hinder us from being accepted with the Lord. respecter of persons:

35 But in Even tho Romans ▪ or Italians ▪ of which Nation Cornelius was, and might probably be worse thought of by the Iews, because they supposed themselves to have been hardly used by them. every nation he that These two particulars include the observation of both Tables of the Law: The fearing of God comprehends piety, that is, the true worship of the true God; and working righteousness, includes all the duties to our neighbour; and both describe a truely good, and holy man, such as Cornelius was; unto whose case this is to be applied. feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.

36 The word of reconciliation betwixt God and man, not onely betwixt God and the Iews, but betwixt him and the Gentiles also; he had sent unto Israel by his Prophets formerly, Isaiah 57.19. God is said to create peace to him that is afar off; the Gentile, as well as to him that is near, the Iew, Psal. 72.7, 8. Isaiah 49.6. and that Salvation was not limited to the Iews onely, might be known unto them by the e •• mples of Melchisedech, Iob, and Naaman, who did no ways belong unto them; but this was now more manifest: God Preaching this peace betwixt himself, and all Nations indifferently by Christ, 1. In his own person Preaching this, Matth. 8.11, 12. and telling them that by his death he would draw all men unto him, Iohn 12.32. 2dly. This peace is Preached to be had by Christ, or onely through Christ; by the Angels themselves, Luke 2.14. And 3dly, by all the Apostles and Ministers of the Gospel, Eph. 2.13, 14. speaking to the Gentiles, St. Paul says, Ye who were afar off, are made nigh by the blood of Christ; and it was their constant Doctrine, that there was no name under Heaven by which men could be saved, but the name of Christ, Chap 4.12. and that it was all one whether they were Greeks or Iews, &c. but Christ is all, and in all, Colos. 3.11. so that in this Doctrine, there is an exact harmony betwixt the Old and Ne • Testament, the Prophets, and the Apostles. The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace Christ is Lord, not of the Iews or one people onely; but of the Gentiles, all Nations also, as Mat. 28.19, 20. Rom. 3.29. by Jesus Christ He is Lord of all.

37 They had heard of the Doctrine of the Gospel by common fame and report, (which could not but spread abroad) all might know that Christ and his Apostles did Preach, tho these might be ignorant of the particular Doctrines which they taught, and which Peter was now sent to instruct them in; or by the word, (in an usual hebraism) the matter of the Gospel may be meaned, as the Life, Death, and Resurrection of our blessed Saviour, which they could not but have heard several reports of: The word I say you know, which was published throughout all Judea, and Luke 4.14. began from Galilee Who, as the Elijah which was promised, Malachi 4.5. was the forerunner of the Lord., after the baptism which John preached.

38 How God It was usual to anoint their Kings, Priests, and Prophets, unto all which Offices Christ was anointed by his Father; hence called Christ, as in the Old Testament the Messiah. anointed Jesus The Apostle is not ashamed of this name, tho given to our Saviour by way of contempt; he gloried in the cross of Christ. of Nazareth with Christ was indued with the Almighty Spirit of God, and with the power of it. the holy Ghost, and with power, who went about All the miracles our blessed Saviour wrought, were works of mercy, for the benefit and relief of those upon whom he wrought them; he could have wrought miracles to destroy and ruine such as would not believe in him, which he was often provoked unto; (nay, his Apostles would have had him but to permit them by fire from Heaven to destroy the Samaritans, Luke 9.54. and he would no • .) doing good, and healing all The deliverances our Saviour so often wrought upon such as were possessed of Devils, was to shew unto them that he was come to destroy the works of the Devil, and to cast him out of the Souls of men, who were Spiritually possessed by him, which also our Saviour did, so that it was a happy calamity for them, which brought them to Christ. that were oppressed of the devil: God was with our Saviour, 1. By his might and Power doing such miracles. 2. In his extraordinary love to him, Matth. 3.17. and always hearing of him, Iohn 11.42. and also, 3. God was with Christ, 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , in the fulness of the Godhead, Colos. 2.11. for God was with him.

39 And we are The Apostles, whom Christ had chosen to go in and out with him, and to be eye and ear-witnesses of all that was done by him, or against him. witnesses of all things which he did both in the land of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; Their killing of our Saviour, is the rather here spoken of, to shew how rightfully the Iews were now to be forsaken, and that they had no cause to complain of the calling in of the Gentiles, being themselves had in such a manner rejected Christ; but especially, that they who were here met, and we, all might consider, how much it cost our blessed Saviour to deliver us from sin, and hell, Gal. 3.13. He was mad •
〈…〉 for us, as Deut. 21.23. that the blessing of Abraham might come upon us, Gal. 3.14. whom they slew and hanged on a tree:

40 Him Lest these Gentiles be deterred from believing in Christ, and take offence at his Cross: St. Peter Preached unto them the Resurrection, which suddenly and powerfully followed. God raised up the third day, and And this he tells them was unquestionable, as appeared by all the ways that any thing can be proved by; Christ was seen, and heard, and felt after his Resurrection, as the beloved Disciple tells us, 1 Iohn 1.1. and manifested his victory over death for us. shewed him openly.

41 Christ after his Resurrection appeared not to the wicked Iews; for being to suffer no more, his enemies were not vouchsafed a sight of him; and thus he did not manifest himself unto the world, Iohn 14.22. Not to all the people, but unto These witnesses were the Apostles, who were chosen by God himself immediately; and the vacancy supplied by lot, which was at Gods direction, Chap. 1.24, 26. The metaphor here used is taken from the ordinary way then in use of chusing men into offices, which is here alluded to. witnesses, chosen before of God, even to us, who did eat Tho in the Gospel-History, we do not read that our Saviour drank after he rose again; yet it is sufficiently implied, being he did eat, and make a meal with his Disciples, Luke 24 30, 42, 43. Iohn 21.12. and eating is put in Scripture for the whole refection, Mat. 15.2. compared with Luke 7.36. and drink with him after he rose from the dead.

42 And he Our Saviour gave this charge to his Apostles before his Ascension, Matth. 28.19. Mark 16.15. Luke 24.27. and foretold that they should execute this his charge, Chap. 1.8. commanded us to preach unto the people, and to testifie that it is Chap. 17.31. he which was ordained of God to be That God hath ordained to judge the world by Jesus Christ, Scripture abundantly testifies, Iohn 5.26, 27. 2 Tim. 4.1. 1 Peter 4.5. And this is here spoken of the Apostle, and was given in charge by our Saviour to be principally Preached of by them all, because the Resurrection of Christ, and the glory of his Kingdom in this world, is clouded by the blindness and hardness of men: as also, because it is of the greatest concernment unto all, that at any time hear the word of God, to be perswaded of this, that Christ, whose Gospel and word they hear, will judge them according unto it. the judge of Such as shall be alive at the coming of our Lord to Judgment, 1 Thes. 4.15. quick and dead.

43 Jer. 31.34. Micah 7.18. To him This our Saviour had told his Apostles, which St. Peter here Preaches to his Auditors: It was included in the very first promise recorded by Moses, Gen. 3.15. The seed of the woman shall break the serpents head; and so continued through all ages of the Church, to be manifest in such degrees as it pleased the wisdm of God to make it known; 'tis certain that all the ceremonial Law concerning Sacrifices, did testifie this very thing; for by it, it did appear, that without shedding of blood there was no remission of sin, as Heb. 9.22. and 'tis manifest by the light of nature, that the blood of bulls and goats, could not take away sins, as Heb. 10.4. give all the Prophets witness, that through b his name whosoever believeth in him, shall receive remission of sins.But through Christs name, for his sake, and by vertue of his merit, who died for our sins, and rose again for our Iustification, Rom. 4.25. We shall receive remission of sins, Heb. 9.13, 14.

44 While That God might mirac • lously shew his approbation of what Peter had said, and to assure Peter of the real Conversion of these Gentiles, which all the Iews did make such a difficulty to believe. Peter yet spake these words Such fiery tongues in a visible shape, as had appeared unto the Apostles, Chap. 2.3. whereby the inward powerful effects of the Spirit upon their hearts, was signified what wonderful effects had this shortSermon? And doubtless, were practisers but as sincere, and hearers as intent, now a days, as then, we should find that the hand of the Lord is not shortned., the Chap. 4.31. and 8.15, 16. holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word.

45 And Such as were not onely themselves circumcised, but born of circumcised parents, who are thus called, Gal. 2.12. they of the circumcision which believed, were astonished, as many as came with Peter, because These not minding▪ or understanding the many predictions of the calling of the Gentiles, thought that Christ was onely promised unto the Iews; and were amazed to see now such an Argument as might convince them to the contrary. that on the Gentiles also was poured out the gift of the holy Ghost.Pouring out, speaks the abundant measure in which the Holy Ghost was given unto them.

46 For they heard them speak with With variety of Languages, or strange Tongues, as in the day of Pentecost, Chap. 2.6. tongues, and magnifie God. Then An ordinary Hebraism for speaking, tho the first part of any Discourse. And Peter knowing that this miraculous Fiery▪ Tongues did shew, that these Men did partake of the same Spirit from whom the Apostles had received them, he makes an inference from thence. answered Peter,

47 This question, as Chap. 8.36. is without question, and denies that any can forbid Water, that is in order to Baptize such as these. As if the Apostle had argued thus▪ They that have the Grace signified or promised, have a right unto the Seal of the promise: But these Gentiles have the Grace • ignified or promised in Baptism; they had the inward part, and therefore the outward part could not be denied unto them. He that hath the Inheritance, may claim the Writings, Wax, and Parchmtnt that belong unto it. Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we?

48 And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. Then prayed That is, in the Name of our Saviour. But this does not imply, but that they were Baptized according to our Saviours prescription, Matth. 28.19. but the Iews by their Baptism, they were become the Lords, (and had given up their names to Iesus Christ) under which Title the Lord, not only our Saviour, but the Father who Anointed him, and the Spirit by whom he was Anointed, is to be understood.
Cornelius and the rest of his Friends, which he caused to be present. At their entreaty Peter and others that came with him (as Acts 11.3.) tarried there, that they might further instruct, confirm, and comfort them: (as the best have ever need to learn, and to grow in Grace and Knowledge) and by this Peter shewed that he looked upon himself and others as not bound to observe those Precepts (of the Wise Men, as they called them) forbidding them all familiarity with the Uncircumcised. they him to tarry n certain days.

div.head: CHAP. XI▪
div.p: AND the apostles The rest of the Believers, who had not only one God to their Father, but one Church to their Mother, and were born of the same Spirit, and were fed by the same Milk of the Word of God., and brethren that were in Judea, heard that the This was a most incredible thing unto them who were of the Seed of Abraham according to the Flesh, and were not acquainted with that Mystery that Abraham should have a Seed of his Faith, upon whom all the Promises were entailed. These looked upon the Gentiles as most execrable persons, such as the Apostle describes Ephes. 2.12. that had no hope, and were without God, and therefore no less than a Miracle, and that well attested, as this was, could make them change their Opinion. Gentiles also had received the word of God.

2 And when Peter was come up to Jerusalem They were such Iews as conversed with them of the Church, and argued against them for taking in the Gentiles into any fellowship with them. But it may be that the believing Iews might for a time be very weak, and offended at it, until they were further satisfied by the following Relation of St. Peter. , they Chap. 10 45. that were of the circumcision Till then they disputed and brought what Arguments they could against it. contended with him,

3 This is the Objection they make against Peter, That contrary to the Tradition of their Elders, and Precept of their Wise Men, he had familiarly conversed with the Gentiles. See Chap. 10 28. this they look upon as Piacular, although no conversation in order to the gaining of the Gentiles unto God, was ever forbidden; but only such as might withdraw the Iews from God. Saying, Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them.

4 But Peter This great Apostle condescends to the least and weakest amongst them, and gives an Account of what he had done, and the Reasons that moved him unto it, if by any means he might gain some, and confirm others. rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order unto them, saying,

5 Chap. 10.9, &c. I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, A certain vessel descend, as it had been a great sheet, let down from heaven by four corners, and it To shew that he was especially concerned in this Vision, it being for his instruction and regulation. came even to me.See this whole Narration spoken to in the foregoing Chapter.

6 Upon the which when I had It speaking his great intention of mind upon it; God so ordering of it, that it might leave the greater impression upon him. fastened mine eyes, I considered, and saw four footed beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.
7 And I heatd a voice saying unto me, Arise, Peter, slay, and eat.He might now use them without any distinction indifferently.

8 But I said, Not so, Lord: for nothing St. Peter here avoucheth, that he had lived in this ceremonial Righteousness, tho he thought himself far from being justified thereby. common or unclean hath at any time He abstained from all the appearances of that Evil. entred into my mouth.

9 But the voice answered me This is twice spoken to St. Peter, that it might be the more unquestionable with him and others: it seeming otherwise very strange; and it may be therefore twice by St. Luke recorded. again from heaven, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.

10 And this was done For the same reason but now mentioned, That God might more abundantly manifest this Mystery of the calling in of the Gentiles, which had been so long hid. three times: and all were drawn up again All this was from Heaven; unto which also it tended, namely, to bring the Gentiles thither. into heaven.

11 And behold, immediately there were So many sent: and such a Journy willingly undertaken, for to gain Instruction in the way of Life. three men already come unto the house where I was, sent from Cesarea, unto me.

12 And Chap. 1 • .19. & 15.7. the Spirit bade me go with them, nothing doubting: Moreover, these Whom they might hear testifie in the same thing, that in the mouths of so many it might be established. six brethren accompanied me, and we entred This Man meant, is Cornelius, concerning the entry into his House, and converse with him, the doubt or controversie was that he was now speaking to. into the mans house:

13 And he shewed us how he had seen an Who by reason of his appearing a Man, is in Chap. 10.30. called a Man. angel in his house, which stood and said unto him, Send men to Joppa, and call for Simon, whose surname is Peter:

14 Who shall tell thee God promises that upon his obedience to this Oracle, in sending for Peter, he should tell him those things that were necessary to be known. words, whereby thou, and all thy house shall be saved.By him and his whole Family unto their Salvation. Whatsoever was formerly the case of such as obeyed the Precepts of Noah (as they were called) after Christ is come, and Preached unto the World, there is no other way unto Salvation, but through him.

15 And as I Whilst Peter was speaking, as Chap 1.1. began to speak, the Holy Ghost fell on them the Holy Ghost fell on them, as in the day of Pentecost, Chap. 2.4. he had fallen on the Apostles, either visibly by Fiery Cloven Tongue; or rather by extraordinarily enduing them with the Gift of Tongues; enabling the most illiterate amongst them to speak in any Language, needful for any to understand, towards their Salvation., as on us at the beginning.

16 Then remembred I the word Of Christ, who is every where so called. of the Lord, how that But these words seem rather spoken by St. Iohn himself, Matth. 3.11. Mark 1.8. which makes no difference. For, First, Whatsoever a Disciple of Christ says in his Name, it is as if it were spoken by himself. He that heareth you, heareth me. But, Secondly, Tho this was spoken by the Baptist, it was spoken by our Saviour also, Chap. 1.5. he said, John 1.26. John indeed baptized By which the great difference is implied betwixt outward Baptism (Administred by whomsoever, tho the Baptist himself) and the inward Baptism of the Holy Ghost; which, as Fire, separates powerfully the skum and dross of sin from us. with water; but Isa. 44 3. Joel 2.38. & 3.18. be shall ye baptized The extraordinary Gifts of the Spirit. with the Holy Ghost.

17 The Apostles Argument is cogent: They who have the Grace signified by Baptism, ought to have the Seal of that Grace; but the Gentiles had the Grace signified by Baptism. Or they who have the inward Baptism, may not he denied the outward. As he that hath a right to an Inheritance, cannot without Injustice be denied the Writings and Seals thereunto belonging. Forasmuch then as God gave them the like gift as he did unto us, who believed on the Lord Jesus Christ, what was I that I could withstand God?To deny Baptism unto any, unto whom it doth belong, is to withstand God, and to keep back the Token of Gods Love from such unto whom it is sent.

18 When they heard these things, they They were fully satisfied with the reason St. Peter had given them of his admitting the Gentiles unto Baptism, and fellowship with him. Wisely inferring from what Peter had said, That it was of God, what he had done, who was to be acknowledged in it. held their peace, and glorified God, saying, Then hath Repentance is the Gift of God, as well as Faith, or any other Grace, 2 Tim 2.25. nor can the greatest guilt affect the heart with true godly sorrow, until God hath quickned it. God also unto the Gentiles granted repentance It is called Repentance unto life, because God hath appointed that it should precede our entrance into life. unto life.

19 ¶ Chap. 8.1. Now they which were So true hath it been from the beginning of the Gospel, that sanguis martyrum est semen Ecclesiae. St. Stephens death, and the persecution upon it, was a great means of disseminating the Gospel. Thus all things work for good. scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen, travelled as far as The Country about Tyre. Phenice, and An Island in the Mediterranean Sea. Cyprus, and The Metropolis of Syria. This explains what was briefly said, Chap. 8.4. and shew'd what places the Disciples were scattered into, and Preached in. They preached to the Iews only because they were not yet persuaded of the calling of the Gentiles; God suffering them to be enlightned by degrees. Antioch, preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only.

20 And some of them were They were such as were born in Cyprus and Cyrene, but had their habitation in Ierusalem; and now upon the Persecution there, fled unto Antiock. men of Cyprus, and Cyrene, which when they were come to Which by this means in time became the Ierusalem of the Gentile-Christians, whither their greatest resort was. Antioch, spake unto the Here they of the dispersion taught not only such Hellenists as are spoken of, Chap. 6.1. who were born of Hebrew Parents, tho living out of the Country of Iudea; but such also amongst the Gentiles (who are generally called Greeks since Alexander's time, who conquered all those Nations round about, and brought in his own Language amongst them) who forsaking Idolatry, and worshipping the True God, were called 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , Devout or Religious persons, such as Cornelius is said to be, Chap. 10.2. And thus God by degrees brought in the knowledg of himself, and his Son Jesus Christ. Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus.Which knowledg only is that which is necessary unto Salvation; and that only which Saul determined to know, 1 Cor. 2.2.

21 And Chap. 2.47. the The Power, Assistance, and Working of God expressed by the Hand; which is the Organ or Instrument Men use in Working. This Hand, or Work of God was manifest: First, In the Miracles which they wrought. Secondly▪ In the Conversion of any by these Miracles. For these alone cannot soften a heart; as appeared in Pharaoh, whose heart was hardened by them. hand of the Lord was with them: and Faith and Conversion are wrought by the Hand of the Lord, and are his Work. But in vain is Faith pretended unto, when there is no change in Heart and Life. What God hath put together, none may put asunder. a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord.

22 ¶ Then tidings of these things came This Pleonasm seems emphatical, to shew with what readiness and delight the Church heard the news of the Conversion of so many to Christ. unto the ears of the church which was in Jerusalem: and they sent forth Of Barnabas we read, Chap. 4.36. who had given such an earnest of Love to God, and true Faith in Christ, for whose sake he sold what he had. Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch▪

23 Who, when he came, and had seen the Which appeared in their Conversion, being made manifest by their professions; and answered by their Pious lives and Conversations. For all which they might cry Grace, Grace. By the Grace of God is also to be understood the encreasing of the Church, and adding to it such as should be saved. grace of God, was This is matter of Joy in Heaven, Luke 15.7. and of all such as are learning their Lesson, and preparing for that Blissful place. glad, and Chap. 13.43. & 14.22. exhorted them all, that with Firm and fix'd resolution, That come what can come, tribulation or distress, life or death, they would keep close▪ to the profession of the Truth of Christ. This purpose of heart is the same with the whole heart elsewhere. Which purpose of heart they would must be joyned, or stick close to Gods Truth and Ways. cleave unto the Lord.

24 For he was Barnabas is here described to be beyond what the Iews called a Righteous Man, who would • ay to his Neighbour, That which is yours, is yours; and that which is mine, is mine: meaning such as would do no wrong. But Barnabas, as the good Man in their esteem, (such an one as the Apostle, Rom 5.7. speaks of, for whom one would dare to die) had actually made, and not called only, that which was his, his poor Neighbours, selling what he had to bestow upon them, as Chap. 4.36. a good man, and Chap. 6.5. full of the Holy Ghost, and of faith, and His good works accompanying his good preaching, might be a great means of the Conversion of so many. much people was added unto the Lord.

25 Then departed Barnabas to Chap. 9.30. Tarsus, for to seek Saul or Paul being Barnabas's Friend and Acquaintance, whom Barnabas had brought to the knowledg of the Apostles, Chap. 9.27. he goes now to seek him, that they might advise and strengthen one another in the Work of the Lord. Saul.

26 And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that Frequency of meeting to partake of the Ordinances of God, is the great reason why the Gospel was so prevalent in this place. a whole year they assembled themselves Or, in the Church. with the church, and taught much people; and the disciples Which will be renowned so long as the World lasts, because here the Banner of Christ was first publickly set up, and Men Listed under him: and this by Divine Authority, for the Word imports no less. And that it was not a name they gave themselves, much less was it a name the Enemies of Christianity gave unto the Professors of it, for they called them Nazareans or Galileans, out of contempt. But God would have Christs Disciples to be called Christians: not only as Scholars were amongst the Greeks called from their Masters (viz. Platonists, Pythagoreans, &c.) to teach us whom we profess to learn of, and to be instructed by; but to mind us of our Unction, (for Christians are anointed Ones) 1 Iohn 2.27. and are •• ade by Christ (in a Spiritual sense) Kings and Priests unto God and his Father, Revel 1.6. were called Christians first in Antioch.

27 ¶ And in these days came These, here meant, were inabled to foretel things to come. A Gift which God did furnish some of his Church withal on such an extraordinary occasion, Ephes. 4.11. whereby they did before-hand signifie future things for the good of the Church, as here. Prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch.

28 And there stood up one of them, named Chap. 21.1 • . Agabus, and signified By a resolution from the Spirit, as one of his Gifts, and not by Judicial Astrology, or any other means real or pretended. For it is a Prerogative of God only, to foretel things to come, as Isa. 41.22, 23. by the Spirit, That there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the This Famine Suetonius and other Heathen writers make mention of, tho some place it one year, and some in another year of Claudius his reign, it may be there were divers famines, or one might continue divers years; but thus God, who provided for the Patriarchs by means of Iosephs foreseeing of the scarcity in Egypt, and elsewhere; provides for his Church now also by a • ike prediction. Gods Omniscience is exerted for his Churches preservation. days of Claudius Cesar.

29 Then the disciples, every man Which is the measure whereby we must mete out unto others, Luke 11.41. we are to give alms of such things as we have, or according as we are able. according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which These brethren or believers in Iudea, were very poor, by reason of the extraordinary malice and persecution of the Iews against them, and therefore recommended by St. Paul unto them of Arabia, (especially to the Corinthians) and to the believers in Macedonia. dwelt in Judea.

30 Chap. 12.25. Which also they did, and sent it To the Apostles; or if they (as 'tis probable) were gone out of Ierusalem, to the Governors or chief of the Churches; for the famine being to come over all Iudea, 'tis most probable, that the other Churches, besides that in Ierusalem, did partake of this bounty. to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

div.head: CHAP. XII.
div.p: NOw about that time, There were several Herods mentioned in Scripture, being all of the family of Herod the great, (by whose name they were called, as Herod that killed the children in Bethlehem, called Hecolonita; another that beheaded St. Iohn, and derided our Saviour, (this Herod was sirnamed Antipas) the Herod here spoken of was called Agrippa; the Son, or as others think, the Nephew of Aristobulus, and was the Father of that Agrippa we read of, Chap. 25.26. being Vice-roy, or King under the Roman Emperor: This Herod did not onely kill some, but punished others with banishment and blows; and especially the Governours of the Church, knowing how much all suffer in them. Herod the king Or, began. stretched forth his hands b to vex c certain of the church.

2 And he killed Who had especially the care of the Church at Ierusalem; one eminent amongst the Apostles, and one of the Sons of Thunder, (or Boanerges) for his zealous and earnest Preaching, and therefore the more hated by Herod; so that which our Saviour had foretold him, came now to pass, Matth. 20.23. that he drank of the cup our Saviour did drink of. There was another Iames, who wrote the Epistle, known by his name, and was called Iames the less; because as some think, he was brought to the knowledge of Christ after the other, of whom we read, Mark 15.40. James the Mat. 4.21. brother of John with the sword.

3 And because he saw All the posterity of Herod the great, by his example studied chiefly to please the Roman Emperors, and to gratifie the Iews whether by right or wrong. it pleased the Jews, he proceeded further, to take Peter also. Then Exod. 23.15. were Or the Passover, which Festival-solemnity lasted eight days; and God over-ruled the hypocrisie of Herod, (for he did not out of piety observe this time) for the preservation of Peter; and Herod might fear some tumult of the people, in so great a concourse, upon Peters death, for which he did defer it; howsoever, the perverseness of the Iews is very remarkable, who were made with rage against Christ and his Apostles, at such times in which they pretended to serve the God of love and peace. the days of unleavened bread.

4 And John 21.18. when he had apprehended him, he put him in prison, and delivered him to There were sixteen Soldiers appointed to keep Peter; the Romans using four Soldiers at a time to keep Centry, and the Iews dividing their nights into four watches, there were enough to relieve the other, and to set a new watch as often as was required for every night; of which four at a time, two were with the prisoner, and perhaps for the greater security, bound with the same chain; and two did always stand at the door or gate; and this they might the rather do, out of great caution, having heard what Miracles Peter did; and that he had been delivered by an Angel out of prison, Chap. 5.19. four quaternions of soldiers to keep him, intending That day in which the Paschal Lamb was eat, on which the Iews would put none to death, that they might not eclipse the joy of that day. after Easter to bring him forth To do with him what they would, leaving him to their mercy, or rather cruelty. to the people.

5 Peter therefore was kept Till a fit time to offer him up as a Sacrifice unto the people; so basely do wicked men stoop for their ends: The onely help or hope poor Christians had, was from prayer, (preces & lachrymae) there are no quaternions of Soldiers can keep the passage shut, that is towards Heaven. in prison; but Or, Instan • and earnest prayer was made. prayer was made Continued, long prayers, without intermission; but also fervent and earnest prayers, 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , with all the might of their Souls; remembring the Apostle now in bands, as bound with him, Heb. 13.3. without ceasing of the church unto God for him.

6 And when Herod would have To be put to death. brought him forth This is a night to be remembred, as that in which God delivered his Israel out of Egypt; when both were come to the utmost extremity, and at the pits brink, then so God does his marvellous work of deliverance, that it ought to be had in remembrance▪ Psal 105.5., the same night Peter was Innocency hath this advantage, and a good conscience▪ acquiesces in the providence of God; it hath Go • to its friend; and if he be for us, who can be against us sleeping between two soldiers, bound with See verse 4 To which may be added, That with one chain St. Peters right hand was bound to the Soldiers left; wit • the other chain his left hand to the other Soldiers right for so was their manner for their greater security, tha • they might not let the prisoner escape, thus persecutors a •• skilful to destroy; but no device can avail against any who • God will save. two chains, and the keepers before the door kept the prison.

7 And behold Chap. 5.1 •
▪ the Whose office it is to minister for the heirs of Salvation, Hebr. 1 14. and who willingly fulfil this will of the Lord, angel of the Lord as Luke 2.9.
