Suddenly and unexpectedly. came upon him, and a Whether this light was from the bright body the Angel assumed, or from some, other cause we are not told; and therefore it is not necessary for us to know; but it was a light onely to Peter, but darkness to his keepers; as the pillar of fire inlightned onely the Israelites, which made them both the more strange and miraculous. light shined in the prison: and he The Angel smote Peter, (as one jogs, or gently strikes another) to awaken him; Thus God was waking, tho Peter slept; and by his providence watches over all his people for their preservation: Chains could not hold any whom God will have free; every thing looses its face, when God suspends or withdraws his concurrence, smote Peter on the side, and raised him up, saying, Arise up quickly. And his chains fell off from his hands.

8 And the angel said The custom being to wear long garments, they were not so fit to go about any business, until they had girt their garments to them; hence Ieremy is commanded to get a girdle, Ier. 13.1. about him, when he was to be sent on Gods errand. unto him, Gird thy self, and bind on thy The sandals were little other than sole-leathers, bound or fastned with thongs. sandals: And so he did. And he saith unto him, Cast The uppermost vest (answerable to a cloak amongst us.) God furnishes his people thus with necessaries, and he will have them use them, so far as they are able to serve them, even then when he is working of miracles for their deliverances. thy garment about thee, and follow me,

9 And he went out and followed him, and wist not that it was The greatness and suddenness of the deliverance, was such, as it amazed him, it seemed incredible unto him; not that he questioned Gods power or goodness; but knowing that he was to suffer for Christs name sake, he might the rather not look for such a deliverance, and when it came, be as one that dreams, as Psal. 126.1. God therefore bringing his people to such extremities, that his Salvation might be the more astonishing. true which was done by the angel: but thought he saw a vision.

10 When they were past the Guard or Sentinels. first and the second ward, they came unto the iron gate The outmost gate that led out of the prison into the City, (not that the prison its self was out of the City.) that leadeth unto the city Chap. 16.26▪ which God worketh a series of miracles in their fit place and time; he could have done them all together, and have opened this iron gate before-hand, when he conducted Peter through the first, then through the second watch; but it is good for Peter and us, to be convinced, that we stand every moment in need of Gods conduct and deliverance. opened to them of his own accord, and they went out, and passed on through one street, and forthwith the angel departed from him.

11 And when Peter was come Out of that amazement, which so many wonderful things had wrought in him, that he could compose himself to reflect upon what he had heard and seen, he knew his deliverance was real and effectual. to himself, he said, Now I know of a surety, that the Lord hath Dan. 6.22. sent his angel, and hath delivered me From Herod who had resolved to have killed him, as he had done Iames, ver. 2. and from the peoples expectation, who had heard the report of Herods resolution, and longed for the fulfilling of it. out of the hand of Herod, and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews.

12 And when he had considered Peter being delivered, meditates upon the greatness of the danger that he had been in, and the goodness of God that had delivered him, and this whilest walking in the street, and going along; no place can exclude good thoughts, and holy meditations. the thing, he came to the house of Mary the The Mother is here described by the Son, as the more known person; here the parent gains reputation, and to be remembred in this Scripture for her Sons sake. Thus a wise Son made a glad Mother, as Prov. 10.1. mother of John, whose surname was Some think, this was • e that wrote the Gospel called by his name. Mark, where many were In this time of persecution the Christians met secretly, and in small numbers as they could; these here mentioned, are thought to be private Christians, because it appears by the 17. ver. that Iames, &c. were not there. gathered together, praying.

13 And as Peter knocked at the This was the outwardmost door to the Porch, or Court before the house. door of the gate, a damsel came Being in a great fear of a surprisal, they ordered one to observe, and give an answer unto any that should come to the house; which wa • the more heedfully done, because it was at an unseasonable time of the night; yet these holy men broke their rest, and exposed themselves to many fears and dangers, rather than not to assemble to serve God, when they could not serve him otherwise. Or, To ask who was there. to hearken, named Rhoda.

14 And when she knew Peters voice, she opened not the gate As one from her self, not knowing what to do for gladness; great and sudden passions, have caused strange extasies, and death it self sometimes: The Spirits in grief flowing too fast unto the heart to fortifie it, and in joy leaving the heart as fast, to meet the object that causeth it▪ for gladness, but ran in, and told how Peter stood before the gate.

15 And they said unto her, Thou art Thou speakest thou knowest not what; thinking her, out of fear to have been discomposed in her mind. mad. But she constantly affirmed that it was even so. Then said they, It is Some have thought, that by Peters Angel, no other was meant than some▪ Messenger from Peter, which they might expect from him in such a case as he was in; now tho 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , (the word here) signifies a Messenger or an Angel, indifferently; yet how could Rhoda then know it to have been Peters voice? A messengers voice being no more like his that s • nt him, than another mans. They did probably mean, some Angel that had assumed Peters shape, and imitated his voice: And the Iews having had a constant opinion, that at least every good man hath a guardian Angel which God appoints to him for a means of his preservation; might be apt to imagine, that this was that Angel whose charge St. Peter was, Matth. 18▪
•• . tho that Angel spoken of, Gen. 48.16. most probably was the Angel of the New Covenant, and not a created Angel, being Iacob blesseth in his name; yet the opinion of tutelar Angels, tho not certain or needful, is to this day thought probable. his angel.

16 But Peter Peter might be unwilling to have his entrance into the house deferred, 1. Out of fear of being taken again, and his life concerned upon it. 2. Out of an earnest desire to see the brethren, whom he might hope to meet with there. 3. Out of zeal to declare the mercy of God towards him; this • ire was kindled in him, and he sought vent for it. continued knocking: And when they had opened the door, and saw him, they were astonished.

17 But he Chap. 13.16. and 19.33. and 21.40. It was usual by the motion of the hand, both to desire silence, and to crave audience. beckening unto them with the hand to hold their peace, declared unto them how the Peter gives God the glory, tho an Angel had been the means of his delivery. Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, Go shew these things unto This Iames was the Son of Alpheus, Matth. 10.3. Mark 3.18. and succeeded the other Iames, (the brother of Iohn, of whom ver. 2.) in governing the Church at Ierusalem. James, and to the brethren. And he departed, and went into Peter could not but know he should be sought after, and therefore durst not abide in one place, lest he should ruine himself, and endanger his friends that should harbour him. Thus the great Apostle, as David formerly, was hunted, as one hunteth a partridge in the mountains, 1 Sam. 26.20. another place.

18 Now assoon as The Soldiers, who were bound with Peter in the same chains, could not but miss him assoon as they did awake, and with admiration find the chains still holding them, tho loosned from Peter. What strange imaginations they might have, is not to be expressed, tho some guess at it. it was day, there was no small stir among the souldiers, what was become of Peter.

19 And when Herod had sought for him, and found him not, he That is judicially; proceeding against them for the escape of St. Peter. examined the keepers, and commanded that they should be They were sentenced to be led away; and 'tis most probably thought, unto the place of execution. The instruments in persecution, God many times meets with in this world; and sometimes by the persecutors themselves. put to death. And he went down from Judea to Cesarea, and there abode.

20 ¶ And Herod was Or, But 〈◊〉 hostile mind, intending 〈◊〉
highly displeased with them of These were two coast Towns in Phenicia; famous, especially the former, for her great trading; and being rich, might be insolent, or possibly might tempt Herod to a war against them, whose conquest would pay the charge of it. Tyre and Sidon: but they came with one accord to him, and having made Blastus Gr. That was over the King • bed-ch •• ber. the kings Or chief of his Bed-chamber: or begged pardon; there being no war yet begun. chamberlain their friend, desired peace; because their These Cities lying upon the Sea, had little land belonging to them, and of old were forced to have their provision from other places, especially from Iudea; thus Solomon gave Hiram (King of Tyre) twenty thousand measures of wheat for his houshold, and twenty measures of pure oil yearly, 1 Kings 5.9, 11. and long after that, they of Iudah and Israel are said to have traded with their wheat in Tyre, Ezek. 27.17. countrey was nourished by the king •
countrey.

21 And upon a This was (says Iosephus cap. 19. lib. 7.) the second day of the sports or games, which Herod had instituted in honour of the Emperor Claudius; or it may be such a day as Herod had appointed to determine the difference in, betwixt him and the Tyrians. set day, Herod arayed in Such, saith Iosephus, as were made of Silver, woven with extraordinary art, and did reflect strangly the beams of the Sun shining upon it: An elevated place, from whence he might the better be seen and heard. royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them.
22 And the people gave a shout, saying, These impious flatterers destroy whom they exalt; for God will pull down his rivals. It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.

23 And immediately An Angel had delivered Peter; and here an Angel destroys Herod; all that Heavenly host fulfil Gods will for the deliverance of his Church, and the destruction of his enemies. the angel of the Lord smote him, because he Priding himself in the acclamation the people had made, and not attributing his eloquence and glory to God, as the giver of them; or rather not repressing or punishing their blasphemy; whereas Peter durst not accept of undue honour from Cornelius, Chap. 10.26. nor the Angel • from St. Iohn, Rev. 19.10. and 22.9. gave not God the glory: and he was, Either breeding in his bowels, or in his flesh, after a more unusual manner; as 'tis recorded of Herod the great, that he was eaten up of Lice. No Creature so little or contemptible, but it can execute Gods Judgments on whom he please. eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.

24 ¶ But Isa. 55.11. Chap. 6.7. & 19.20. Col. 1.6. the word of God The Word of God is compared here to Seed, as in our Saviours Parable, Matth. 13.19. grew and The number of believers multiplied through the Word, which was sown, as Seed is scattered abroad. So true it is, that Persecutors by their pulling down of the Church, do but build it up. multiplied.

25 And Barnabas and Saul returned They returned unto Antioch, from whence they were sent, Chap. 11.26, 30. to carry the benevolence of the Church of Antioch, to that of Iudea. from Jerusalem, when they had fulfilleed This was the Ministry or Service they were appointed to do. their
Or, Charge. ministery, and took with them Of whom before, Verse 12. John whose sirname was Mark.

div.head: CHAP. XIII.
div.p: NOW there were Chap. 14.26. in The true Church, which hath a being, and whose builder and maker is God. Other Churches (as that of the Circumcision) are no Churches or Congregations of the Faithful. the church that was at Antioch, certain These two Offices might be in the same person, as he that had the Gift of Prophesie, and could foretel things to come, might be a teacher to instruct the People; but yet they were frequently appertaining to several persons, one excelling in one Gift, another in another. prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called This Simeon is thus distinguished from Simon Peter, and from Simon the Canaanite, this name of Niger being given him by the Romans. Niger, and Lucius of This hath been thought the name of Luke, it being more after the Latin termination; and that it might be he that wrote the Gospel called by his name, and this Book of the Acts. Howsoever we meet with this name, Rom. 16.21. And St. Paul sends Salutation unto him that was so called. Born at a place so called, or brought up in the Synagogue of the Cyrenians. Of which Chap. 6.9. Either this Manaen was Herod's Foster-Brother, or had the same Tutors and Instructors with him, their Education being together. This Herod was Herod Antipas, who set at nought our Saviour, and killed the Baptist. And yet Manaen, as another Moses, kept his integrity in that Pharaoh's Court. And as Moses, Heb. 11.25▪ he chose rather to suffer affliction with the People of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season. Thus there was an Obadiah in Ahab's House, 1 Kin. 18.3. and divers believe in Nero's Family, Phil. 4.22. Cyrene, and Manaen, which had been Or, Herods Foster-Brother. brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.

2 As they The word importeth the exercise of any publick Office, Sacred or Civil. But in the former verse mention being made of Prophets and Teachers, these words are in sense too conjoyn'd with them; and informs us, that whilst they were Preaching to, and Instructing of the People, (for there is no Ministry or Service which God likes better than to convert and save Souls) and that all might be more effectual, as being done with greater earnestness and intention of mind, whilst they fasted. ministred to the Lord, and fasted, the The Holy Ghost by some inward instinct in those Prophets before spoken of, who had warrant to declare it as from him. holy Ghost said, Chap 9.15. & 22.21. Rom. 1.1. Separate me These two were to be separated as the first-born under the Law, Exod. 13.12. and after them, or in their stead, the Levites, Numbers 3.12. So were Paul and Barnabas in especial manner separated for the calling in of the Gentiles, that great Ministry or Service which God had for them to do. Barnabas and Saul p, for the work Matth. 9.38. Rom. 10.15. Heb. 5.4. whereunto I have called them.

3 And Chap. 6.6. when they had A good preparation to enter into any business with, whereby they acknowledged that all success must come from God. Our Blessed Saviour himself would not enter upon his Ministry till he had Fasted fourty days, Matth. 4.2. compared with the 17th. fasted and prayed, and laid Barnabas and Saul being called to be Apostles already. This laying on of their hands upon them signifies; First, Their being set apart to thi • particular imployment they were now to be sent about. Secondly, The Approbation of the Church to that Heavenly call they had. Thirdly, Their praying for Gods Blessing upon them, and Success upon the work they went for. their hands on them, they sent them away.

4 ¶ So they being sent forth by the holy Ghost, departed unto A Sea-town of Cilicia, nigh unto Antioch, and over-against Cyprus, built by Seleucus, and was a Town of some note, but mentioned here only as in their passage to Cyprus. Seleucia; and from thence they sailed to Cyprus.

5 And when they were at The chief City of Cyprus, now called Famagusta, scituate on the East-side of the Island, over-against Syria. Salamis, they preached the word of God They preached here, and elsewhere in the Synagogues, either because they found no such convenient places to Preach in; (these being large Structures, and many resorting to them;) or rather, because tho they were sent unto the Gentiles, yet it was not till after the Iews should have refused the Gospel, as may be seen throughout all this Book, and in the conclusion of it, Chap. 28.28. in the Synagogues of the Jews: and they had also John to their Minister.As Chap. 12. & 25.

6 And when they had gone through the Isle This City was on the West-end of Cyprus. So that going from Salamis they went through the Island; this place was famous for the worshipping of Venus. unto Paphos, they found a certain There were many Magicians about this time amongst the Iews, who by their false Miracles endeavoured to bring the real Miracles of our Saviour into contempt. As the Magicians and Sorcerers of Egypt, by their enchantments for a while, did seem to do such wonders, as Moses had wrought by the Finger of God, Exod. 7.11. sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus:

7 Which was with the Whether he was Pro-Consul, or Proprietor, it is in effect the same; for he it was that Governed the Island. deputy of the countrey Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; who called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired This desire was extraordinary, and wrought by God, in order to the fitting him for the further mercy of his Conversion, and Salvation; where such a desire is, it shall be granted: ask and ye shall have, Luke 11.9. to hear the word of God.

8 But Exod. 7.11. 2 Tim. 3.8. This is another name of him that was called Barjesus, which was not unusual, as Simon Bar-jonah, Matth. 16.17. This, Elymas ▪ may be taken appe •• atively, and Elymas the sorcerer (for signifies the Magician or Sorcerer; but being it was a proper name unto others we read of, it may be so here. so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith.

9 It is observable, that St. Luke never before called this great Apostle by the name of Paul: and henceforth never calls him by the name of Saul; tho there be no great difference in these names. Saul might be more acceptable to the Iews ▪ amongst whom hitherto he had conversed. And Paul a more pleasing name unto the Gentiles, unto whom he was now sent, and with whom for the future he should most converse. He was called Saul as he was a Iew born, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; and Paul, as he was a Denison of Rome. The Romans having that name in good account in several of their chief Families. Then Saul (who also is called Paul) filled Zeal for Gods Glory, and Faith and Power to work the ensuing Miracle. with the holy Ghost, set his eyes on him▪

10 And said, O full of all subtilty and all
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 signifies a facility or readiness in doing mischief; and that such who are given to Sorcery are easily drawn to commit any kind of sin whatsoever. mischief, Matth. 13.38, John 8.44. 1 John 3.8. thou Because he did his work who is the Destroyer ▪ in hindring what he could the Salvation of Sergius Paulus and his Family. child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease To make the way of God crooked, which is straight; and rugged, when indeed it is smooth: that is, to lay what rubs he could to keep any from coming unto, or continuing in the ways of God. to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

11 And now behold, The hand of the Lord is put for any powerful action of God, whether in Mercy or Judgment: here it is put for the Divine Power wherewith God strikes his Enemies. the hand of the Lord is upon thee, and thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun God did in Judgment remember Mercy, inflicting this blindness only for a season, that it might be rather a Medicine than a punishment. for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he
went about, seeking some to lead him by the hand.

12 The Gospel which Paul Preached. Then the deputy when he saw what was done, believed, being Finding in it (though a wise Man) depths beyond his fathoming: and all accompanied with such a power in doing of Miracles, and changing of Hearts, and Lives; as might well amaze so prudent, and considering a man. astonished at the doctrine of the Lord.

13 Now when Paul and his company loosed from Paphos, they came to A City in Pamphylia: not that there were any other Cities of that name; but because this Region was more commonly known, it being Perga in a Country in the lesser Asia, bordering on Cilicia. Pamphylia: And John The departure of Iohn; of whom before, Verse 6. and Chap. 12.25. was blame-worthy, as Chap. 15.38. Some think he shunned that labour and suffering which he saw attended the Gospel; others supposed that he returned to Ierusalem out of too fond an affection for his Mother, who lived there; and it may be that he retaining a great aversion from the Gentiles, might abhor to go amongst them: howsoever, let him that stands, take heed lest he fall. departing from them, returned to Jerusalem.

14 ¶ But when they departed from Perga, they came to So called to distinguish it from the other Antioch mentioned in the first Verse, which was a City in Syria, as this in Pi • idia, next to, or part of Pamphylia. Antioch in Pisidia, and went into the synagouge Either to joyn with the Iews in their worship, which was not then unlawful, or to get an opportunity more publickly to Preach the Gospel unto them: they were no sooner come thither, but they mind that great business they went about. on the sabbath-day, and sate down.

15 And after the The reading of the Law was commanded by Moses; and they say, that Ezra commanded the reading of the Prophets also in their Synagogues, which was used; as we may see in the 27th Verse. And so divided into several Sections, that once a Year they might be all read over. reading of the law and the prophets, the They were such as had the over-sight of this Service of God in their Synagogues, that it might be performed according to the prescription. rulers of the Synagogue sent unto them, saying, Ye men and An usual compellation which the Iews gave one another, owning them to serve the same God, and professing a suitable respect for them. brethren, If ye have any word of exhortation for the people After the reading before spoken of, there followed a Sermon, or Exhortation; which the Apostles are desired to make, the Rulers of the Synagogue, as 'tis supposed, having had some previous knowledg of them., say on.

16 Then Paul stood up To procure silence and attention, as Chap. 12.17., and beckning with his hand, said, Men of Israel, and Besides the Native Iews, the Proselytes, and such out of all Nations who left the Idolatry of the Gentiles, and vow'd the only True God, met together in the worship of God; these were the 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 spoken of, Chap. 17.4. It shews also what they are to do that would hear the Word of the Lord with profit; viz. to attend unto it in the fear of his Name. ye that fear God, give audience.

17 The God was the God of Israel after a peculiar manner. God of this people of Israel Having chosen them before all Nations, to make him known unto them, to be served and worshipped by them. chose our fathers, and And God exalted them in the time of Ioseph; and whilst the memory of that great preservation wrought by his means, did continue, till another King arose that knew not Ioseph. exalted the people Exod. 1.1., when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt, Exod. 6.6. & 13.14, 16. and with an The many Miracles done by the Power of God towards the Israelites deliverance out of Egypt. By which the Apostle would have them remember, that they owed all which they challenged from their Progenitors, to the Grace and Blessing of God only; and that God may do with his own as he please. high arm brought he them out of it.

18 And Exod. 16.35. about the time of fourty years This is Recorded, Psal. 95.10. and remembred by the Apostle, Heb. 3.8, 9. And to be admired through all Ages, that God should be so patient, or a People could be so perverse: some instead of 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , read 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , there being but one Letter difference, (and such as are usually changed into one another,) and then it speaks Gods providing for this People all that while, and carrying them as in his Bosom, as a Nurse bears the sucking Child, Numb. 11.12. Deut. 1.31. or as an Eagle beareth her young ones on her Wings, Deut. 32.11, 12. But it seems God did not bear with their Fathers, but destroyed them in the Wilderness, 1 Cor. 10.5. First, God bare long with those that perished. Secondly, The succeeding Generation took not that warning which did become them, but followed their Fathers steps; and whilst one Generation was wearing away, and another coming, this space of Forty years was spent, through the abundant compassion of God towards them; who did not consume them as they tempted him to do, in a moment. 2 Mac. 7.27. according to the 70. And so Chrysost •• . suffered he their manners in the wilderness.

19 And when he had destroyed These seven Nations are mentioned, Ioshua 3.10. seven nations in the land of Canaan, he Josh. 14.1. divided their land to them The Lot being disposed only as God would, Prov. 16. ult. And it was but reasonable that God having miraculously got this Land (for the Israelites did rather go to take possession of it, than to fight for it) and assumed a special right unto it, that he should divide it to whom he pleased, and in what proportions he thought good. by lot.

20 And after that he gave unto them Judges 3.9. These Judges were persons deputed by God to govern and deliver that People; their Commission was attested usually by some extraordinary thing done by them, and their power (as being mediately from God) was absolute judges, about the space of The computation of years here mentioned, hath been very much controverted: That which hath the greatest probability with it, is, Either first, to have recourse to the 17 Verse, and begin this Aera there, with Gods chusing of their Fathers, and ending it at the time of the decision of the Land by lot, as Verse 19. for from the birth of Isaac, to this distribution of the Land, are reckoned 447 years; which may well be said here, About 450 years: but then the sense is, after that, such things mentioned in the 17, 18, 19. Verses were done; which were in the compass of 450 years, God then gave them Judges. Or, as others do refer these words to what follows, and begin the Aera or computation from the going of the Children of Israel out of Egypt, and ending it at the expulsion of the Iebusites out of Ierusalem, which may make up this account: But then this passage of St. Paul is not intended to shew how long the Judges Ruled, but when it was, or about what time that they Ruled; As also to shew what a long time it took up to gain that People a quiet possession of that promised Inheritance, their sins still keeping good things from them. four hundred and fifty years, until Samuel the prophet.

21 And afterward they desired Their great sin in desiring a King was, because by that desire they rejected God, who had at that very time a Prophet (Samuel) by whom he governed them, 1 Sam. 8.7. & 10.19. They had been under a Theocrasie ever since they came out of Egypt; their Laws, and their Governors being appointed by God; had their condition been as that of other Nations, their desire had not been a provocation. a king: 1 Sam. 8.5. and God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, by the space of These words, by the space of fourty years, are to be joyned with the foregoing Verse, and the other foregoing words in the Verse read with a Parenthesis: and thus they shew how long Samuel the Prophet (as he is here called) exercised his Prophetical Offices, which was the space here mentioned, partly before Saul was Anointed King, and in part afterward; in which, as another Moses, he cared for, and went in, and out, before the People of God, the like space of fourty years. This computation of St. Paul might also agree more with the Septuagint, and be according to the then current account, which (not being of more consequence) St. Paul would not controvert at this time, having greater matters to speak of unto them. fourty years.

22 And when God had taken Saul away by death; for he would not suffer David to hasten it. he had removed him, he raised up unto them 1 Sam 16.13. Psal. 89.20, 21. David to be their king, To whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man Favoured or beloved by me, and obedient to me; my servant, as God speaks of him, Psal. 89.20. after mine own heart, which shall fulfil And here, that he should fulfil all Gods will, to wit, in governing his people; for he hath a Testimonial upon record in Gods word, Psal. 78.72. He that is according to Gods heart, fulfil all the wills of God, and do nothing by partiality, thus also; but if it be Gods will either for him to do, or to suffer any thing, he is ready to set his fiat to it; as he dally prays (understandingly) that the will of the Lord may be done. all my will.

23 Of this Christ was the Son of David, and so frequently called, Matth. 1.1. Luke 18.38, 39. with reference unto the promise made, Isaiah 11.1. spoken of Chap. 2.30. Rom. 1.3. mans seed hath God according to his promise, raised Because he lived amongst the Iews, and Salvation was first offered unto them by him, as verse 46. unto Israel a Saviour Our Saviours name is added, to shew that he truely was according to his name, and what he was said to be, as Matthew 1.21. Jesus:

24 Mat. 3.1. When John had first preached Iohn the Baptist did not speak of Christs coming, as the other Apostles had done, as of a thing a great way off, or at a distance of time; but he spake of it as of a present matter, before his and their faces, and in their view; Behold the lamb of God, Iohn 1 29.36. before his coming So it is called, Mat. 3.2, 8. Mark 1.4. Luke 3.3. Repentance being a due qualification for such as hope to receive the mercies of God in Christ, unto life Eternal., the baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel.

25 And as John fulfilled The course of his Ministry, or of his life; in respect of either, he ran as one in a race. his course, he said The sense of these words ye have Iohn 1.20, 27., Whom think ye that I am? I am not That is, the Messias, which they were in such expectation of, and so inquisitive about, he. But behold, there cometh one Christ began his life, (as to the flesh) after Iohn; and he began his Ministry after him, and in that respect may be said to come after him. after me, whose shoes of his feet I am not A proverbial expression, whereby the meanest office is implied, Mat. 3.11. which the Disciples or servants could do for their Masters. worthy to loose.

26 He speaks to the Iews according as the manner was amongst them; to the Iews he become as a Iew. Men and brethren, children of the stock of Abraham, and Some think, the devout Pisidians, or men of that Countrey, are here meant; but rather it may insinuate the Apostles hope concerning these Iews, that they were such as feared God; which hope they ought the rather to have carefully answered. whosoever among you, feareth God, Mat. 10.6. Chap. 3.26. Verse 46. to you is 1. Christ who is the incarnate word, or the word made flesh, Iohn 1.14. or the Gospel, which is glad tidings of Salvation; as if the Apostle had minded them; that it was not any business which belonged unto others alone, which he was speaking about; but of such things as pertained unto their Salvation; and such a Salvation (this Salvation) as never greater was, or ever will be published; this is certain, that we are concerned in it for our selves, if we accept or neglect this Salvation, it is for our selves: Oh that in this respect self-interest were more prevalent with us! the word of this salvation sent.

27 For The common people had their they that dwell at Jerusalem great Council; both had a hand in our Saviours death., and their rulers Chap. 3.17., because they But if so great a fault was capable of any alteration, the Apostle gladly mentions it, that it was done out of ignorance; they knew neither Christ the word, nor the word (of the Gospel) concerning Christ, tho that they may be made sensible, that this their ignorance was not invincible▪ knew him not, nor yet the voices of the prophets Chap. 15.21. which are read He minds them that it was their sin, having had means whereby they might have come unto the knowledge of Christ. every sabbath • day, they have See Chap. 4.28. Luke 24.25, 26. fulfilled them in condemning him.

28
•• rk 15.13, • 14. • 23.21, 22. • 19.6. And tho they found He was a Lamb without blemish; neither had he offended the rabble that was so slanderous against him, unless by such vast goodness and kindness towards them, he branded them for ingratitude. no cause of death in him, yet Matth. 27.22. The Iews did condemn him, but they could not put him to death; the Romans, under whom they were subject, having reserved the power of life and death wholly unto themselves, and therefore they desired Pilate to confirm the •• sentence, and to cause it to be executed. desired they Pilate that he should be slain.

29 And when they had fulfilled As the giving him vinegar to drink, piercing his side, &c. Psal. 69.21. Iohn 19.28, 30. ▪ all that was written of him, they took him down See Chap. 5.30. from the tree, and Ioseph of Arimathea, and Nicodemus, Matth. 27.60. Iohn 19.39. laid him in a sepulchre.

30 Mat. 28 •• Chap. 2.24. But Lest they should be offended at our Saviours dying so shameful and cursed a death, and to take away the scandal of the cross; he shews, that his Resurrection was as glorious, as his death could be ignominious; being by it declared to be the Son of God with power, Rom. 1.4. God raised him from the dead:

31 And he Mat. 28.16▪ Chap. 1.3. was seen Fourty days betwixt his Resurrection and Ascension, Chap. 1.3. many days of them Christ was seen, not onely by the Apostles, but of the Galilean women which came up with him unto Ierusalem, Matth. 28.1. and by above five hundred at once, 1 Cor. 15.5, 6. so plentifully would God have this great article of our faith, and object of ou • hope to be confirmed unto us. which came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses unto the people.

32 And we declare unto you Or the Gospel, which is nothing else but the glad tidings of our Salvation from Sin and Hell. glad tidings, how that the Or the Gospel, which is nothing else but the glad tidings of our Salvation from Sin and Hell. promise which was made unto the fathers,This promise was frequently made, and renewed to their Ancestors, and ty • ified by many deliverances, especially from Egypt and Babylon.

33 God hath fulfilled the same unto us their children, in that he hath Some refer these words to the Incarnation, others to the Resurrection of our Saviour: Our Translators lay the stress upon the preposition, with which the verb is compounded; and by adding again, intend it to be understood of the Resurrrection; and there is ground for it in the context: for the Resurrection of Christ, is that which in the 30. verse is propounded by St. Paul, as his theam or argument to Preach upon. raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second p • alm, These words quoted, tho they do not seem to be a proof of Christs Resurrection at the first view; yet if we weigh them well, they answer St. Pauls purpose; Thou art my son, Psalm 2 ver. 7. is ushered in with; I have made thee King, ver. 6. and followed with, I will give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, which was in especial manner to be fulfilled after the Resurrection; as our Saviour manifests, Matth. 28 18, 19. Heb. 1. •
▪ Thou art my son Not as if Christ at his Resurrection began to be the Son of God; but then he was manifested to be so, Rom. 1.4. which before, whilest he was in a suffering condition, was not so apparent; some of the Ancients have understood these words, of the Eternal generation of the Son of God; Eternity being an everlasting point, and one and the same day for ever., this day have I begotten thee.

34 And as concerning that The former verse was not intended so much by St. Paul for a proof of the Resurrection, as it was to shew how faithful God was in fulfilling that promise there spoken of; here the Apostles design is, to evince Christs Resurrection, and that it was agreeable to the Prophesies which were concerning him. he raised him up from the dead, now no more to return to corruption, he said on this wise These words are found, Isaiah 53.3. and the sure mercies of David there; and here spoken of, are such mercies as were promised to David, (David being to be taken positively) now the mercies which were promised to David, are all included or surmounted in this; that by this Son of David, (our Lord and Saviour frequently and truly so called) God would erect and establish an everlasting Kingdom, which could not be done, unless Christ rose again, and obtained the victory over death and the grave., I will give you the Gr. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , holy, or just things: which word the 70. both in the place of Is. 53.3. and in many other places, use for that which in the Hebrew is, mercies. sure mercies of Daeid.All the promises God hath made unto his Church in any age concerning Christ, are sure and faithful, holy and just▪ The words have been variously rendred and changed; but no words can sufficiently express their stability and excellency.
35 Wherefore he saith These words are quoted out of Psal. 16, 10, 11. see Chap. 2.27. also in another psalm ▪ Thou shalt not suffer thine holy On • to see corruption:

36 For David Or, After he had in his own age, served the will of God. after he had served his own generation Some point these words otherwise, reading them thus; David after he had served his generation, by the will of God fell asleep. Which contains indeed a truth, viz. that God hath appointed every ones time in the world, and that the issue of life and death are his; but thus they would prove little to Davids praise; for who dies otherwise, but according to the determinate counsel of God? But this is remembred to Davids glory, that according to the will of God, he was a publick good, and he liv'd and govern'd by the rule and square of Gods word. by the will of God, Notwithstanding which he fell asleep, and saw death; but such as did not deserve so terrible a name. 1 King. 2.10. Chap. 2.29. fell on sleep, and was laid Buried amongst his Ancestors. unto his fathers, and saw corruption:And his body corrupted as theirs; now this verse explains the former, and draws the argument home, in that it proves, that the words before mentioned, could not be meant of David; but of one that he typified, and represented.
37 But he whom That is, on the third day, according to the Gospel. God raised again, saw Was not under the power of death so long, as to be preyed upon so far by it. no corruption.

38 ¶ Be it known unto you therefore The usual compellation given in these cases., men and brethren, that Luke 24.47. 1 John 2.12. through Having spoken concerning Christs Resurrection, which onely can be meant of him in his humane nature, here, according unto that nature the Apostle calls him, Man. this man is preached unto you As in Chap. 10.43. This forgiveness of sins, is that which the Apostle so much would recommend to all to seek after, and magnifie Christ for; it being onely through him; and he could not be overcome by death, who could deliver us from sin. the forgiveness of sins:

39 And Rom. 3.28. and 8.3. Heb. 7.19. by him all that believe It is a forensick word, opposed to be condemned; all that believe in Christ with the heart, by his merit and mediation shall be absolved, and shall not come into condemnation; and thus this agrees with the former words, and shews us whence remission of sins is to be had; if any will take this word, as signifying also to be purged from sin; yet 'tis evident, that the Law can bring neither of these benefits unto us: The Law declares what is sin, and what the curse is that is due unto sin, but not how to be delivered from them; it shews the spot, but not how to wash it off; and the sore, but not how to heal it; but on the other side we are bidden to glory in the Lord (Jesus) Who of God is made unto us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, 1 Cor. 1.30. are justified To which may be added, that there were some sins which by the Ceremonial Law there was no Sacrifice appointed for: And for such sins which a Sacrifice was appointed for, it was not possible that the blood of bulls and goats should take them away, Heb. 10.4. which may make more to admire the grace of the Gospel, by which we are Sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all, Hebrews 10.10. from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.

40 Beware therefore, lest that come upon you which is spoken of Habakkuk 1.5. He cautions these Iews, lest the same thing threatned by the Prophet to their Fathers, come also upon them; for sin is as odious unto God as ever, and God is as jealous of his honour which sin robs him of, as ever he was. in the prophets,

41 These words are cited from that place in Habakkuk, according to the reading of the Septuagint; St. Paul not being willing to alter the words, the Iews that were dispersed, being so used to that translation, especially the sense being the same with the original Hebrew: This quotation of the Apostle, might also be taken from Isaiah 28.14, 16. Behold, ye For which cause, in that place of Habakkuk they are commanded to consider the Heathen, and are sent to School unto them they contemned so much, who had had God for their Teacher, had they not despised his word. despisers, and Grow pale or shame and fear. wonder, and Ye shall be destroyed by the Romans your enemies, as your Ancestors were by their enemies perish▪ for I work a This work was a work of Gods just revenge on 〈◊〉 then, by the Chaldeans; but threatned to come on th • e (without repentance) by the Romans. work in your days, a work which Which • estruction should be so great, tho it was incredible to them now, though it should have been told them. ye shall in no wise believe, though a man declare it unto you.

42 And Or as some read, the Apostles, Paul and Barnabas, were gone out of the Synagogue of the Iews. when the Jews were gone out of the synagogue, the Proselites, or such devout persons formerly spoken of, who had relinquished Paganism, and came to be instructed in the knowledge of the true God by the Iews. Gentiles besought that these words might be preached to them Or in some day betwixt the Sabbaths; that the Apostles took all advantages, if there were a Festival (which was also called a Sabbath, Levit. 16.31. and in the 23. Chap. of Levit. frequently) they would Preach in season and out of season; howsoever, because we find the Apostles did meet again with them on that day seven-night after, it is most probable that their desire was so to be understood, See verse 44. the Or, In the week between, or in the Sabbath betwe •• . next sabbath.

43 Now when the congregation The Congregation was dissolved, by the offence the Iews generally had taken at the Doctrine of the Apostles. was broken up, many of the Jews, and These Proselites were so called, from their coming over from Paganism, to own the true God, see Chap. 2.10. religious proselites followed Paul and Barnabas; who speaking to them, Chap. 11.23. and 14.22. perswaded them to continue This grace of God, the Apostles so earnestly exhorted them to continue in; was, 1. Their present state of being firmly resolved to serve God, whatsoever opposition or temptation they should meet with to the contrary, which was wrought in them by the grace of God. 2. The Doctrine of Justification by the grace of God, which St. Paul had Preached unto them, verse 39. Or 3. the whole Gospel, and Doctrine therein contained, which is called the grace of God, Heb. 12.15. aad the true grace wherein we stand, 1 Peter 5.12. in the grace of God.

44 ¶ And the next sabbath day came almost the The Citizens generally resorted thither. whole city together Some ou • of curiosity, some to cavil at it, tho some also out of love to it; here was doubtless a mixt Congregation. to hear the word of God:

45 But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled The Iews could not endure that the Gentiles should be equalled to them, (being as much concerned against the Gentiles being exalted, as against their own being depressed) with envy, and spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, Envy; as a vicious humour, made them disrelish the wholesomest, and most saving truths: contradicting the Doctrine of the Gospel, and blaspheming the Preachings of it; or going from one degree of opposition unto another, until they came to the highest enmity against both. contradicting and blaspheming.

46 Then Paul and Barnabas Being nothing affrighted with the reproaches and blasphemies they met with, which but increase their zeal, as a little water does the fire in the Smiths forge. waxed bold, and said, Chap. 3.26. Rom. 1.16. It was There was a necessity, that the word of God should be first Preached to the Iews, 1. Because Christ was promised to the children and heirs of their Ancestors. 2. Because Christ did command it to be thus Preached, Matth. 10.5, 6. Luke 24.47 Chap. 1.8. 3 Christ himself thus Preached it, declaring that he was not sent, (comparatively) but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, Matth. 15.24. necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but Exod. 32.10. Isaiah 55.5. Matth. 21.43. Rom. 10.19. seeing ye put it from you By this their contradicting and blaspheming, they shew as evidently that they are thus unworthy of everlasting life, as if a judge had determined so, or passed such a sentence upon his Tribunal, or Judgment-seat., and judge your selves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we Chap. 18.6. and 28.2 • . turn to the Gentiles.

47 For so hath the Lord Because that Prophesie must be fulfilled which we find, Isaiah 49.6. The Apostle infers aright, that they were commanded to publish Christ unto the Gentiles; For how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? Rom 10.14. commanded us, saying, I have set thee to be All knowledge is ignorance, and all light is darkness without Christ. a light Luke 2. •• . of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth.

48 And when the Gentiles heard this There can be no true rest or peace in any, to whom Christ is not manifested; the Apostle telling us, that we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, Rom. 5.1. And the Kingdom of God is peace and joy in the Holy Ghost., they
were glad, and They magnified the goodness of God, which appeared in the Gospel unto them. glorified the word of the Lord: and as God who ordered the end, odereth the means, and gives them opportunities to hear the Word, and by it graciously worketh Faith in them whom he hath appointed to Eternal Life; without which Faith, purging the heart, there's no hope of life Eternal. many as were ordained to eternal li • e, believed.

49 And the Concerning Salvation to be found only by Christ, and the Gentiles to be admitted to partake of that Salvation. word of the Lord was published throughout Like Leaven which a Woman took and hid in three Measures of Meal till the whole was Leavened, Matth. 13.33. all the region.

50 But the Jews stirred up
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , as was said of the Men, such as had relinquished the Idolatry of their Country and Ancestors, acknowledged the True God, the maker of Heaven and Earth. the devout and Of great repute and esteem; Women being accounted more earnest in what way soever they take; and to be sure Eve was first seduced, and in the transgression. honourable women, and In some Cities there were but Five, in some Ten, in others Twenty, in whose hands the Government of the City was ordinarily put; and these the Persecutors (knowing what an influence their Authority must needs have) by all means labour to seduce. the chief men of the city, and 2 Tim. 3.11. raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts.

51 Chap. 18.6. But This was according to our Saviours command, Matth. 10.14. Mark 6.11. Luke 9.5. so often is it mentioned, and so considerable a matter it is for us to know, and dread the punishment appointed for such as refuse the Gospel, and contemn the Salvation offered by it. they shook off What this was Symbolical of, is not expressed. The Hebrew Proverb says, The dust of an Ethnick City or Country doth pollute a Man; and they might by this represent, that the Inhabitants of such a City or Place, who did not entertain the Gospel, and the Ministers thereof, they would repute as the vilest sinners, and they should by God be dealt with accordingly. the dust of their feet against them, and came unto See Chap. 14.1. Iconium.

52 And the Either Paul and Barnabas in a more especially manner: Or, also such as at Perga had believed the Gospel, and came with them to Antioch, were filled with joy. disciples were So as no place was left for meaner contentments. First, By reason of the pardon of their sins. Secondly, The promise made to them of everlasting Life. Thirdly, The Gifts of the Holy Ghost which they had, at that time, as an earnest and pledge to assure the other unto them. filled with joy, and with the holy Ghost.

div.head: CHAP. XIV.
div.p: AND it came to pass in A City in Lycaonia. Iconium, that they went Paul and Barnabas, as they were wont to do, shewing as great constancy in performing of their duty, as their Enemies did obstinacy in persecuting them for it. both together into the Synagogue of the Jews, and With such evidence and demonstration of the spirit and of power. so spake, that a great multitude, both of the Jews, and also of See Chap. 13.43. the Greeks, believed.

2 But Or disobedient Iews, who did not believe the Truths, or obey the Precepts of the Gospel. the unbelieving Jews Urging, perswading and pressing of them, who of themelves (tho as yet ignorant of Christ, and his Word) would not have been so cruel. stirred up the Gentiles, and made their minds evil affected against The Apostles themselves, and others that were converted by them, whose commo • Father, God through Christ was, and were accordingly endeared one to another. the brethren.

3 To strengthen the new Converts against the opposition they met with in the way of Christ, willingly partaking with them in their afflictions for Christs sake. Long time therefore abode they With great courage, and humble confidence, as knowing in whom they had believed. speaking boldly First, In the Lords cause, a business which he had sent them about. Secondly, And in the Lords strength, who enabled them in it. in the Lord, Mark 16.20. • eb. 2.4. which gave testimony unto the word of The Gospel, First, Wherein the Grace of God is manifested. Secondly, Whereby it is offered. Thirdly, Wherewith, to such as receive, it is conveyed. Fourthly, And out of Grace disputed and allowed to some, hidden and withdrawn from others. his grace, and granted God by his miraculous confirming the Doctrine of the Apostles, that it was from him. signs and wonders to be done by their hands.

4 But the multitude of the city was As it was about our Saviour and his Doctrine, Iohn 7.43. divided: and part held with the Jews, and part with Paul and Barnabas, who were called to be Apostles, 1 Cor. 9.5, 6. the apostles.

5 And when there was an assault made both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews, with their Such as were called the chief Men of the City, Chap. 13.50. rulers, to use them Thus they that were called to the Marriage of the Kings Son, Matth. 22.6. entreated the Servants despitefully. 1 Thess. 2.2. 2 Tim. 3.11. despitefully, and to They would have used them as such who were not worthy to live, and then have taken away their lives from them; as they did by our Saviour, first they spat upon him. And then Crucified him. stone them.

6 They were ware of it, and The Apostles did not flee so much to save their lives, as to husband their time best for the glory of God in other places; and this they were commanded to do, Matth. 10.23. When they persecute you in one city, flee unto another. fled unto There were Cities further in the Country of Lycaonia, than Iconium was. Lystra and Derbe, cities of A part of the lesser Asia, nigh unto the Mountain Taurus. Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about:

7 And Thus was verified what St. Paul observed, Phil. 1.12. That all those things fell out unto the furtherance of the Gospel; which spread the further for the scattering of the Apostles and Preachers of it: and Thousands had not heard of Christ, if persecution had not driven the Ministers of the Gospel unto them. God working good out of evil, and causing the Sun when it leaves one part, to shine upon another. there they preached the gospel.

8 ¶ And there sate a certain man at Lystra, impotent in his feet, being a creeple from his Such defects as are from Nature, are incurable by Art, and only to be helped immediately by the God of Nature. mothers womb, who This is observed and enlarged upon, to make the miracle the more appear to be the only work of God, Chap. 3.2. never had walked.

9 The same heard Paul speak: Who stedfastly beholding him, and perceiving that he had This Paul might know by a Prophetical Spirit; and that extraordinary Gift of discerning of Spirits might be in this case bestowed upon him. But withal, it is not unlikely but this Lame Mans attention to the Word, eyes gesture, and countenance, might speak as much. faith to be healed,

10 Said with a loud voice, Isa. 35.6. Stand upright on thy feet As Chap. 3.6, 8. To shew, that he was perfectly recovered of this Lameness: as all miraculous cures (being the Work of God) were perfect.. And he leaped and walked.

11 And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lift up their voices, saying in Which was a Dialect of the Greek Tongue, that Language being in the lesser Asia ordinarily spoken. the speech of Lycaonia, Chap. 28.6. The gods are come down to us in the The Heathens (especially their Poets) did frequently believe such kind of Apparitions. Probably at first from the appearing of Angels unto the Patriarchs and others, which by tradition they might have heard of. likeness of men.

12 And they called Barnabas Whom the Heathens took for their chief God., Jupiter; and Paul Mercury was feigned to be the Messenger of their gods, (and therefore represented with wings;) as also the Interpreter of the gods, which caused their applying of his name to Paul. , Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker.

13 Then the Priest of Jupiter which was The Temple of Iupiter, whom they took for the Patron of their City, was in the Suburbs. before their city, brought oxen, and These were usually in the form of Crowns put upon the Oxen which they intended to Sacrifice; and by this sign, shewed that they were Dedicated to Iupiter, whom the Heathen blaspemously called, The King of kings, and placed him setting in his Chair or Throne with a Crown on his Head. garlands The Gates or Doors of the House where the Apostles • odged. unto the gates, and would have done sacrifice with the people

14 W • ich when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul heard of Which was a sign of their greatest detestation of, and sorrow for such abominations., they Matth. 26.65. rent their clothes, and Expressing their greatest zeal for the Glory of God, and earnestness to hinder the Idolatry of this People. ran in among the people, crying out,

15 And saying, Chap. 10.26. Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are We stand in need of Food and Raiment, are liable to Diseases and Death, as well as you are. men Jam. 5.17. of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these So Idols are frequently called, 1 Kings 16.13, 26. Ieremy 14.22. because they disappoint the hopes that are placed in them, and are empty of any good which is expected from them, and have nothing but what vain Men (their makers) bestow upon them. vanities unto the The True God is called, The living God, Deuter. 5.26. & Ioshua 3.10. in opposition to those false gods, who usually were only dead men, which out of Love or Fear were Deified; as also in that he lives from himself, and gives life to every living Creature. living God, Gen. 1.1. Psal. 33.6. & 146.6. Rev. 14.7. which By this also the True God is distinguished from false gods, as Ier. 10.11, 12. And is a good Argument against all Idol-worship: For Divine worship is a Tribute we owe and pay to him that made us, Psal. 100 3, 4. It should be considered with what a respective compellation the Apostles speak unto this Heathen rabble, calling them, Sirs, or Masters; a term, surely then not unlawful to be given to our equals or betters. made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:

16 There were two main Objections which these Heathen Idolaters might make against the Gospel, and the Worship of the True God: And they are, First, From the Antiquity; Secondly, From the Universality of that false worship▪ both which the Aposte here gives a criptical Answer unto, telling them, That the reason why so many, and for so long a time, had followed Idols, was from the just Judgment of God upon them, as Psal. 81.12. Rom 1.24, 28. Chap. 17.30. Who in times past suffered all nations to walk in their Ways of our chusing, and not of Gods commanding, are false ways. own ways.

17 These words are to prevent that cavil, Why does God yet complain? And informs them, that tho God had not given them, nor their Ancestors, his Laws wrote in Tables of Stone, as he had given to the Iews; yet they had had the Law written in their hearts, which they had no • obeyed, tho Gods manifold Mercies, his Works of Creation and Providence had testified unto them, that he only was to be Feared and Worshipped. How many Witnesses hath God against sinful man, when every Creature and Providence speaks his Power, Wisdom, Goodness, &c. and call upon us to love and obey him? Every Creature tells us that God made it, &c.
Rom. 1.20. Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us Matth. 5 45. rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness

18 So hard a matter it is to perswade any to leave off these sins they are accustomed unto; or, to rectify such Errors in Religion which men are brought up in. And with these sayings scarce restrained they the people, that they had not done sacrifice unto them.

19 ¶ And there came thither Such as mention was made of, Chap. 13.50. certain Jews from Antioch and • conium, who A strange and incredible sickleness: But that we know how the same Multitude who cried Hosanna, did more suddainly alter their note, and cry against our Saviour, Crucify him, Crucify him ▪ so incertain a thing is worldly honour. perswaded the people, and 2 Cor. 11.25. 2 Tim. 3.11. having The malice of Satan is every way great; if he cannot destroy the Souls of these blessed Apostles, by making of them to accept of Divine worship, he will do his utmost to kill their Bodies. stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead.

20 Howbeit, as the disciples Either, in order to bury him, thinking him to be dead, as well as his Persecutors did; or, else to defend him, as much as possibly they could, from the rage of his Enemies in that popular fury. Their spite was most against Paul, because he spake most, and Preached unto them the way of Life. stood round about him, he Being by the Power of God suddainly restored to his strength again. rose up, and came into the city: and the next day he departed with Barnabas to A city near to Lycaonia, some say▪ in it. Derbe.

21 And when they had preachd the gospel to that city, and had Had made many Disciples by Teaching, and also by Baptizing of them, Matth. 28.19. For as by Circumcision they were made Moses's Disciples, so by Baptism they are made Christs Disciples. taught many, they returned again to Lystra, and to
• conium, and to Antioch.

22 It is not enough to Sow the Seed of the Word, but it must be Watered also, frequent endeavours must be used, that it may be fruitful. Thus the Apostles return to visit such as they had Preached unto. The persecution they had endured encreasing their resolution for God, and their strength from him. Confirming the souls of the disciples, and Chap. 11.23. exhorting them to continue in the faith, and saying that Luk. 22.28, 29. Rom. 8.17. 2 Tim. 1.12. we must Lest they should be offended at what they saw St. Paul had endured, or themselves might be called to endure, they Preach unto them the Doctrine of the Cross, not hiding from them the miseries which in this World the profession of Christ, and his Truths might bring upon them. God hath indeed dealt all along thus with his People. The troubles which the Israelites met with in the Wilderness, in their Journy towards an Earthly Canaan, did Typify the Calamities which God • People will meet with in this World, as they Journy towards the Heavenly Canaan, or Ierusalem, which is above. through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.

23 And when they Ti • . 1.5. had The word properly signifies a stretching out of the Hand, such as was used when they gave their suffrages in the Election of their Magistrates, whereby was shewed for whom they gave their Voice; and afterwards it was commonly used for to constitute or appoint; or, as here, to ordain to any Office or Place; which might the rather be done by stretching out, or laying on of the Hands of the Apostles, because by that means the Holy Ghost (or a Power of working miracles) was frequently bestowed, Chap. 8.17, 18. which in those times was necessary to Authorize their Doctrine to the Infidel World. ordained them Such as might instruct and govern the Church. elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they They commended the Disciples as their Jewels and chiefest Treasure; as all sufferers are to commit their very Souls to God, 1 Pet. 4.19. commended them To Christ, the best and faithful Keeper, that he should keep and further them in Grace and Goodness; to whose Providence they wholly had committed themselves. to the Lord, on whom they believed.
24 And after they had passed throughout Going the same way back which they had came, a • appears by Chap. 13.13, 14. Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia.

25 And when they had preached The Gospel, the Word of the Lord; or Christ who is the Word, and who is the Sum of what the Ministers of the Gospel Preach about. the word Mentioned, Chap. 13.13. A City; or as some will, a Country in Pamphylia by the Seas • de. But the Bounds of Provinces were often altered by the Romans, and some made larger, and others lesser. in Perga, they went down into Attalia:

26 And thence sailed to That Antioch which was in Syria, as appears Chap. 13.1, 2, 3. to what this relates, and is a sufficient proof that they had not sought God in vain, and that there is no better preparation or provision towards any business, than faithful prayer unto God concerning it; doing our duty, and leaving the event unto his dispos • ng. Antioch, from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God, for the work which they fulfilled.

27 And when they were come and had gathered the church together, they Chap. 1 • . •
▪ 12, 27. 1 Cor. 16 •
▪ 2 Cor. 2. ••
rehearsed all
that God had done God being with them, and they being labourers with God, 1 Cor. 3.9 2 Cor. 6.1. They shewed how much God had honour'd them in making them his Instruments in the Conversion of so many Souls. with them, and how he had opened He had given the Gentiles an opportunity of knowing and believing the Gospel. The Fleece alone had been wet before, and all the Ground round about it dry; and now all the Ground is wet, and that Fleece was dry. To allude to Iudges 6.37, 39. by which this mystery was presignified, and can only be resolved by that of our Saviour, Matth. 11.25, 26. Even so Father, for so it seemed good in thy sight. the door of faith unto the Gentiles.

28 And there they abode To confirm them, as Verse 22▪ and also as our Saviour withdrew himself from the Multitudes, they chose there to refresh themselves a while here, out of the heat of contention and persecution. long time with the disciples.

div.head: CHAP. XV.
div.p: ANd These were such as did pretend to believe, but were false Brethren; some think Cerinthus to have been one of them. certain men which came down from Judea, taught the The Gentiles who were converted unto the Faith of Christ; or Proselytes of the Gate (as they were called) who were not Circumcised, and now pro • essing the True Faith. These, the Pharisaical pro • essors, would have excluded from any hopes of Salvation, altho Circumcision was not commanded, but unto the posterity of Abraham, Gen. 17.10, 11, 12. and Abraham himself was Justified before he was Circumcised, Rom. 4.10. brethren, and said, Gal. 5.2. Phil. 3.2. Col. 2.8.11, 16 Except ye be circumcised Lev. 12.3. after According unto the Law of Moses, for God by him did renew and establish that Ordinance unto that People; altho it was long before his time, both Commanded and Practised, Iohn 7 22. the manuer of Moses, ye cannot be saved.

2 When therefore That meek Apostle, who was willing to become all things unto all men, yet here enters into a holy war with them that would introduce circumcision into the Christian Church; because, 1. He would have no works of the Law to be an ingredient into our Salvation; but the free grace of God in Christ to be all in all. 2. That our freedom from all the Coremonial Law, acquired by the death of Christ, might not be diminished. 3. That the spreading of the Gospel might not be hindred, but that Christ might be accepted, and honoured amongst all; now if circumcision had been retained, it would have kept possession for all the other ceremonies to have continued, or re-entred, there being the same reason for the one as for the other; and the circumcised person was obiged by his circumcision to observe them all, Gal. 5.3, 4. Paul and Barnabas had no small dissention and disputation with them The Church at Antioch, where his controversie was moved., they determined that
〈◊〉 . 2.1. Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem Iames, Peter, and Iohn, who are thought to have been then at Ierusalem, the rest being probably gone to Preach Christ in other parts. unto the apostles and elders about this question.

3 And being brought on their way The brethren or believers of Antioch, out of respect, went part of the way with them; as also thereby shewing, that Paul and Barnabas did not go upon their own business, or mind onely; and that there was no dissention betwixt them, and the Church there. by the church, they passed through Phenice, and Samaria, declaring It is a conversion or turning indeed, from error to truth, from impurity to holiness; that is, from darkness unto light, and from the power of Satan, to the ever living God, Chap. 26.18. the conversion of the Gentiles: and they caused great Nothing more rejoyces a good man, than the bringing of Souls unto God, and the enlarging of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ. joy unto all the brethren.

4 And when they were come to Jerusalem They we • e owned with respect and thankfulness, for their great work and labour in the Lords Vineyard., they were received of the church, and of the apostles and elders, and they declared all things See Chap. 14.27. that God had done with them.

5 But If these words be taken for St. Lukes, (the Pen-man of this Book) then they declare, that in the Church of Ierusalem there were some that did abet the opinion of the necessity of circumcision; but if (as most probably we may) do take them for the words of St. Paul, they then are part of his narrative to the Church there, of what had hapned at Antioch. there Or, Rose up, said they, certain. rose up certain of the sect of the These Pharisees were a Sect amongst the Iews, (so called from 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
separavit, and may be Englished Separatists) separating from converse with others▪ by reason of an opinion they had of their own holiness, Luke▪ 18.11. Pharisees which believed, saying, That it was needful to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses▪

6 ¶ And the Unto whom Paul and Barnabas were sent about the decision of this question, verse 2. apostles and elders came together for to They had been informed of it, and now they met to deliberate about it. consider of this matter.

7 And when there had been They argued on both sides, and considered what might be said for either opinion; some of them that met here, seem at first to have been for the retaining of the circumcision; for we know but in part, and from the collision of adverse parties, such sparks fly out, that many a man hath lighted his candle at them. much disputing, Peter rose up and said unto them, Men and brethren, ye know how that From the beginning of our having received our commission to Preach, as Mat. 28.19. or more particularly, from the time of Cornelius's conversion, Chap. 10.22. and 11.12. which is thought to have been about fourteen or fifteen years before that Peter Preached Christ, by the command of God, unto the Gentiles. a good while ago, Chap. 11.2 •
▪ God made choice among us, that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the Gospel, and believe:

8 And God God knew the desires of the Gentiles, that they did sincerely desire to please God, and to see his Salvation: This great attribute David improved, 1 Chron. 29.17. and highly recommended his Son Solomon to consider of, 1 Chr. 28.9. which if believed▪ would make us also to serve God with a perfect heart, and a willing mind. which knoweth the hearts, bare them witness, God himself was a witness for these Gentiles beyond all exception, when he gave them the ordinary and extraordinary gifts of the holy Ghost; by which he testified, that they belonged to Christ, whose Spirit this was; Thus the testimony of Iesus is the spirit of prophesie, Rev. 19.10. and the Spirit, according to our Saviours promise, Iohn 15.26. doth testifie of him.
Chap. 10.44. giving them the holy Ghost, even as he did unto us:

9 And put God had now broken down the middle-wall of partition betwixt Iew and Gentile, and distributed his graces to these also, Ephes. 2.14. which was signified by the rending of the vail from the top to the bottom, Matthew 27.51. whereby such as were formerly without, might see, and injoy the benefit of those great things which had been hidden under those shadows and types. no difference between us and them, From Idolatry, and other impieties in which they had lived; which is the inward circumcision of the heart; and whosoever is thus cleansed, ought not to be reputed amongst the unclean. Chap. 10.43. 1 Cor. 1.2. 1 Pet. 1.22. purifying their hearts Faith is the instrument, God is the efficient cause of our Justification and Renovation. by faith.

10 Now therefore why Why would you make a doubt of, and put it to a trial, whether God did in good earnest admit the Gentiles to his favour, and whether he remains firm and constant in such his kindness towards them; they did tempt God also, by disliking the calling of the Gentiles, and would have brought Gods will, were it possible, unto theirs; not submitting their wills, as they ought, unto Gods, for he that sins in any kind, does tempt God; that is, he tries Gods patience, Power, and Righteousness. tempt ye Cod Mat. 23.4., to put a So the Law of Ceremonies is called, Gal. 5.1. and was a yoke indeed, if we consider, 1. Their variety, 2. Their difficulty▪ 3. Their chargeableness, 4. Their inefficacy, being onely shadows of good things to come, Col. 2.17. yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?

11 But Eph. 2.8. Titus 3.4. we believe that through the All saving-grace may be well so called, it being purchased onely by Christ, and bestowed upon us from the Father through Christ. grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, we shall be saved even The Iews their Fathers; these were saved through the grace of the Messiah which was to come; and the Apostle urges this (against the imposing of the Law) to the Iews; because neither their Ancestors nor themselves, could be justified by the Law, but onely by grace. as they.

12 ¶ Then The Apostles and Elders themselves, gave attention to what Barnabas and Paul declared; and by their silence did tacitely approve of what they had said. all the multitude kept silence, and gave audience to Barnabas and Paul, declaring what The Conversion of the Gentiles in its self, and not onely the signs which did attend it, is truly wonderful: The saving of any one Soul is a miraculous work. miracles and wonders God had wrought among the Gentiles by them.

13 ¶ And Barnabas and Paul had finished their narrative. after they had held their peace Who was sirnamed the just, and was the Son of Alpheus, and a kinsman to our Saviour, now being President of this Councel., James That is, began to speak. answered, saying, Men and brethren hearken unto me.

14 Or Simon (the name of Peter); but St. Luke being himself an Hebrew, writes it according as they pronounced it; and not so contracted as the Greeks wrote it. Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them There were some at all times probably amongst the Gentiles, who did fear God, as Iob and his three friends; but they did not make a people or such a number as is here spoken of. a people for his name.God takes out of the World a people for his name, that is, 1. For himself, as Prov. 18.10. the name of the Lord, is put for the Lord himself. 2. For to call upon his name, as also for to be called by his name. 3. For his glory and honour, and to magnifie his name.

15 And to this agree Amos 9.11, 12. the words of the In the plural number, tho onely one cited; 'tis an ordinary enallage; but also it shews the harmony amongst the Prophets, they all speaking by one Spirit; what one said, is as if all had said it. prophets; as it is written,

16 In the days of the Messiah. After this The word may be taken in both voices. If Actively, it signifies Gods returning unto the Gentiles, from whom he had departed: If Passively, it foreshews their returning unto God, whom they had forsaken. I will return, and will build again The House expressed by a Tabernacle (as frequently in Scripture) because that Anciently they dwelt only in Tabernacles. And this for the Throne of David, who was a Tipe of Christ, whose Kingdom is over all. God does promise less than he does perform, for he did not only restore the Tabernacle of David, in Christ; but raised it to a far greater Splendor and Glory in its Spiritual State. And tho St. Iames here does not exactly keep unto the words of the Prophet, he speaks their sense and meaning. the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down: and I will build again the ruins thereof, and I will set it up:

17 That In the Prophet, it is remnant of Edom, Amos 9.12. which is here called the residue of men; for as Iacob or Israel shadowed out the Church; so Edom, or Esau (the other Son of Isaac) represented those who were rejected, Rom. 9.13. The Prophet also adds, by way of Explication, all the Heathen ▪ as the Apostle does here, all the Gentiles. the residue of men may seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles upon whom Who shall be mine, or appropriated unto me; also called by his Name, they being called Christians from Christ, whom they believed in. my name is called, saith the Lord The calling of the Gentiles was Gods Work, and therefore so far from being excepted against, that it ought to be marvellous in our Eyes., who doeth all these things.

18 This the Apostle adds, that they might not be offended with the seeming novelty and surprize of the calling of the Gentiles, and abrogation of the Ceremonies; for it was no other than what God had before determined to do, and therefore they ought to rest satisfied in the Wise and Holy appointments of God. Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.

19 St. Iames here gives his opinion, confirming andapproving what Peter had done in Conversing with, and Baptizing of the Gentiles. Wherefore See ver. 2 • . my sentence is, that we Whom he would not have afflicted or disturbed with such things as were not necessary, left that it should hinder the Conversion of the Gentiles, and the Church should lose the substance for a shadow. trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God:

20 But that we write unto them, that they abstain from Eating of Meat that was offered to Idols, (as Verse 29.) in a case of scandal, and for the present state of the Church was forbid, tho afterwards in other cases indulged, 1 Cor. 10.27. pollutions Exod. 20. • . 1 Cor. 8.1. & 10.20. of idols, and 1 Thess. 4.3. from Fornication is here mentioned amongst indifferent things; not that it ever was so, but because it was amongst the Gentiles reputed to be so, even by them who punished Adultry severely. By these two some think all sins against both the Tables of the Law to be forbidden, because by one sin against each Table, all the sins against any command may Synecdochically be understood. fornication, and from things Such Creatures had not their Blood let out; and therefore were not to be fed upon, by the Law of God, Gen. 9.4. given as soon as the use of Flesh was allowed for Food. strangled, and They were also much more to abstain from Blood, when shed out of the Body of any slain Creature, Lev. 3.17. Deut. 12.23. That Blood was forbidden, might be to teach them meekness, and to abstain from revenge. It is certain, that such Nations as feed on Blood, are most barbarous and cruel. It is also probable, that these being included in the Precepts which they called, The Precepts of Adam or Noah, and to which all the Proselytes of the Gate were obliged to yield obedience: the Apostle would have the observance of them to be continued upon them that came from amongst them, over unto Christianity. For tho all these Ceremonies were dead (with Christ) yet they were not then deadly, and did wait a time for their more decent burial. If any wonder that the Councel did not treat of, and write about greater matters; As of worshipping God the Father, through the Son; of denying of our selves, and taking up the Cross; he ought to consider, that the question they met upon, was about other matters, and that those great things were never in question amongst such as feared God. from blood.

21 For The reason why St. Iames would not have the Ceremonies buried as soon as they were dead, was because the Iews had been so long confirmed in them, and bare such a love unto them; and he would purchase Concord betwixt them, and the Gentile converts; tho the Gentiles should bear with some inconvenience into the bargain, as not presently using all the liberty which through Christ they had a right unto. Moses of old time hath in every city them that preach him, Chap. 13.2 • . being read in the synagogues every sabbath-day.
