22 Then pleased it A happy concord, all agreeing as one Man, by one Spirit. the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men That Paul and Barnabas might be the better credited, and that by such as had been of a contrary Judgment: so hard it is to remove suspitions, and to root out pre-conceived opinions. of their own company to Antioch, with Paul and Barnabas; namely, The Brother of that Ioseph mentioned Chap. 1.23. Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Called Silvanus also. Silas Noted for their Holy living, or great Knowledg, or Office in the Church., chief men among the brethren.

23 And wrote letters by them after this manner The Letter was wrote in the name of them all, that it might have the greater force, and better acceptance; that so strong a Cord might not be broken by the false Apostles., The apostles, and elders, and brethren send greeting unto the brethren which are of the Such as out of Gentilism, or Paganism, were converted unto Christ; to whom the determination of this case was of greatest concern: their right of belonging unto Christ, and having any hopes of Salvation being questioned, unless they would be Circumcised. Gentiles in Antioch, and Syria; and Cilicia.

24 Forasmuch as we have heard, that certain which went out For, Verse 1. These false Apostles were such as came from Iudea; that is, from the Church there. It is Satans great policy to divide, that he may rule; he will have at least one share wherethere is mo • e than one. No such sad divisions, as Church-divisions, when that some of our selves Preach pe • verse things, as Chap. 20.30. from us, have As if in the professing of Christianity there would be no Salvation, unless Judaism be imbraced, and Circumcision admitted. No greater trouble to a considerate mind, than about the concern of Salvation, when they say, Where is thy God? troubled you with words These they did well put together; for by Circumcision they engaged to the observance of the whole Law of Moses: And by the Decreeing the omission, that whole Law of Ceremonies is declared void, and of no effect. What Truth and Unity build up, Discord and Error pull down., subverting your souls, saying, Ye must be circumcised, and keep the law; to whom we gave no such commandment:

25 It seemed good unto us, being assembled with With one Mind, as if they had all but one Soul (they had but one Spirit, the Spirit of Truth) as Chap. 2.1. and 5.12. Their Unanimity adding great strength to the Decree they sent. one accord, to send chosen men unto you, with our beloved Barnabas and Paul;

26 Because that the false Apostles at Antioch had vilified Paul and Barnabas, and opposed their Doctrine and Practice in admitting of the Gentiles by Baptism into the Church, the Councel here at Ierusalem take occasion to vindicate, and to commend them, especially for their suffering so much for Christ, of which we read, Chap. 13.50. and 14.19. It being most reasonable to believe, that they had not done or said any thing for their own sakes, who had done and suffered so much for Christ and his Truths sake. Men that have hazarded their lives, for the For Christs Honour, and the Truth of his Gospel. Rom. 1.5. name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

27 We have sent therefore Judas and Silas, who shall also tell you o the same things by
• r.
• ord. mouth.They shall inform you of the truth of what is contained in this Epistle, that you may be more assured, it is not forged or counterfeited. Of these Men, viz. Verse 22.

28 For it seemed good That is, unto us, assisted by the Holy Ghost. The Holy Ghost is deservedly first mentioned, that the Apostles might testifie that they desired to say, write, or do nothing in which they had not the Spirit of God directing of them: And they mention the Spirit, that the Antiochians, unto whom they wrote, might be assured they were not Human inventions which they recommended, but that they had the Authority of God for them. to the holy Ghost As Ministers, or Gods Stewards, who acquainted them with these things, in discharge of their duty, and that they might appear themselves to be faithful., and unto us, to lay upon you no greater The Yoke spoken of, Verse 10. burden th • n these To be sure several of the things here spoken of, are not absolutely necessary unto Salvation; or simply, and in their own nature necessary, as to abstain from Blood, &c. but tho they are not necessary always, and at all times, yet in this place, and at this time, they were necessary for the peace of the Church, and to avoid giving of offence to the converted Iews, and to nourish Brotherly love betwixt them and the Gentiles. necessary things;

29 Chap. 21.25. That ye Of th • se see more largely, Verse 20. abstain from They were wont to carry home, and Feast upon part of the Sacrifices they had offered unto their false gods; nay, they did not, withou • reproach, eat of any greater Beasts (as Oxen and Sheep) but they always first offered some of them unto their Idols. And it was accounted no small impiety to eat 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , part of any Beasts which they had not first offered up to some or other of their gods. meats offered to idols, and For this reason they might not eat of any thing that died of its self, as Deut 14.21. because the Blood was not gone ou • of it. Levit. 17 14. from blood, and from things strangled, and from Mentioned here, because so commonly practiced amongst the Gentiles, and yet not esteemed a sin. Hence also, 1 Thess. 4.3. the Apostle lay • a very great charge against it. fornication; from which if ye keep your selves, ye shall do well. The ordinary Apprecation wherewith their Letters were concluded, in which they wished health and strength to the party they wrote unto; instead of which word, some ancient Copies read 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 : which is rendred, walk in the Ho • y Ghost; or, the Holy Ghost carrying, or enabling of you. A wish or prayer becoming these holy Men that made it. They who have found the necessity of the Spirits assistance, de • ire it above all things, for such as they wish well unto. Fare ye well.

30 So when Paul, Barnabas, Iudas, and Silas; which two last were sent with the former. they were dismissed, they came to Antioch: and when they had gathered From whom they were sent, Verse 1, 2. and that this determination of the Councel might be more publickly known, as all things concerning our common Salvation ought to be. the multitude together, they delivered the epistle.

31 Which when they had read, they rejoyced It could not but much rejoyce the Gentile-Believers, that they were exempted from Circumcision, and the Ceremonial Law. And it gladded the Believing Iews also, that the Controversy was determined, and Concord established amongst them; but much more might they all rejoyce to understand the Grace of the Gospel; and that we are not justified by the deeds of the Law, but by faith in Christ, Rom. 5.1. This word also signifies Exhortation, and it was matter of Joy to be put upon such excellent duties, as our most Holy Religion recommends, and to be deterred from such erroneous Evils as it forbids. All that God requires of us, being only to eschew evil, and to do good, Isai. 1.16.17. 1 Pet. 3.11.
• or the Or, Exhortation. consolation.

32 And Judas and Silas being Not properly so called from any Gift of foretelling things to come, Eph. 4.11. but as Doctors and Teachers in the Church, expounding Moses and the Prophets, and shewing how and what they speak concerning Christ; proving out of them, that he was the Messiah, as Philip had done, Chap. 8.35. prophets also themselves, exhorted the brethren with many words, and See Chap.
• 4.22. & 18.23. confirmed them.

33 And after they had tarried there A competent time; some make this space to be a year. a space, they were let go They were dismissed with earnest Prayers for them; for by Peace is meant all kind of Good, which they desired for them, as Matth. 10.13. in peace from the brethren Such of them as were at Ierusalem, who also had sent them. unto the apostles.

34 Notwithstanding it pleased Tho having performed his message, he was discharged, and might have returned; yet for the further benefit of that Church, he continued at Antioch. Silas to abide there still.

35 Paul also and Barnabas Iudas only returned to Ierusalem, to acquaint the Apostles with the reception their Letter had met with, and what obedience was readily given to their Decrees. continued at Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord So that when these went away, the Church at Antioch was not left destitute of faithful Pastors. When God gives the word, great is the multitude of preachers, Psal. 68.11., with many others also.

36 ¶ And some days after, Paul said unto Barnabas, Let us go It is not enough that they had sown good Seed, but they must take care left it be plucked up, and Tares sown in the stead of it, by the wicked one, Matth. 13.19. A Husband-mans work is never at an end, neither is the labourers in Gods vineyard. again and visit our brethren, in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see Not so much looking after their Bodily welfare, as how their Souls fared, whether they continued in the Faith, and Integrity of life. how they do.
37 And Barnabas determined to take with them Chap. 12.12▪ 25. & 13.5. 2 Tim. 4.11. Philem. 24. John, whose surname was This Iohn or Mark ▪ was Sisters Son to Barnabas, as Coloss. 4.10. Mark.

38 But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them This deserting of Paul and Barnabas by Iohn, is mentioned, Chap. 13.13. from Pamphylia, and went not with them The work unto which the Spirit had called them, Chap. 13.2▪ which was to offer Life and Salvation unto the Gentiles, and to gather them into the Fold of Jesus Christ. This Objection was very considerable, and ought to have weighed more than this Iohns propinquity, or nearness in Blood anto Barnabas. to the work.

39 And the contention was so sharp between them, that they As Abraham and Lot parted, Gen. 13.9. yet keeping the Unity of the Spirit in the Bond of Peace; loving of▪ and praying for one another; as we may judg, being both good Men. But they verified here what they had said at Lystra, Chap. 14.15. we are men of like passions with you ▪ yet God over-ruled these very divisions betwixt Paul and Barnabas, for his own Glory, and the inlargement of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ. Several places being by this means blessed with the Gospel. And this reflection upon this Iohn Mark, is thought to have made him for the future more diligent and valiant in the cause of the Gospel, which occasioned that kind Salutation from St. Paul unto him, Coloss. 4.10. departed asunder one from the other: And so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto An Island in the Mediterranean Sea. Cyprus;

40 And Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto The favour of God, as Chap. 14.26. which the wisest and holiest Men stand in need of in all their undertakings; as also his gracious conduct and assistance. the grace of God.

41 And he went through Where there were several Brethren by reason of the dispersion that was upon Stephens death, Chap. 11.19. and 15.23. unto whom also the fore-recited Letter was wrote; Syria, and Cilicia putting them in mind of the Gospel of Christ, which they had heard and believed; and encouraging of them to persevere in the profession of it, and being ready to answer any Objection that could be brought against it., confirming the churches.

div.head: CHAP. XVI.
div.p: THen came he to Of these Cities see Chap. 14.6. Derbe and Lystra: And behold, a certain disciple was there, Phil. 2.19. 1 Thess. 3.2. named Who was known unto Paul from his Childhood, 2 Tim. 1.5. and accompanied him in many Journies, 2 Tim. 3▪10. and is called by him, his work-fellow▪ Rom 16.21. Timotheus, the son of a Called Eunice. certain woman, which was a Jewess, and Being one of them that had believed in Christ in Iudea, and had a holy Woman to her Mother, named Lois. Altho it was not Lawful for a Iew to marry a Woman of another Nation, yet some think that a Iewess might marry to a stranger, as Esther married to Ahasuerus. believed▪ but his father was a Greek:Of Gentile extraction, and therefore not Circumcised; yet he is accounted to have been a Proselyte.

2 Which Chap. 6.3. was Tho Timothy was well known unto Paul, yet ye would not Ordain him without the testimony of others concerning him, of his holy life, and knowledge in the Scripture, 2 Tim. 3.15. which he did excel in. well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and iconium.

3 Him would Paul have to go forth with him; and took and circumcised him, because of the Jews which were in those quarters: For they knew all that his father was Timothy was un
• ircumcised, altho his Mother was a Iewess; for according 〈◊〉 their Thalmudists, the Mother could not cause her Child to be Circumcised against the mind of the Father. a Greek.Who could not yet be perswaded that the Law of Circumcision was abrogated. Paul who became all things to all Men (that he might save some) Circumcised Timothy that he might not offend the Iewish Converts, 1 Cor. 9.22. but would not Circumcise Titus, Gal. 2.3. lest that he should harden them, and offend the Gentiles. These indifferent things require a single Eye, to the Edifying of the Church, and the Salvation of Souls.

4 And as they went through the cities, they delivered them the The determination of the Councel, mentioned Chap. 15.20, 29. decrees for to keep, that were • rdained of the By common consent, and not of one only, whosoever he were. apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem.

5 And so were the churches established Being rightly perswaded in the nature and use of things indifferent; and in general, of things necessarily to be believed. in the faith, and So that this visitation of the Churches had a double benefi • . First, It strengthned them that were already converted. Secondly, 〈◊〉 added more unto their number. increased in number daily.

6 Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and Galatia were parts of Asia minor. Phrygia, and the region of Galatia, and were They were forbidden of the Holy Ghost by some Revelation, (tho the manner is not known.) forbidden of the holy Ghost to preach the word in For that time, tho afterwards Paul preached there about two Years together, Chap. 19.10. Thus God (the great Housholder) orders the Candle to be removed from one Room unto another; sends, or takes away the Light of the Gospel, to whom, and as often as he pleaseth. Our Calling, as well as our Election, is free; and we may say with our Saviour, Matth. 11.26. Even so Father, for so it seemed good in thy sight. Asia.

7 After they were come to A little Country near Troas. Mysia, they assayed to go into Another Province nigh unto the same place, over-against Thracia, bordering upon the black Sea. Bithynia: but The Spirit of Jesus, or of God, as some Copies read. the Spirit The Journyings of them that preached the Gospel, as well as their words, were directed by God; they might not say, Do, or Go, but according to the will of God. suffered them not.
8 And they passing by Mysia, Chap. 20. • . 2 Cor. 2.12. came down to Either the relicts of the famous City of Troy; or, the Country thereabouts, in which the City of Antigonia was built. Troas.

9 And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: There stood An Angel i • the appearance and likeness (in habit and demeanour) to one of that Country. a man of A Grecian Province in Europe, extending to the Archipelago. Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and As to our Souls with the saving Light of the Gospel; God sends the Ministers of the Gospel to help such as would otherwise perish; with the Gospel, Salvation comes. help us.

10 And after he had seen the vision As soon as Gods will was manifested, they make no delay, not objecting against the Journey., immediately St. Luke, the Penman of this Book was one of them that went, (the others were Paul, Silas, and Timotheus) and therefore speaks in the Plural Number. we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering, that the Lord had called us for to preach the Gospel unto them.

12 And from thence to A City so called from Philip the Father of Alexander the Great, who repaired a ruined Town, and caused it to be called by his name. Philippi, which is the Or, the first city.
Or the first City in the passage from Samothracia unto Macedonia. chief city of that part of Macedonia, and Where many Roman Citizens went to inhabit; and whose Inhabitants had the freedom of the City of Rome. To the Church in this City Paul wrote an Epistle. a colony: and we were in that city abiding certain days.

13 And on the Gr. Sabbath-day. sabbath we went out of the city by a river side In those places where there were not enough to build a Synagogue, or could not obtain leave to do it, the Iews in those Countries chose more private places to meet in, which usually were near Rivers, or by the Sea-side, removed from the noise and observance of the Multitude; and these places were called Proseuches, from the Prayers which were usually made there; and to one of these, Paul and the rest went, taking that occasion to meet with them whom they might preach the Word of Life unto., where prayer was wont to be made; and we sate down, and spake unto The Women are here named, as being more numerous in those Oratories, or such as most willingly heard and attended unto what was spoken. the women which resorted thither.

14 ¶ And a certain woman named So called from the Country of that name, she being born in Thyatira. Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of A City therein; and now lived with her Family at Philippi. Thyatira, which Being a Proselyte, and one of them who had left the Heathenish Idolatry, and owned the one, only, and true God; but as yet unacquainted with the Gospel of his Son our Saviour. worshipped God, heard us: whose Hear • , in Scripture-sense, signifies both the Understanding and the Will: thus with the heart man believeth unto righteousness, Rom. 10.10. Her understanding was enligh • ned, her heart changed; she now loved what she before hated, and hated what before she loved. heart This was the Lords work: according unto what our Saviour himself had said, Iohn 6.37, 44▪ No man can come unto 〈◊〉 except the Father, which hath sent me, draw him.
〈…〉 we may in a sense open our hearts, by using such means 〈◊〉 God hath promised to succeed for that purpose, Revel. 3.20. and especially when in a sense of our inability and necessity, we implore the free Grace of God, and engage him to work in us according unto all his good pleasure. Otherwise creating a clean heart within us, as 'tis called, Psal. 51.10. is beyond the power of Nature. the Lord opened, that she Hearing is an instructive sense, and Faith cometh by it, Rom. 10.17. but it must then be accompanied with attention. attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.

15 And when she was baptized When Lydia had right to Baptism, by reason of her Faith in Jesus Christ, all her Family, whom she could undertake to bring up in the knowledg of Christ, were admitted to that Ordinance also; as all the Servants, and such other as were born in his House, or bought with his Mony, were Circumcised with Abraham, Gen. 17.12, 13. Now the Gospel does not contract in any respect, but enlarges the priviledges of Believers in all things. And if they might under the Law have their Children and Servants admitted into a Covenant with God (which could not but rejoyce Religious Patents and Masters, who value the Relation they and theirs have to God, above all Earthly things) surely under the Gospel none of our Families are excluded, unless they wilfully exclude themselves., and her houshold, she besought us, saying, If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and abide
• here. And Gen. 19.3. & 33.11. Judg. 19.21. Heb. 13.2. As the two Disciples that were going to Emaus constrained our Saviour, Luke 24.29. with all earnest intreaties, and loving violence. she constrained u • .

16 ¶ And it came to pass, as we Towards the place where their publick Prayers was usually made. went to prayer, a certain damsel, possessed with a spirit Or, of Python, the name of Apollo, from the place where he was worshipped (which was afterwards called Delphi) and from whom all Evil spirits, that pretended to Divination, were called Pythons; as that the Woman made use of to delude Saul by, 1 Sam. 28.7. Or, of Python. of divination, met us, which brought her masters Chap. 19.24. much gain by soothsaying:

17 The same followed Paul, and us, and cried, saying, The Devil might be forced by God to confess this; or, he might do it voluntarily by Gods permission: First, To draw men on to believe him in other things, being he commended the Servants of God, and spake the truth in this. Secondly, That by flattering of St. Paul, he might puff him up, and occasion him to sin. But an Evil spirit (or an Evil man) when he dissembles as if he were good, is then worst of all. These men are the servants of the most high God, which shew unto us the way of salvation,

18 And this she did many days. Bu • Paul being St. Paul was grieved; either, for the Maids sake, who suffered so much by her being possessed with this spirit; or, for their sakes who were seduced by him. grieved, turned and said to the spirit St. Paul (as our Saviour had done, Mark 1.25.) refuseth the testimony of the Devil; for he being the Father of Lyes, Ioh. 8.44. makes every thing he says to be suspected▪ as 'tis an usual punishment of Lyars, that they are not believed when they speak the truth; and the Devil never speaks any truth, but with an intention to deceive., I command thee By the Authority and Power of Christ. in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he Mark 16.17. came out the same hour.

19 ¶ And when her For she was a servant, or slave; and being very advantageous, might have many that had a share in h • r. masters saw that the hope of their The profit could not but be considerable, for they were to come with the rewards of divination in their hands; as they did to Balaam, Numb. 22.7. gains was gone, they caught Paul and Silas, and drew them into the Or, Court. market-place, unto the See the next Verse. rulers.

20 And brought them to the The same who are called Rulers: and the word here shews, that they were under the power of the Sword, and ruled by the Romans; tho the Rulers spoken of in the former Verse, might be the Civi • Magistrates of the City, and the Magistrates here mentioned might be the Commanders of the Forces therein; they carried them, as they did our Saviour, from one 〈◊〉 the other, the more to disgrace them, and to obtain the greater punishment for them. magistrates, saying, These men They mention their being Iews, because it was a most odious name unto all Men, by reason of their different Opinions in Religion, and diversity of manners in conversation from all. being Jews, do
〈◊〉 . 18.17. Chap. 17.6. exceedingly trouble our city,

21 And teach customs which are not lawful for us to receive, neither to observe, being There was at Philippi, as appears, Verse. 12. a Colony of the Romans, and they were governed by their Laws, by which they might make no innovation in Religion, without the consent of the Senate, and afterwards of their Emperors; which here these persecutors alledge. Romans.

22 And the Generality, and Unanimity alone, cannot Authorize Opinions or Practises. multitude rose up together against them: and the magistrates rent off their clothes, 2 Cor. 11.25. 1 Thess. 2.2. and commanded to beat them.
Pauls and Silas's Clothes▪ to disgrace them the more, or in order unto their being scourged, tho some think that the Magistrates rent their own Clothes in detestation of the pretended Blasphemy which was laid to Pauls charge; as the High Priest did, Mark 14.63.

23 And when they had laid Partly, by the Lictors or Executioners; and partly, by the furious Rabble. many stripes upon them, they cast them into prison, charging the This Jaylor (of whose Conversion we read hereafter) his name was Stephanas, as may appear if you compare 1 Cor. 1.16. with what follows by St. Luke in this Story. Of him also we read, 1 Cor. 16.15, 17. Jaylor to keep them safely.

24 Who having received such a charge, thrust them into the Thus they dealt with Ioseph, Gen. 39.20. compared with Psal. 105.18. and with Ieremiah, and with Iohn Baptist. Sanctorum sors est, & non moleste ferenda. inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks.

25 ¶ And at No time or place where Prayer is not accepta •• e unto God, and prevalent with him: nay, it sounds the sweeter when on the Waters of affliction a good Man pours it forth unto God. mid-night Paul and Silas prayed, and sang That they were counted worthy to suffer for Christ: And being all things are over-ruled for the 〈◊〉 and conduce to the advantage of them tha •
〈◊〉
• od, Rom. 8.28. they owe unto God thanks for all things through Jesus Christ; which is also required of them, Ephesians 5.20. praises unto God: and the prison ••• heard them.

26 Chap. 4.31. And How soon is Prayer answered, when the fulness of time is come? So nigh is God unto all that call upon him, Psal. 34.17. & 145.18. suddenly there was a An Earthquake did usually precede some wonderful matter; as Matth. 28.2. And altho God could have delivered these his Servants without an Earthquake; yet to shew the more that their deliverance was his Work, and it was no artifice, or force of their own, he manifested his Power after this manner. great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately Chap. 5.19. & 12.7. all the doors were opened, and every ones bands Either, by the Earthquake, or some secret power of an Angel, or by God himself immediately, that the Apostles and others might know, that the Souls of Men should be unloosed and set free by them, whose Bodies for that purpose were now freed by God. were loosed.

27 And the keeper of the prison By the Earthquake, which being upon an extraordinary occasion, could not fail to do all that God intended by it. awaking out of his sleep, and seeing the prison-doors open, he drew out his sword, and would For fear of suffering a more cruel death: for all Jaylors, who let any Prisoner escape, were to suffer the same punishment that the Prisoners were thought to have deserved; and self-murder was very ordinary amongst both the Romans and Grecians. But whatsoever their Philosophers have said of it, it must needs have been a very great provocation against God, to shew so great an aversion from Gods Will, disposing of them and their concerns in this World, and challenging or daring of him to do worse by them in the Wo •••
• o come. Men must have sad comforts, and take 〈…〉 resolutions, that come to this once. have killed himself, supposing that the prisoners had been fled.

28 But Paul cryed with a loud voice, saying, Do thy • elf no h • rm? for we are The other Prisoners were smitten with amazement; neither did they mind (or it might have been kept from them) that the doors were opened, and their chains loosed: but as for the Apostles, the same God who wrought this deliverance for them, might inform them of the intent of it; that by this means the conversion of the Jaylor and his family was intended; and that their Doctrine might be magnified, which had been so much vilified. all here.

29 Then he called Or lights, which Prisons are not usually without. for a light, and sprang in, and came What a suddain and great change can God make? He comes trembling to those feet which he had put into the Stocks so lately. trembling, and By which he would only give a civil respect unto them, it being an ordinary Rite amongst the Eastern Nations (as endless Examples in Scripture-witness) to pay their Respects: and from them it spread its self into Greece: which Respect Paul and Silas do not refuse, because it was barely civil, and did shew the humility and brokenness of the Jaylors heart. Yet Peter would not accept of the like from Cornelius, Chap. 10.25, 26. because it was more than a bare civil Respect which Cornelius would have given him. fell down before Paul and Silas;

30 And brought Into his own apartment in the prison, or to some more open and free place. them out, and said A term of respect given by the Romans and Grecians to such whom they honour'd, as now the Jaylor did these seemingly most contemptible men. Luke 3.10. Chap. 2.37. and 9.6., Sirs He might have some knowledg of a future state, which he here enquires after, 1. By the very light of Nature. 2. Tradition. 3. The Doctrine of the Philosophers. 4. By his frequenting with Iews and Proselytes. Men under fears, and in dangers, as to the things of this world, are brought to look after another world (as every one prays in a storm): but this is onely when God is pleased to sanctify such fears and disasters; otherwise all the plagues of Egypt do but harden them the more, Exod. 7.3., what must I do to be saved?

31 And they said John 3.16, 36. and 6.47. 1 John 5.10., Believe This is the sum of the Gospel. Christ apprehended by faith, serves for Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification, and Redemption, as 1 Cor. 1.30. But then this precious Faith must be such as works by love, as purifies the heart, Chap. 15.9. as overcomes the world,
• John 5.4. as quenches the fiery darts of the devil, Eph. 6.16. and is deservedly called, a most holy faith, Jude 20. on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved Thou shalt by this means come to obtain that life thou dost so much desire after; and not only thy self, but (God that gives more than we ask) thy children and family shall be saved; in as much as the Covenant, where it is entred into, is not only with them, but with their children., and thy house.

32 And th • y sp • ke unto him the Expounding more at large that which they had briefly propounded in the foregoing verse, as concerning the Natures and Offices of Christ; especially his suffering for our sins, and rising again for our justification. word of the Lord, and to Their fellow Prisoners not exempted, unto whom it was a joyful confinement, being by this means made God's Freemen. all that were in his house.

33 And he took them He did not delay to shew forth the fruits of his faith, and real conversion. the same hour of the night Which his stripes had made, using such means as might asswage their pain, and heal their wounds., and washed their stripes; and was baptized, he and See on, ver. 15. and 32. Of Baptism administred without any delay, upon their profession of Faith in Christ, we have had Examples, Chap. 8.38. and 10.47. and in the 15th verse of this Chapter. all his, straightway.

34 And when he had brought them Which was close unto, or a separate part of the Prison, into which they did ascend, heing before in a low Dungeon. into his house Luke 5.29. and 19.6., he set Paul and Silas had been long fasting; and in any season of the night it was a mercy to them to have a Table spread for them. meat before them, and Finding the effects of his faith, peace with God, and joy in the Holy Ghost; which was not a little augmented, in that he had his Family admitted into the Cove • ant of God's Grace, they also believing, and being baptized. r • joiced, believing in God with all his house.

35 And when it was day, the magistrates sent Their Messengers, or Officers, which did carry a Mace, or a Rod, from whence they had their name. the sergeants Probably being terrified with the Earthquake, which if it had not been general, they could not yet have heard of. Their consciences might also accuse them for having unjustly punish'd them for a good deed which they had done, only to gratifie the rage of the multitude; a •
•• so because they had acted against the custom of the 〈…〉 tho they did not yet know that they had the 〈…〉
Roman Citizens), and had beaten strangers without any legal trial, or form of Law., saying, Let those men go.

36 And the keeper of the prison told this Being glad that he might release them. Neither does he bid them go, as desirous to be rid of them; but not requiring any fees, he lets them go to preach the Gospel, and fulfil their Ministry, with his prayers and well-wishes. saying to Paul, The magistrates have sent to let you go: now therefore depart, and go in peace.

37 But Paul said The Officers who were sent to the prison with the message about their liberty. unto them The Magistrates who commanded them to be beaten, are justly charged with the beating of them; as if they had themselves done it., They have beaten us It was no small aggravation of their injustice, and these holy mens sufferings, that they had, for the greater spite unto them, openly scourged them. openly For they were not tried, or permitted to speak for themselves. uncondemned Having the priviledg of Roman Citizens; which was sometimes given to whole Communities. Now such by their Laws might not be bound, much less beaten (and least of all uncondemn'd) without the consent of the Romans.
Chap. 22.25., being Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily, but let them come This the Apostle stands upon, not so much for his own, as for the Gospel's sake, that it might not be noised abroad, that the Preachers of it were wicked and vile men, and did deserve such ignominious punishment. Tho they were as innocent as doves, it became them also to be as wise as serpents. themselves, and fetch us out.

38 And the sergeants told these words unto the magistrates, and they For the Romans (under whom these Magistrates were) made it by their Laws to be Treason thus to abuse any of their Citizens. God over-ruled their fear of man, for the deliverance of his servants. feared when they heard that they were Romans.

39 And they came and Two things the Magistrates had to desire of them, 1. That they would excuse the wrong done unto them, which they feared lest the Romans might revenge. 2. That to avoid further mischiefs (as they thought) they would leave the City. But the words here used do signifie also, that they comforted them, as well as besought, or exhorted them: Both by word and deed they sought to make amends for the injury they had offer'd unto them; and desired them to depart for their own safety, lest the people should express their rage and madness more against them. besought them, and brought them out, and Mat. 8.34. desired them to depart out of the city.

40 And they went out of the prison, and entred into the house of Lydia: and when they had seen the brethren, they In respect of the tribulation they had endured, and were still to endure, or exhorted them to prepare for suffering▪ and to submit unto God in it, and to make an holy use of it. com • orted them, and departed.Of whom, ver. 14. They do not shun dangers, so as to neglect their duty.

div.head: CHAP. XVII.
div.p: NOw when they had passed through A City near to Philippi; so called, because the Sea came up to it on both sides. Amphipolis, and A City near to Thessalonica. Apollonia, they came to This Thessalonica was one of the chiefest Cities of Macedonia; Unto the Church in this place St. Paul wrote two of his Epistles. This City was built by Philip, in memory of a Victory he obtained over the Thessali. Thessalonica It seems that there was no Synagogue in either of the other places; but that the Iews of the other Cities resorted unto the Synagogue in this; all these three Cities being in Macedonia. The sending a way of Paul and Silas, chap. 16.39. to gratifie the mad multitude, was a means to bring the word of salvation to those places., where was a synagogue of the Jews.

2 And Paul, as Who was faithful unto him that had called him, and took all occasions to do his Master's work. his manner was, went in unto
them, and three sabbath-days reasoned with them The Law and the Prophets▪ which they owned to be of Divine Authority; And from the holy Scriptures alone all knowledg in the things of God, and of our salvation, must be fetched. If any speak of these matters not according to them, it is because they have no light in them, Isa. 8.20. What Scriptures St. Paul alledged 〈◊〉 not set down; but they were such as our Saviour 〈…〉 use of, Luke 24.27. for the same purpose. This was customary with Paul, to preach these things unto the Iews first; as Chap. 13.46. till they had put the word of God from them by their incredulity. out of the scriptures.

3 The Scriptures which he had quoted. The very entrance into God's Word giveth light, Psal. 119.130. Opening and Making the truth concerning our Saviour, which he preached, so plain to the eye of their understanding, as any thing which is exposed to the view of our bodily eyes. alledging, that Christ must Comparing the words of the Prophets concerning Christ, with those things which were done and suffered by him, Psal. 22.6. Isa. 53. throughout, Matth. 16.21. Luke 24.26, 46. needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead: and that this That Jesus whom Paul preached was the true and only Messiah, and that what was written of the Messiah, was fulfilled in him. Jesus Or, whom I said. whom I preach unto you, is Christ.

4 Chap. 28.24. And some of them believed, and Were so affected towards them, as that they were willing to take the same part or lot with them. The word imports the nearest and intimatest friendship▪ and union; even such as is conjugal. consorted with Paul and Silas: and of the Such of that Nation as were become Proselytes, who had renounc'd the Idolatry and wicked conversation of the Heathen, amongst whom they lived; and had joyned themselves to the Iews; at least so far as to hear the Law and the Prophets read and expounded in their Synagogues; and did worship but one God, and did injury unto none. Of these we frequently read in this book; as ver. 17. and chap. 13.42, 43. and 16.14. devout Greeks a great multitude, and of the chief women A considerable number of these believed; yet chap. 13.50. such had stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas. not a few.

5 ¶ But the Jews which Or were not convinced, or perswaded by St. Paul's Sermons and Arguments. believed not, moved with Or Zeal; which as fire in the chimney, its due place, is useful and necessary; but when scatter'd abroad, and out of its place, is most dangerous and destructive envy, took unto them certain Such as stand in Markets, and publick places, gazing, and having nothing to do. lewd fellows To what mean and base acts do not blind zeal, and the rage of persecutors descend? of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uprore, and assaulted the house of Some think this to be the Greek name which the Hellenists did use for Ioshua, or Iesus. This man was one of the dispersion, who came from Iudea into Syria; and from thence into Macedonia; and is famous so far as the Word of God is preached, for being the Host to Paul and Silas; and is mentioned Rom. 16.21. Jason, and sought to bring them For to slay them. Nothing but their blood could quench the thirst of their persecutors: But having no just cause for the spilling of it, they are willing to have others to bear the odium of it. out to the people.

6 And when they Being withdrawn, to avoid the popular rage against them, they charge Innovation upon them, as knowing how jealous Rulers are of any alteration. Thus whatsoever mischiefs befel the State, or whatsoever was odious and abominable, was in the Primitive times still charged upon the Christians. The Enemies of God's Church cloathe his servants in beasts skins (painting, and representing them in what forms they please), that every one may hunt and worry them. found them not, they drew Jason, and certain brethren unto the rulers of the city, crying Chap. 16.20▪ , These that have w turned the world upside down, are come hither also;

7 Whom Jason hath Privily, and with design. received: and these all do contrary to the decrees The Romans before they were brought under their Emperors (and after that), did not suffer any to be called King without their allowance and approbation; which was also much valued by such unto whom that Honour was bestowed by them. of Cesar, saying Luke 23.2. 〈◊〉
▪ 19.12., That there is another Besides Cesar, who was called the Lord of the World. This is like to the charge laid against our Saviour; but most maliciously both then and now, and wholly against their own consciences; For they themselves expected the Messiah to be a King, Ioh •
18.36, 37. and refused and rejected him, because his Kingdom was a spiritual Kingdom, and not of this World. king, one Jesus.

8 And they troubled Hearing something to have been done against the Roman State, under whom they were, and not knowing what it might come to, or how it might be construed. the people, and the For fear of an insurrection and tumult. rulers of the city, when they heard these things.

9 And when they Either being satisfied with their answer, or having Bail for their appearance, if need were; the word only hinting their being satisfied, or contented; as Mark 15.15. had taken security of Jason, and of the other, they let them go.

10 ¶ And Chap. 9.2 • . the brethren immediately sent away Paul and Silas by night unto B • rea: who coming thither, went into the They went still first unto the lost sheep of the House of Israel. In which Paul's invincible love which he speaks of, Rom. 9.2. does manifestly appear. The Iews had every where endeavoured his destruction; he still requites them (what he may) in promoting their salvation. synagogue of the Jews.A City also of Macedonia, not far from Pella, and Thessalonica.

11 Th • se were The Iews of Berea did excel those of Thessalonica, not so much in birth as in disposition: They were not so prejudiced and obstinate; they patiently heard Paul, they seriously thought upon what he had said, and compared it with the Scriptures. And thus God gave them the preparation of the heart; and they brought their empty Vessels. No wonder then that the Oyl of Grace ran into them, and filled them▪ The Iews do call their Learned men, the sons of Nobles; and according to that expression, these Bereans that had acted so ingenuously and wisely, were said to be more Noble. more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readine • s of mind, and Truth dares abide the Test; only false wares need a dark shop to put them off in. Isa. 34.16. Luke 16.29. John 5.39. searched the The Scriptures only are our infallible Rule; for they come from God, 2 Tim. 3.16. who cannot lie, Titus 1.2. scriptures daily, whether those thing • were so.

12 Therefore many of them believed: also of honourable women which were Greeks, and of men not a few.God blessing his own gifts, and giving still unto them that had, and made use of them: And would we also lay aside all filthiness, and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the ingrafted Word, which is able to save our souls, Iames 1.21. we should find the hand of the Lord not to be shortned, but his Word as powerful, as piercing, as converting as ever.

13 But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledg that the word of God was preached of Paul at Berea As the waves are stirred with the wind; a fit Metaphor to represent the fickle multitude by; that as the Sea now rolls one way, then another; or as tottering buildings that shake with every wind., they came thither also, and stirred up the people.

14 And then immediately the brethren sent away Paul That they might give over the pursuit of him; or at least, be disappointed if they did pursue him, being he went on foot to Athens. , to go as it were to the sea: but The fury of the persecutors not being so hot against them as against Paul, who was more known or maligned than Silas or Timotheus: Or these might abide there longer, having their Relations in Macedonia. Silas and Timotheus abode there still.

15 Who accompanied him, and had undertaken to secure him. And they that conducted Paul, brought him unto The Greece of Greece, or the Eye of Greece; as Greece was accounted the Eye of the World; and yet with all its Learning did not attain to saving knowledg, until Paul came and preached it. Satan •• malice still causes the Gospel to spread. Athens: and Chap. 1 • .5. receiving a commandment unto Silas and Timotheus, for to come to him with all speed, they departed.

16 ¶ Now while Paul wait • d • or them at A • hens, his spirit was Moved, and sharpned, being highly affected with divers passions, 1. With grief for so learned, and yet blind and miserable a place. 2. With zeal, and an holy desire to instruct and inform it. 3. With anger and indignation against the idolatry and sin that abounded in it. stirred in him, when he saw the city Or as the marginal reading hath, full of Idols. For we read, that there were more Idols in Athens, than in all Greece besid • s; and that it was easier to find a God there (that is, a • Idol) than a man; their Images being as numerous as their Inhabitants. wholly given Or, Full of Idols. to idolatry.

17 As ver. 2. still giving the Iews, if there were any, the priority; or having by that means an opportunity to speak unto the Proselytes of the Gentiles.
▪ Therefore disputed he in the synagogue with the Jews, and with Who are the devout persons here meant, see Chap. 13.43. the devout persons, and in Because of the concourse thither; throwing the Net of the Gospel where there were most Fish; and he himself preaching, as he exhorted others to do, in season and out of season, 2 Tim. 4.2. the market daily with them that met with • im.

18 Then▪ certain Both these sects of Philosophers were the most opposite to Christianity of all others: 1. The Epicureans (so called from one Epicurus) did generally deny, that the World was made, or that it is governed by God; as also, that there were any Rewards or Punishments for men after death, holding nothing to be good but what was so to their senses: And if so, were indeed swine rather than men. 2. The Stoicks were so called from the place where they met at first; and held as bad Opinions as the other did; and denied, that their Wise men were inferior to their Gods; and in some respect preferred them before their Gods; which their Seneca was not free from, Epist. 73. And no wonder if such men oppose the Gospel what they may. philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountred him: And some said, What m will this Or, Base fellow. babler say? Other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of They might amongst the Athenians bring in by publick Authority as many Gods as they would, but none out of their private Opinions; which was the fault charged upon Socrates. strange gods: because he preached unto them So ignorantly, or maliciously did they pervert St. Paul's words, that they accuse him for making the Resurrection a God too. Probably they heard him often naming▪ the word, and magnifying of the Resurrection, as without which, we were without hope. Jesus, and the resurrection.They make Paul so contemptible, comparing him to such as live by the off-falls of Corn, which was used to be gathered up as they fell down in measuring, and left to be fed upon by the meanest and poorest of the people.

19 And they took him, and brought him The city of Athens was divided into five Wards, or parts; one of which was called Areopagus, from the Temple of Mars, which stood upon an hill in it; nigh unto which Temple, or in some part of it, was their chiefest Court kept; and here they judged of all Religious Affairs: here they condemned Diagoras, Protagoras, and Socrates; and hither they bring Paul, tho rather to enquire of him (there being the resort of Learned men) concerning his Doctrine, than to condemn him for it. unto Or, Mars hill. It was the highest Court in Athens. Areopagus, saying, May we know what this new doctrine, whereof thou speakest, is?

20 For thou bringest certain The greatest Objection which these men had against the Gospel, was, that it was strange and new. That it is not new, was apparent, it having been in the Old Testament (as the ripe fruit is in the blossom) so long ago; and their own Superstitions were but so many Apish imitations of God's Worship. And 〈◊〉 these things were strange unto them, they might thank themselves, who had not made due enquiring after them; and had by their not improving the light of Nature, provoked G • d to withhold further manifestations unto them, Rom. 1.24, 28. strange things to our ears: we would know therefore what these things mean.

21 For all the Athenians, and Which must needs have been a considerable number, Athens being then a famous Haven-Town and University; and these strangers might easily take this itch after News from the Natives, who are noted for it b •
Theophrastus, D •
mostbenes, &c. strangers which were there, spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.

22 ¶ Then Paul stood in the midst Or, Court of the Areopagites. of See ver. 19. Ma • shill, and said, Ye men of Athen • , I perceive that in all things ye are Sometimes this word is taken in a good sense; many then, as now, taking Superstition to be Religion. But it is often taken in a bad sense. Thus Theophrastus says, that a truly pious man is a friend of God; 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 ; but the superstitious man is a flatterer of God. Now this word being then of a kind of middle signification, the Apostle would seem not to bear too hard upon the Athenians, who were devout and religious, according to the measure of their knowledg, and whom he desired to win by love and gentleness. too superstitious.

23 For as I passed by, and beheld Any thing unto which Divine Worship and Honour is given. your Or, Gods th •• you worship. 2 Thes. 2▪4. devotions, I found an altar with this inscription It is storied, That in a Plague-time, when the Athenians had wearied themselves with their supplications unto all the gods of their Countrey, they were advised by Epaminondas (a devout man amonst them), to erect an Altar unto that god who had the power over that Disease, whosoever he was; which because they did not know, and would be sure not to omit in their devotions, they erected an Altar unto him under the Name of the Unknown God. Some say, there was a more general Inscription, To the Gods of Asia; Europe and Africa, to the unknown and strange Gods; tho the Inscription the Apostle mentions in the singular Number, might be usual too: for the Athenians, who entertain'd all manner of Gods, fearing lest there should be any which they had not heard of, for their greater security, as they imagined, would have an Altar for such also. Now▪ this Vnknown God, St. Paul says, which was worshipped by them, was the true God: For, 1. They had an apprehension, that Christ was the true God, whilst that wonderful Eclipse at his Death was effectually considered amongst them. Hence it is said, that Dionysius, cried out, Deus ignotus in carne patitur. Now the unknown God▪ suffers in the Flesh. 2. The God of the Iews, whose Name the Iews took to be so ineffable, that they would not undertake to speak it; and who was not wholly unknown to Plato and Pythagoras; and who is truly invisible and incomprehensible, might upon that account be thus stiled amongst them., TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye g ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.

24 God that made the world, and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, As if he could be tied to them, or circumscribed by them▪ Yet God did in some respect dwell in his Temple, where he did manifest himself more clearly than in other places: But that was a type of Heaven, the Throne of God. Chap. 7.4 • . dwelleth not in temples mode with hands:This seems to be directed against the Epicureans, who held, that the World was without beginning.

26 And hath made of 1. To teach all charity and compassion towards one another, being so nearly allied to one another. 2. As also to admire God more in that variety that appears in mens shapes and voices, but especially in the diipositions of their minds; whenas they all come from one stock and stem. one blood, all nations of men, for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined The Apostle asserts the providence of God against these Athenian Philosophers, that nothing comes by chance, or a satuitous concourse of Atomes; but that God is in every thing, tho men know it not, or rather will not consider it, Iob 7.1. and 14.5, 14. This Doctrine was preached by Moses, who tells the people, that God is their life, and the length of their days; that they might love him, and obey his voice, and cleave unto him, Deut. 30.20. the times before appointed, and the Deut. 32.8. bounds of their habitation:

27 The Apostle tells these Philosophers, to whom he spake, the true use of their Philosophy, to improve their knowledg of natural things; to beget in them by it an admiration of the God of Nature: for as from him, so for him are all things. Rom. 11.36. That they should seek the Lord, if haply they And although God himself is incorporeal, yet the things which he made are palpable; and did they seek as they ought, they might find a great deal of God out by the creatures, in which his Wisdom, Power and Goodness is manifested, Rom. 1.20. might feel after him, and find him, though he be God filleth all things, especially he is near in the effects of his Wisdom, Goodness and Faithfulness, by which he orders and disposes of all things, to the falling off of a hair from our Heads. not far from every one of us:

28 For in him He is the God that made us, that preserve • us, and not we our selves; he keeps us as in the hollow of his hand, and compasseth our paths. Our breath is in our Nostrils, and when we send it forth, we have none to take in again, unless God furnish us with it, as out of his own hand. we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his off-spring. Aratus a Greek Poet; not that St. Paul thought to derive any Authority from these Poets, unto what he had said; but that he might shame them the more by the Testimony of their allowed Authors. Such Quotations as these are (as the bringing in of a Greek into the Temple) very rare; yet besides this, we meet with the like, 1 Cor. 15.33. Titus 1.12.

29 Forasmuch then as we are the off-spring of God, Isa. 40.18. we Taking man in his natural principles, consisting of Soul and Body, he is not made of Gold and Silver, much less can God be made of them. Our Soul, in which we bear the Image of God, cannot be expressed by any Graving or Painting; much less God whose Image it is. There are two things to be considered in every Image, its matter, and its form or shape; The matter of an Image, let it be never so precious, is much inferior to Man; for, it lies in the earth (be it Gold or Silver) for man to trample upon, until he dig it up, and take it out▪ As for the form of the Image, it is that which men p • ease to give it, and man is a kind of Creator of it; howsoever it is his workmanship, and the work is more ignoble than the workman; at least not to be adored by him▪ ought not to think that the G • dhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone graven by art and mans device.This is spoken by the Apostle in a Poetical expression; according unto what he had cited. We are indeed the Children, and in our Souls bear the Image of God. But as many as have the spirit of Adoption, they partake of Gods Holiness, and imitate his Goodness, and are more like unto him, by whom they are begotten again unto a lively hope, 1 Pet. 1.3. and at the Resurrection they will appear unto all to be his Children, when they shall be acknowledged his Heirs, and Coheirs with Jesus Christ, Rom. 8.17. According to mans will and pleasure, for the Image cannot determine its self to be made as it would.

30 And the Chap. 14.16. times of this ignorance To prevent an Objection, lest any should think that they might continue in their unbelief, and fare as well as their Progenitors, God is said to have overlooked them; as if he had counted them unworthy of his Care and Providence: And therefore he did not correct or instruct them. When any are left to go on in their sin, without God's instruction or correction, it is a sad sign that God scorns to look upon them, or to use any means to recover them. God winked at; but Under the Gospel we are so far from having liberty to do what we list, that we are more nearly concerned to repent and become Holy, Rom. 13.11. Titus 2.11, 12. 1 Pet. 1.14, 15. and that all men, every where, without exception of time or place, are under this command of Repentance; and cursed indeed will he be that does not observe it. L • ke 24.47. now commandeth all men every where to repent:

31 Because he hath That God will judge the world, his enemies have with trembling acknowledged; but when God will judge the world, he hath conceal'd it from his friends; yet the time is already set, Psal 96.13. 2 Cor. 5.10. and we ought to be daily prepared for it. appointed a day in the which Chap. 10.42. he will judge the world Shall not the Judge of all the world do right? in righteousness, Our blessed Saviour, called here man, suitably to his death and resurrection which St. Paul Preached of, as also as man he is thus highly exalted for his debasing of himself for our sakes, Ph • l. 2.9, 10, 11. by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath An undeniable proof or argument, it being so difficult a matter to believe a world to come, when we see all things remain as they did in this world; and especially to believe▪ that in the general judgment, Christ whom they had Judged, Condemned and Executed, should be Judge: God therefore did glorify him, by raising him from the dead, that they and we might not be faithless, but believe, Rom. 1.4. given Or, Offered 〈◊〉 . assurance unto all men, in that he Chap. 2.24. hath raised him from the dead.

32 ¶ And when they heard of the resurrectio • of the dead, The Epicureans, whom Paul had spoken against in his Doctrine of the Resurrection from the dead, and Judgment to come. some mocked: and 'Tis thought the Stoicks, who did not think the Resurrection to be impossible, but did acknowledg Rewards and Punishments in the world to come; yet, tho • his seem most likely, the Grace of God is free and powerful, and can subdue any unto its self. We are sure that there be different Soils into which the Seed of the Word is cast▪ Matt. 13 others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.
33 So Paul departed Leaving what he had said, to God's Blessing, and their Consideration. from among them.

34 Howbeit, certain men In more than ordinary friendship, they were as glewed to him; great was their love to the Apostle, by whom their eyes were opened; nay, by who • e Ministry they were raised from the dead. clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the One of that great Councel mentioned vers. 19. whose conversion might have a great influence upon many. Areopagi • e, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.Who is thought to have been an honourable woman. Such are mentioned; vers: 12. or she might have been specially eminent for some Grace or Goodness she excelled in, and therefore hath a name upon record in the Word of God.

div.head: CHAP. XVIII.
div.p: 2 And found a certain Jew named Rom. 16.3. 1 Cor. 16.19. Aquila, born A Country between Cappad • cia and the Black Sea, Acts 2.9. whither the Progenitors of A • uila, in one of the dispersions, might flee from Iudea to inhabit there. in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome) and came unto them.The Roman Emperor, who, at the beginning of his Reign gave liberty to the Iews freely to exercise their Religion, but about eight years after took away that priviledge from them, which S • etonius makes mention of▪ tho very much mistaking the reason: With the Iews, 'tis thought that the Christians were banished too; for the Pagan Romans did not care to distinguish betwixt them, they both worshipping but one God, and agreeing in opposing their Idolatry.

3 And because he was of the same The most learned amongst the Iews did always learn some handy-craft, and it was one of those things which they held a Father was bound to do for his Child, viz. to teach him some Trade. And one of their Rabby's sayings is, That whosoever does not teach his Child a Trade, does as bad as if he did teach him to play the Thief. St. Paul wrought with his hands, not so much because as yet there was no Church there that could maintain him; but 1. because▪ he would not be burdensome unto them, they being, probably most mean persons that believed there, as appears, 1 Cor. 1.26. Or 2. That he might shew how that he did not covet theirs, but them; and to gain nothing but Souls amongst them. Yet he asserted his right, and the right of Ministers, by Divine appointment, to live of the Gospel, 1 Cor. 9.6, 11, 12. craft, he abode with them, and e Chap. 20.34. 1 Cor. 4.12. 1 Thes. 2.9.
• rought (for by their occupation they were tent-makers)Tents were used by Soldiers, and in those hot Countries by others also, being usually made of Skins sewn together to keep off the violence of the weather.

4 And he Or Argued and Disputed, giving his Reasons out of Scripture, and answering their Objections, reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and not only using cogent Arguments; but, as some understand the Verb, such as did prevail upon them. perswaded the Jews, and the Not such as were of the Jewish race, and after the dispersion used the Scripture in the Greek Tongue; but such as were Gentile-Greeks, Greeks by descent. Greeks.

5 And when Silas and Timotheus According as was ordered by him, Chap. 17.14, 15. were come from Macedonia, Paul was More than ordinarily affected, the Spirit of God influencing his Spirit; so that he felt an anguish or pain at the heart (as 2 Cor. 2.4.) such was his grief for the contumacy of the Iews; so great was his desire that they might be saved. pressed in spirit, and testified unto the Jews, that Jesus Or, is the Christ. was 1. The Christ, or Anointed, that excelled all other Christs or Anointed ones, being anointed with Oil above measure. 2. The Christ that was promised by the Prophets. Christ.

6 And Chap. 13.45. when they opposed themselves, They blasphemed Paul, miscalling of him, but especially Christ, whose dishonour grieved Paul most. and blasphemed, he His upper Garment, as the ma • ner was, Matt. 26.65. that none of the dust of that place where such blasphemy was spoken, might stick unto him. See Chap. 13.51. Matth. 10.14. shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your b • ood be Or you are guilty of your own deaths and damnation, 2 Sam. 1.16. Matt. 27.25. Felo de se; this expression is borrowed from the Witnesses laying their hands on the head of the guilty person; or the Sacrificer's laying his hand on the head of the Beast which was to be slain, Exod. 29.10. Le • . 1.4. upon your own heads; free from their blood, or the loss of their Souls, having warned them, and shewn the way of Life unto them, Ezek. 33.4. He had blown the Trumpet, and warned the people. I Ezek. 3.18. am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

7 ¶ And he departed thence, and entred into a certain mans house, named Some read Titus, some both Titus and Iustus, making Iustus a sirname, as Acts 1.23. Col. 4.11. after the manner of the Romans. Justus, one that Had forsaken the Polytheisme of the Heathen. worshipped God, whose house joyned hard to the synagogue.

8 1 Cor. 1.14, • 5. And Crispus There were several Rulers in a Synagogue, which we find frequent mention of, as Matth. 9.18. Mark 5.22. Their Office and place was to advise, and give order about the affairs of the Synagogue, that all things might be performed according to their prescribed Rules; the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed on the Lord with all his house: and amongst whom are reckoned Gai • s, Soshenes, 1 Cor. 1.1. and Ep • netus, Rom. 16.5. many of the Corinthians, hearing, believed, and were baptized.

9 Then Chap. 23 11. spake the Lord to Paul in As Chap. 16.9. it may be by an Angel. the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and 'Tis doubled again and again, as of greatest consequence, 1. To the Corinthians, whose Salvation by this means might be procured. 2. To Paul himself, whose Soul howsoever should be delivered, he having discharged his duty, Chap. 20.26, 27. The fierceness of the enemies of God, and his Truth, should kindle a greater fervour in his Servants for his Glory. Should Satan have better Servants than God? Should they dare for their Master, beyond what the Servants of God are willing to do or suffer for him? Isa. 62.1. Ier. 1.17, 18. hold not thy peace:

10 For I am Because he would be with him, to supply, support and deliver him; as 'tis promised to Ieremiah, Ier. 1.18. and to all the faithful Ministers of Christ, Matth. 28.20. This promise was fulfilled to Paul, and to other of Gods Servants, whatsoever troubles they met with, even when they were • illed, they were not hurt, Rom. 8.36, 38. with thee, and no man shall set on thee, to hurt thee: for I have The other reason why Paul was commanded to tarry, was, because there were many that God would have called by his Ministry, and thus those who were not his people, God calleth his people, as Hosea 1.10. & 2.23. much people in this city, Christ, in this Vision, useth two Arguments to perswade Paul to continue Preaching the Gospel at Corinth; 1.

11 And he Gr. sat there. He sate there, as his fixt place; which implies his continuance and constancy in the work of the Ministry. coninued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

12 ¶ And when This Gallio was Brother to that deservedly famous Seneca, (who was Tutor to Nero) and hath great commendations given him, as being a man of an excellent disposition, beloved by all men, an enemy to all vice, and especially a hater of flattery. Gallio was the This man was Proconsul, deputy of Governing Achaia and all Greece absolutely; or with the power of a Consul. Achaia, the Jews made insurrection Wicked men in their evil deeds are unanimous▪ for Satan knows that his kingdom would not stand, if it were once divided. with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgement-seat▪

13 Saying, This fellow perswadeth men to worship God Of the Romans, who, to avoid tumults and confusions, did forbid any to set up any new worship without leave; and the Iews in these parts having here no power to punish St. Paul as they had at Ierusalem, maliciously incite the Governour against him: Or by the Law here may be meant the Law of Moses, which they accuse Paul to have broken, and so not to be comprehended in that license which they had to exercise their Religion. contrary to the law.

14 And when Paul was now about to To make his Apology, and to speak in his own defence. open his mouth, Gallio said unto the Jews, Chap. 25.11. If it were a matter of As Murther, Theft, or any such injury, which Judges do usually determine of. wrong, or wicked lewdness, O ye Jews, I would endure any trouble to hear and understand it, I should think it my duty to suffer you to say as much as you would in your case. reason would that I should bear with you.

15 But if it be a question of Which have been spoken about the controversies of Religion; words and as whether Jesus was to be called Christ or the Messiah; and whether his Disciples might be called Christians. names, and Concerning Circumcision, as whether none may be saved without it. of your law, look ye to it; for I will be no judge of He acknowledges his unfitness and unwillingness to determine such things as did not belong unto him, or he did not understand. such matters.
16 And he He commanded them to be gone, having dismissed their Case; and if need were, added threatning and force. drave them from the judgement-seat.

17 Then all the Not the converted Greeks, tho St. Austin thought they beat Sosthenes as an enemy to Paul (yet surely they had not so learned Christ) but the unbelieving or Gentile-Greeks, who cared for neither Paul, nor Iews, but favoured Gallio, who would have them driven away. Greeks took Some think him to have been the same with Crispus, Verse 8. others to have succeeded him in that Office: And some think that he was chief Ruler of another Synagogue (for in great Cities there might be more than one); and others, that there might be several called chief Rulers over one and the same Synagogue. So • thenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgement-seat: And Gallio cared Either slighting the Iews and all their controversies, or prudently to decline intermedling with them.
• or none of those things.

18 ¶ And Paul after this tarried there yet A year and an half in all, as some think, which is mentioned, verse 11. by a Prolepsis; or besides that year and an half there spoken of. a good while, and then took Ordering every thing as if he were to have taken his last farewel of them, as it fell out accordingly: Howsoever holy men live in a constant expectation of their dissolution. That the Wifes name is here put before the Husbands, have caused various conjectures; and 'tis observed, that in St. Paul's Epistles, whereas there are three times only mention of them • oth together, viz. Rom. 16.3. 1 Cor. 16.19. 2 Tim. 4.19. the Wives name is twice placed first, to shew, that in Christ Jesus there is neither Male nor Female, Gal. 3.28. his leave of the brethren, and sailed thence into Syria, and with him Priscilla u and Aquila: having Chap. 21. • 4. shorn his head in Which was a Town at the entring into the Haven belonging to Corinth, Rom. 16.1. Cenchrea: To wit, St. Paul had; and therefore had shaven his head according unto the Law, Numb. 6.18. To the Iews he became as a Iew. for he had a vow.

19 And he came to The Metropolis of the lesser Asia, where afterwards that famous Church was, unto which St. Paul wrote an Epistle, as also St. Iohn wrote another, Rev. 2.1. Ephesus, and lest That is, Aquila and Priscilla, at Ephesus, to confirm the believing Ephesians: whilst Paul, them there: but he himself entred out of an extraordinary love for his Nation, although he had suffered all those indignities from them▪ yet he would give them precept upon precept, and line upon line. into the synagogue, and reasoned with the Jews.

20 When That is Aquila and Priscilla, whom Paul would not yield unto. they desired him to tarry longer time with them▪ By Gods wonderful Providence (which over-rules all our inclinations) Paul having greater things to do and suffer for the Glory of God elsewhere. he consented not:

21 But bade them farewell, saying, I must by all means keep The Feast of the Passover; which is meant where Feast is put absolutely, unless some after expression qualifies it: not that this holy Man did out of Conscience to the Feast, intend to observe it; for Christ is the end of the law to them that believe, Rom. 10.4. but because of the vast concourse from all places to Ierusalem at that time; which would give him an opportunity of making Christ known to such multitudes, and to gain their Souls unto him. this feast that cometh, in Jerusalem: but I will return again unto you, Tho he was an Apostle, and had the Spirit of Prophesie, and might know whether he should return or no; yet he does not absolutely promise them to return to them; but conditionally, if the Lord will, to teach us what caution we should use in all our Promises and Resolutions, as Iam. 4.15. being we know not what a day may bring forth. Besides, in our owning of Gods Will and Pleasure, we acknowledg a Providence of God in all things, especially in our concerns; which we desire to refer all unto. 1 Cor. 4.19. Heb. 6.3. if God will. And he sailed from Ephesus.

22 And when he had landed at Not that Cesarea that was in Syria, but that which was in Palestine, called Cesarea Stratonis; and which was the safest way to Ierusalem; for the way by Ioppa, tho shorter, was accounted more dangerous. Cesarea, and gone up and saluted the Either the Church of Cesarea in his Journey, or that at Ierusalem at his Journeys end; which for its populousness might be called, eminently, The Church. church, he went down That Antioch that was in Syria. to Antioch.

23 And after he This work might take up the constant care and indefatigable pains of the Apostle. had spent some time there, he departed, and went over all the countrey of Where he had Converted many. Galat • a and Se •
Chap. 16.6. Phrygia in order, Tho the Seed be duly sown, yet it must be seasonably watered: and redit labor actus in orbem. strengthning all the disciples.

24 ¶ 1 Cor. 1.12. And a certain Jew named Who is thught also to be called Apelles, Rom. 16.10. Apollos, born at His Parents having lived there. Alexandria, an A rational, ptudent, and learned Man. Tho the Kingdom of God is not in any excellency of Speech, 1 Cor. 2.1, 4. yet this Egyptian Jewel may be used to Adorn the Tabernacle. eloquent man, and In quoting, explaining, and urging of them. mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesu • .

25 This man was Catechised, or taught, viva voce. instructed Christ, who hath by his Precepts and Example taught us the way to happiness; in the way of the Lord; and being very zealous to promote Gods Glory, and mens Salvation, as Rom. 12.11. servent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, Who Baptised with Water, but could not Baptize with the Holy Ghost, Matth. 3.11. that is, they had not those extraordinary Gifts of the Holy Ghost which followed upon Baptism after that Christ was Ascended, and the Spirit poured out, Chap. 2.4. But Iohn was a preacher of repentance, and of faith in Christ, pointing at the Lamb of God; and he Baptized his Disciples into this Doctrine; which is the same with the Baptism and Belief of the Apostles afterwards. Only now they knew many things more fully than were revealed in the Baptists time. Chap. 19.3. knowing only the baptism of John.

26 And he began to speak boldly in the Synagogue. Whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them If we allow Priscilla to have contributed towards the Instruction of Apollos, as doubtless we may, it is certain it was only in private discourse; which being joyned with a • eek and humble behaviour, might be very effectual for the Conversion of Souls, 1 Pet. 3.1, 2. Thus Timothy was indebted for his knowledge in the things of God, to his Mother and Grand-mother, 2 Tim. 1.5. but otherwise it is not Lawful for a Woman to Teach, 1 Tim. 2.11, 12., and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.

27 And when he was disposed to pass into To Corinth, which was in Achaia. Achaia, the Who were at Ephesus. brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him▪ Who, when he was come, 1 Cor. 3.6. helped them much which had believed through Apollos helped them much by his Eloquence, Zeal, and Constancy; which all are the Gifts of God; but especially, that they believed, was through Grace; for Faith is the Gift of God, Eph. 2.8. and it was given unto them to believe, Phil. 1.29. grace.

28 For he With great constancy, perseverance, and enduring of opposition. mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing As Chap. 17.3. by the scriptures, that some think that Christ ought to be the Subject, and Jesus the Predicate: and then the sense is, That Christ is our Jesus or Saviour. The Messiah that was sent from God, is the Saviour of the World. Jesus Or, is the Christ. was Christ.

div.head: CHAP. XIX.
div.p: ANd it came to pass, that while 1 Cor. 1.12. Apollos was at Corinth, Paul having passed through the The North parts; in which were Pontus, Bithynia, Phrygia, and Galatia, Chap. 18.23. upper coasts, came to Ephesus: and finding certain disciples,

2 He said unto them, Have ye received The extraordinary Gifts of the Holy Ghost, as Prophecying, speaking with Tongues, healing of the Sick, &c. as appears by Verse 6. and Iohn 7.39. for it could not be, that they who were Instructed and Baptized by Iohn, should be ignorant of the Essence or Person of the Holy Ghost; for the Baptist had seen him descending upon our Saviour; as is remembred by all the Evangelists which speak of his Baptism, Matth. 3.16. Mark 1.10. Luke 3.22. beside other Scriptures which testified of him; and St. Iohn had spoken of him unto all he Baptized, That our Saviour would Baptize them with the holy Ghost, and with fire, John 1.32, 33. the holy Ghost since ye believed? And they said unto him, We have not so much as heard This answer must be understood, according to the question, of those Gifts now mentioned; and which by the imposition of the hands of the Apostles were given, especially at the Ordination of such as were sent to Preach the Gospel, it being necessary for the Planting of the Church, (those miraculous Gifts assuring those, unto whom they P • eached, that their Doctrine was from Heaven;) as also • o assure the Apostles themselves of the success of their Ministry, and the conversation of such they Preached unto, as Chap. 10 44, 47. And this acception of these words is parallel'd, 1 Sam. 3.7. where it is said, That Samuel knew not yet the Lord; the meaning is, That he knew not that God was wont so to speak unto any; otherwise that holy Man, as young as he was, both knew God, and served him. whether there be any holy Ghost.

3 And he said unto them, Unto What Doctrine did you make profession of? And what Religion did you Seal unto at your Baptism? what then were ye baptized? And they said, The Doctrine that Iohn taught, and the Religion that he professed and preached. Thus the Iews are said, 1 Cor. 10.2. to be Baptized unto Moses, being engaged to believe the Doctrine, and observe the Law delivered by Moses. Now the Baptist, as Chap. 18.25. preached indeed Christ, but many things concerning him he could not preach, unless as of things to come: as his Death, and Resurrection. The Baptist being Beheaded before our Saviours Death, and the Holy Ghost was not poured out in that extraordinary manner, until after our Saviours Resurrection and Ascension; which pouring out of the Spirit, these Disciples at Ephesus, having been Baptized by Iohn in Iudea, and afterwards returning home, might not have heard of. Unto Johns baptism.

4 Then said Paul, Matth. 3.11. John verily baptized with the At which the Baptist did exhort them to Repentance; and they by it were obliged to repent; by which is manifest, that the Baptism of Iohn, and of Christ (which he commanded, is one and the same. Iohns Baptism did respect Christ, and oblige the Baptized to believe in him, as also to repent: and more, it was a Seal unto them of the Remission of their sins, as is expresly observed, Mark 1.4. so that the Baptism of Iohn, and the Baptism of the Apostles afterward, had the same Sign, and the same thing signified in them both (the inward and outward part, the Heavenly and Earthly part were the same in both;) as also they had both the same end; and therefore they were both the same. Add to this, That unless th •
