Baptists and the Apostles Baptism were the same, Christ and his Member • (the Church) are not Baptized with the same Baptism: It must be acknowledged that there are some Circumstances in which they differ; Iohns Baptism respected baptism of repentance, saying unto the people, That they should believe on him which Christ to come; that is, in the exercise of his Ministry (which was not so fully exercised till after Iohns death;) but especially, those great things (his Death, Resurrection, and Ascension, &c.) were to come in Iohns time, which now are accomplished. should come after him▪ that is, Including the Father, and the Holy Ghost, and mentioning Christ, to difference his Baptisms from the several Baptizings and Washing then in use. on Christ Jesus.

5 The Disciples, or those that Iohn preached to, (for these Ephesians were not amongst those few that Paul Baptized, 1 Cor. 1.14.) who when they heard what the Baptist said in the foregoing Virse, they were Baptized; as in the same terms 'tis said, Chap. 2.37. when they heard what St. Peter had said, they were pricked in their hearts, &c. and were Baptized. As for Pauls imposing his hands upon them that are said here to be Baptized, it might very well be, That the Twelve Disciples, Verse 7. might have been Baptized by Iohn, and now Receive the Holy Ghost in those extraordinary Gifts by the laying on of the hands of St. Paul: for to what end should these Disciples who were Baptized with St. Iohns Baptism, be again Baptized by Paul? It is true, they had further manifestations of the Mystery of the Gospel brought unto them; but if men should be Baptized for every degree of Knowledg or Grace which they do acquire, how many Baptisms had they need to have, who ought daily to grow in Grace and in Knowledg? It is evident, that the Apostles themselves were only Baptized with the Baptism of Iohn, for there were none else to Baptise them. And Baptism being an Ordinance for our Regeneration, and New Birth; as we can be born but once in the Flesh, we can be but once also born in the Spirit; and no more may Christians be Baptized twice, than the Iews could be twice Circumcised. When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

6 And when Thereby Ordaining and Authorizing of them to preach the Gospel. Paul had Chap. 6.6. & 8.17. laid his hand • upon them, the In those extraordinary Gifts of Tongues, &c. whereby they were sitted to preach the Gospel unto any Nation or People unto whom they should be sent. holy Ghost came on them; and they Chap. 2.4. & 10.46. spake with tongues and They Prophesied, either in its proper sense, being enabled to foretel things that were to •• me; or in a larger and more improper sense, praising and magnifying of God, and declaring the hidden Mysteries of the Gospel; expounding the Scriptures; especially the Prophesies concerning Christ, as 1 Cor. 14.1. prophesied.
7 And all the men were about Or exactly Twelve; answering to the Apostles, and that Blessed Number so often mentioned in Scripture. twelve.

8 And he went into the Of the Iews at Ephesus. For in the greater Cities the Iews had their Synagogues in which they had their Prayers, read, and expounded the Law; as also a School for teaching of their Theology; in which they treated of hard Questions, and more difficult matters; which might occasion the Apostles frequenting that place. synagogue, and spake boldly for the space of three months, disputing and perswading the things concerning The Gospel; which is so called, Rom. 14.17. because the Kingdom of Grace is by it set up in us here, and we are fitted by it for the Kingdom of Glory hereafter. But it might be also so called, because the Iews had dreamed of a political Kingdom of the Messiah, and the Christians would own that Christ was indeed a King, but that his Kingdom was a Spiritual Kingdom. the kingdom of God.

9 But 2 Tim. 1.15. when divers The Sun hardeneth what it doth not soften, and causeth a ste •• h from Dung-Hills, as well as a sweet smell from the Mountains of Spices; and Christ is for the falling▪ as well as for the rising of many. were hardened, and believed not, but spake evil See Chap. 9 2 of So the Doctrine of the Gospel, by reason of its excellency above other ways. By way, the Hebrews understand any course or means to an end. Hence we read of the way of Peace, the way of Salvation, the way of the Lord. that way before the multitude, he departed from them Not frequenting any more the Synagogue of the Iews, where they met only with contradiction of their Doctrine, and blasphemy against their Saviour., and separated the disciples, disputing daily in the school of one Some have taken this word Appellatively, as denoting some great Man or Ruler, who maintained a School, or place for Instruction; but 'tis rather a proper name of some private Teacher amongst them: for the Iews had not only publick Schools, where their Consistories did meet, but private Schools, where their Law was Ta • ght. Tyrannus.

10 And See Chap. 20.31. this continued by the space of two years; so that Many of all sorts: all they which dwelt in Asia the lesser, or Asia strictly so called, lying about Ephesus; the Heathens came thither to worship their Diana; the Iews came about their Affairs thither, either in their Trades, or Law-suits. Asia, heard the The Gospel, which is the Word concerning the Lord Jesus; or, the Word which he appointed to be preached and published. word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.
11 And Mark 16.20. Chap. 14.3. God wrought Not common or ordinary things, or such as might happen by chance. special miracles by the As Chap. 5.12. by his Means and Ministry. hands of Paul:

12 So that from his body were brought Our Habit and Attire being so different from what was used so long since, it cannot but occasion some variety in rendering these words. Which some think to signify two things; and some but one and the same part of their Clothes or Dress; the words are both Originally Latin; the former so called from its use to wipe away sweat; the other from its being usually tied about such as wore it. unto the sick, handkerchiefs or aprons, and the God by such small and unlikely means wrought these Miracles: 1. That the Power of Christ (whom Paul preached) might the more clearly appear. And that, 2dly, Such as were absent might have a high value for Christ and the Gospel, tho they had never seen Paul, or heard him preach. Such extraordinary works were also wrought by God to magnify the words preached by Peter, Chap. 5.15. as our Saviour had foretold and promised, Iohn 14.12. diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them.

13 ¶ Then certain of the Who wandered up and down, making it their trade and livelihood: as Juglers amongst us. vagabond Jews So called from their obtesting the evil spirits in the name of God. Of these Iosephus tells strange Stories, Antiq. lib. 8. and thinks that the way of their exorcising was derived unto them from Solomon, and that they used the Name of the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Iacob; as also of Zebaoth, and Adonai, as Origen tells us. Some think, that tho there is certainly no power in the Words and Syllables which they pronounced, yet that the True God being rather willing to be known and owned by those Names, than that any should call on the names of the false gods, did sometimes put forth his power in casting out of Devils at such times, a •
Matth. 12.27. Howsoever, there being no warrant in the Word of God for any such practice, and no promise to act Faith in Prayer upon; were the words never so serious, and the Name of God and his Attributes never so much (seemingly) manifested, it is a most abomiaable Impie • y., exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits, the Instead of, or together with those other Names formerly mentioned. name of the Lord Jesus, saying▪ We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.

14 And there were seven sons of one Sceva a Jew, and One of the chief of the 24. Courses into which the Priests were divided, 1 Chron. 24.4. or such as (according to the corruption of those times) had been High Priests, and were laid aside, or were of the High Priests Family, and hoped to succeed him. chief of the priests, which did so.

15 And the evil spirit answered and said I acknowledge that Jesus hath Power to command me to go hence;, Jesus I know, and I know that Paul, as his Minister, hath Authority over me. and Paul I know; but who But what pr •• ensions have ye to command m • now? Tho the Devil is a lyar, and the Father of lyes, yet none lye to their own disadvantage, but rather to their advantage, as they take it; and Satan may therefore be believed in what he here says, because it is to his disgrace; that will he, nill he, he is under the command of God, tho but signified to him by the least of his Ministers or Servants. are ye?

16 And the By the power of the evil spirit, which by the permission of God did act in him, Matth. 8.28. Mark 5.4. Luke 8.29. Satan retains still his natural power, tho he hath wholly lost his moral or spiritual power unto any good: and that his violence proceeded no further, is to be ascribed only to the bounds which God had set him; which he, being in Chains, could not exceed or go beyond; not for his want of malice, but power. man in whom the evil spirit was, leapt on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.

17 And this was known to all the Jews and Greeks also dwelling at Ephesus; and They feared (after this example of Gods not holding them guiltless that had taken his Name in vain) to prophane the Name of Christ, and much more to blaspheme or speak against it. fear fell on them all, and the His Authority, which the unclean spirit could not resist; and his Doctrine and Ministers, whose Defence God had undertaken. name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.

18 And many that That believed the power which God alone had over Satan, and were convinced of their sin and danger in being led captive by him. believed came, and Openly declared their evil deeds. They durst keep the Devil's counsel no longer, but expose and manifest it, that their sores being laid open, the Balm of the Gospel might more effectually be put into them. Thus Rom. 10.10. with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
Mat. 3.6. confessed, and shewed their deeds.

19 Thus their good works justified their Faith, without which it had been dead, Iames 2.24, 26. Many also of them which used Or rather idle and vain Arts, as Judicial Astrology, calculating Nativities, and all Magical Arts, which the Ephesians, of all others, were most addicted to, and famous for, and may be here called various Arts, because they were so called by the Ephesians, who practised them; as also because these Arts are about Curiosities, not necessary for us to know. Otherwise they are Diabolical Arts, or rather devillish Cheats. curious arts, brought their books together These Books were not sold, and the price of them brought unto the Apostles, because it was look'd upon as the price of a Whore, which was an abomination, and might not be offered unto God, Deut. 23.18., and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it What this sum amounts to, is not so certain, because it is not agreed what these pieces were. Some make them Roman, or Grecian Coin; and others understand by them, Shekels, which are the Iewish money, and would make this sum so much the greater. Take them for so many Pence, a piece of money commonly so called, which weighed the Eighth part of an Ounce of Silver; as Matth. 18.28. They make 6250. Ounces of Silver, or so many Crowns, and so much more as Silver is worth more per Ounce. Such indignation have true Converts against the sins they have been guilty of, that they will not retain any thing that might occasion their return unto them: Were it a right Eye, they would pull it out. fifty thousand pieces of silver.

20 So Chap. 6, 7. and 12.24. mightily The encrease which the seed of the Word had made, was very remarkable; or it is a great instance of the power of Gods Word, when it makes men willing to part with their beloved and accustomed sins, and not to stand upon saving or gaining; as Isa. 55.11. grew the word of God, and prevailed.

21 ¶ Rom. 15.25. Gal. 2.1. After these things were ended, Paul Resolved with himself, or purposed in his heart, as Dan. 1.8. Yet in this his determination he had the influence and guidance of the Holy Ghost, and that in a more than ordinary manner; as we may see by the continued series of this History, how he came to all these places here mentioned. purposed in the spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia, and Paul travelled thorow these Countries, and went to these Cities, because he hoped for a greater Harvest, where he might scatter the seed so far abroad. Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying▪ After I have been there Chap. 18.21., I must also see Rome.

22 So he sent into Macedonia two of them that This great Apostle 〈◊〉
• or any to minister unto him, out of State, but out of Necessity, being he could not himself attend to all the Offices of the Church. These were employed by Paul, not so much to procure any Accommodation for himself by the way, as to further a collection for the poor brethren at Ierusalem, 2 Cor. 9.3, 4. ministred unto him, Timotheus and There seems to have been two of this Name mentioned in Scripture; The one, Rom. 16.23. and the other, 2 Tim. 4.20. The latter is here spoken of. Erastus; but he himself stayed In Ephesus, which was in Asia, where Paul now was. in Asia for a season.

23 When all things seemed to have been quiet: so incertain are the servants of Christ to have any quiet here. And 2 Cor. 1.8. the same time there arose no small stir about The Doctrine of the Gospel; as Chap. 18 25. See Chap. 9.2. that way.

24 For a certain man named Demetrius, a silver-smith, which made These shrines were only, either 1. Pourtraits of the Temple of Diana, in which was graven, or (by any other Art) represented that famous Structure which was afterwards burnt by Erastrotus: Or 2dly, They were Medals in which their Idol Diana was expressed according to her Image, spoken of, ver. 35. And they are called here, Temples, or Shrines, because they did resemble and represent that Shrine or Temple. And these the superstitious people carried home to their houses and friends; not only to evidence what a pilgrimage they had performed, but to incite the more their devotions towards this Idol. silver shrines for Diana, brought Chap. 16.16. no small gain unto the craftsmen.

25 Whom he called together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, Sirs, ye know that Gain. Getting, or keeping a livelihood are great temptations; and a little pretext of piety with them, do keep up the superstition and false worship that abounds in the world. by this craft we have our wealth:

26 Moreover, ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath perswaded and turned away much people, saying, that they be no He tells them indeed what was St▪ Paul's Doctrine; but he conceals the Reasons of his Doctrine: for there can be nothing more evident to any considering man▪ than that there is but one God who made all things▪ as Psal. 115.34. Ier. 10.10. gods which are made with hands?

27 So that not onely this our craft is in danger to be Not 〈◊〉 that we shall have no more to do, and be without work; but that it will be a reproach unto us to have had such an imployment. set at nought; but also that the This is made an aggravation to the loss of their all, that Religion should suffer too. How much more ought it to concern those who have a sure foundation for what they do profess? temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnific ••• e should be destroyed, whom This Temple is said to have been burnt down the same day that Alexander was born; and that it was two hundred and twenty years in re-building, at the charge of all Asia. all Asia, and the 〈◊〉 worshippeth.Tho the Romans might worship any God (of those multitudes) which they allowed; yet they might leave their Estates onely to a very few amongst them: but Diana, of the Ephesians, was one of those few▪ as also one of those twelve whom they accounted (Dii, or D • ae majorum Gentium) Gods and Goddesses of the highest quality, or first rank.

28 And when they The Argument from their profit wrought very much upon them, especially meeting with their prejudicate Opinions, having pretended antiquity and universality to confirm them. heard th • se sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is To shew their abhorrence of what Paul had taught; and desiring her glory might be perpetual, whom Paul thought not worthy to be honoured at all. Diana of the Ephesians.

29 And the whole city was filled Tumults and noise▪ All conditions of men, high and low, prom • scuously being met in such uproars. with confusion: and having caught One born at Derbe, but living at Thessalonica; as Chap. 20.4. Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel, they rushed with one accord into the theatre.Of whom we read, Chap. 27.2. Colos. 4.10. A place or Structure built for publick uses; whence, 1. Their Sports or Plays in any publick solemnity were beheld. 2. Their Speech or Orations in their common Assemblies were heard. 3. Where they punished also their Malefactors; it being accommodated with 〈◊〉 steps or seat • higher than one another, and of vast exte • t for these 〈◊〉 . Hither, according to their custom, they resort, to 〈◊〉 any one would speak upon this occasion to them; or rather to get these Christians condemned and executed for their supposed Sacriledg and Blasphemy.

30 And when Paul would have Being desirous either to appease the tumult; or if the worst came of it, to die for Christs sake. entred in unto the people, the p disciples suffered him not.By their intreaties: to whom this good Apostle's Life, from whom they had received the Faith, was more dear than their own.

31 And certain of the Such as had the oversight of the Plays and Shows in honour of their Idol-gods, and were usually their Priests; and were of four Countries, from whence they had their names of Asiarchs, Bithynarchs, Syriarchs, and Cappadociarchs. Whosoever these were, the Providence of God is to be adored, who could out of his greatest enemies, raise up deliverers for his servants. chief of Asia, which were his friends, sent unto him, desiring him that he would not adventure himself into the theatre.

32 Some therefore An excellent description of a popular tumult. Whether this Assembly was afterwards made legal by the Magistrates resorting thither (tho it was not called by their Authority), and is therefore called here, 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , is not so useful to enquire. cried one thing, and some another: • or the assembly was confused, and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together.

33 And they drew Alexander Where he could not be seen and heard, unto some more convenient place, from whence he might make a vindication or defence for them; and that most likely in behalf of the Iews, who were equally obnoxious to the rage of the people for being against their Idolatry, as the Christians were. This Alexander is thought to have been that Alexander of whom we read, 1 Tim. 1.20. 2 Tim. 4.14. tho some think that this was another of that name. out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. And Alexander To procure silence; as Chap. 12.17. beckened with the hand, and would have made his defence unto the people.

34 But when they knew that he was a Jew, all with Unanimity makes not the cause to be good, if it 〈◊〉 bad at first. one voice about the space of two hours cried out, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.And by consequence an enemy to their Idolatry; and as they might imagine, at least, a friend to St. Paul ▪

35 And when the Or Secretary, who Registred their Acts, and intervened in all their Meetings. town-clerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, w • at man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians Each Countrey and City had their peculiar gods which they worshipped, and took for their Patrons; as Ephesus did this Goddess Diana. But the word here signifies a Sacrist, or one that looks to the Temple to keep it clean; especially that hath the charge of more solemn shews or sports in honour of any supposed Deity. And these Ephesians took it to be their no small glory, that they were employed in such as belonged to Diana. is a Gr. the Temple-keeper. worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image Tho the Maker's Name (Canetias) is upon Record, yet it having lasted whilst the Temple was six or seven times repaired, at least, if not renewed, and none ever remembring when it first was brought in amongst them, the crafty Priests perswaded the credulous people, that it was fallen from Heaven, thereby getting more honour unto it, and profit to themselves. which f • ll down from Jupiter?

36 Seeing then that these things He did more cunningly than honestly endeavour to evade their clamour, and still their rage, by telling them (how fallaciously soever) that neither Paul, or any other Christian or Jew, had 〈…〉 with their goddess or worship. For they 〈◊〉
• ere against all images that were made with hands 〈…〉 was not such an one, it being fallen down from Heaven. We must consider he was but a Pagan; and his design was only to still the people: And populus vult decipi. cannot be spoken against, ye ought to be quiet, aed to do nothing rashly.

37 For ye have brought hither these men, which are neither robbers of churches, nor yet For they had not enter'd into their Temple. blasphemers of your goddess. Paul had barely preach'd this Truth amongst them, not upbraiding them for their Idolatry: as Michael, the Arch-Angel, brought no railing Accusation against the Devil, when he contended with him, Iude 9.

38 Wherefore i • Demetrius and the craftsmen which are with him, have a matter against any man, Or, the Courtdays are kept. the Which is fittest to determine all questions and controversies. For men would be partial to their own cause; and every one challenge to be in the right. law is open, and there are Who under the Roman Emperors or Consuls, had power to hear and determine of all matters. deputies; let them That so both parties may be heard. implead one another.

39 But if ye enquire any thing concerning Relating to the good Government of the City, or maintaining the Establish'd Religion, which ought not in such a confused manner to be treated of. other matte • s, it shall be determined in But in an Assembly called • y lawful Authority, which the Romans did usually call, a • least, three times every month. a Or, ordinary. lawful assembly.

40 For we are He wisely minds them of their danger: For being under the power of the Romans, it was no less than the loss of their Liberties to abet any Faction or Sedition; And to make a concourse or meeting tumultuously together, was capital, unless it were upon the sudden invasion of an Enemy, or to put out some raging fire. in danger to be called in question for this days uprore, there being no cause whereby we may give an account of this concourse.

41 And when he had thus spoken, he The people were perswaded quietly to depart to their homes. Thus God one way or other, sometimes by friends, and sometimes by foes, kept his Church and People from being ruined: and his hand is not shortned. dismissed the assembly.

div.head: CHAP. XX.
div.p:
ANd after the uprore was ceased, Paul called unto him the disciples Took his Farewel of them (and as the manner of those Countries was in meeting and parting with friends), he kissed them, Luke 7.45. and far more anciently, Gen. 31.55. And this was the true ground of that Kiss of Peace, or the Holy Kiss, recommended, Rom. 16.16. 1 Cor. 16.20. 2 Cor. 13.12. and esewhere; which was only a civility then in use., and embraced them Yielding to the present fury of Demetrius; not so much for his own safety, as for the good of the Church, that it might not be further persecuted for his sake; and that elsewhere it might by his Ministry be enlarged and built up., and 1 Tim. 1.3 •
departed for to go into Macedonia.

2 And when he had gone over those parts, and had given them Which after so great a stir and opposition against them, the Disciples could not but stand in great need of, that they might not be offended at the Cross of Christ; as also mingling consolations with his exhortations; as the word indifferently signifies, as the case would well bear; there being a special blessing promised unto such as are persecuted for righteousness sake, Matth. 5.10. 1 Pet. 3.14▪ much exhortation, he came Attica; in which Province Athens was: Otherwise Macedonia was in Greece largely taken. into Greece,

3 And there abode three moneths: And when the Jews Some have thought that their laying in wait, might be to rob him of the Collections which he carried with him for the Saints at Ierusalem; but most likely it was rather to take away his life, whom they hated for his zeal and diligence in the Gospel. laid wait for him, as he was about to sail into Syria Shunning their treachery and plotting against him. He would not tempt God by running into dangers, tho his cause were never so good., he purposed to return Being the same way that he had came to Corinth. through Macedonia.

4 And there Their Names are set down, as being men called and known at that time in the Churches; and that what they did for this holy Apostle, might be remembred in all Ages. accompanied him into Asi •
Who is called also Sosipater, Rom. 16.21. It is added in some Copies, that he was the Son of Pyrrhus; which in Greek is the same with Rufus in Latin. , Sopater of A City of Macedonia, Chap. 17.10. Be • ea; and of the Thessalonians Of whom, Chap. 19.29. as also of the others, mention hath been formerly made., Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of D • rbe, and Timotheus Of Ephesus, a City in Asia. Tychicus; of whom, Ephes. 6.21. Col. 4.7. 2 Tim. 4.12. and of Trophimus we read, Chap. 21.29. 2 Tim. 4.20. These seem to have been the Apostles or Messengers of the Churches spoken of, 2 Cor. 8.23. in the number of whom St. Luke is to be reckoned, but being the Penman of this Book, he declines mentioning of himself by name; but his praise will be for ever in the Gospel▪ 2 Cor. 8.18, 19.; and of Asia Tit. 3.12., Tychicus and Trophimus.

5 These going before, tarried for Whereby it appears, that St. Luke was one of them that accompanied St. Paul, tho neither here nor elsewhere doth he express his own Name. us at Either the City of Troy, or the Countrey thereabout so called. Troas.

6 And we sailed away Where they embarked, and sailed on the River first, then on the Sea. from Philippi, after the Tho St. Paul would not have the Gentile-Converts to be burdened with the Ceremonial Law, yet that he might not offend the Iews, for a while he complied with their Rites, Chap. 18.21. they being indeed dead, but not yet deadly; and therefore he stays his Journey all the time of the Passover-solemnity, instructing them in the mean while of the Nature and Use of such things. days of unleavened bread, and came unto them to Troas in five days, where we abode seven days.

7 And upon the This was the day which the Lord had made, it being called from his Resurrection, which was on this day, The Lord's Day, Rev. 1 10. On this day the Disciples met, and Christ honoured them with his presence, Iohn 20.19, 26. And when he was ascended, this day was appointed for the Christians to meet in, 1 Cor. 16.2. which must necessarily infer the abrogation of the Saturday, or Iewish Sabbath: For it being part of the Command, Six days shalt thou labour, they could not in ordinary have rested the last day of the week and the first day too, without sinning against that Law of God. first day of the week, when the disciples came together To take a meal in common together; which they called Agapae, or the Love-Feast; so great an harmony and natural love was manifested in it; which was concluded with celebrating the Lord's Supper. And this is chiefly, if not only intended in this place: The Love-Feasts being abused; were soon laid aside; but the other must continue until the Lord come, 1 Cor. 11.26. to Chap. 2.42, 46. 1 Cor. 10, 16. break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow, and continued his speech A long Sermon indeed; at least, it would be now thought so: And yet we must have the same Spirit, or we are not Members of that Catholick Church. until midnight.

8 And there were There being many present; and it being in the night▪ because of the persecution that the Christians met with. Le • t they should be reproached for doing any thing indecently, they by this means exposed themselves, and all that was done amongst them, to the common view and notice of all. many lights in the Where 'tis supposed they did ordinarily meet; as Chap. 1.13. upper chamber where they were gathered together.

9 And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long Discoursing and arguing: For it does not seem to have been a continued▪ speech, by the word here used. preaching, he sunk This fall is thought by some to have been caused by Satan (through Gods permission), that he might the more disturb Paul, and hinder, or put an end to his Sermon; which by the ensuing Miracle, God turned to a quite contrary effect. down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead.

10 And Paul went down, and As Elijah on the Widow of Zarephath's dead Son, 1 Kings 17.21. and Elish •
on the Sh •• amites Son, 2 Kings 4.34. fell on him, and embracing him, said, Trouble not your selves; for Not but that he had been really dead; as ver. 9. but that upon the Apostle's prayer (which is to be understood, tho it is not here expressed) God had restored the young man to life: or howsoever, because St. Paul knew infallibly he should presently be restored to life, even whilst he spake. his life is in him.

11 When he therefore was come up again, and had Either in the Eucharist; as ver. 7. or in taking his ordinary refection and breakfast. This was of long continuance, and speaks the patience and zeal of Christians in those times, and will rise up in Judgment against a careless and negligent Generation., broken bread, and eaten, and talked a long while, even c till break of day, so Going that part of his Journey on foot, as the rest of his company did go by Sea; as ver. 13. he departed.

12 And they brought the young man alive, and were not a little They rejoiced not only that the young man was restored to life, but that by this means the Gospel was attested to, and many confirmed in the belief of it. comforted.

13 ¶ And we went before to ship, and sailed unto A City in Mysia, called also Apollonia, not far from Troas either by water or land. Assos, there intending to take in Paul: For so had he appointed, minding Paul's going on foot might be the • ather, that so he might have the better opportunity to scatter the seed of the Gospel as he went, going thorow Towns and Villages▪ and conversing still with some or other, more than in Sea-journeys can be expected. So greedy of winning souls to Christ was this holy man, that he ordered every step, as near as he could, towards it. But St. Paul might desire to go alone thus on foot, that he might enjoy more free and full communion with God, having only God and his own soul to converse with. himself to go a
• oot.

14 And when he met with us at Assos, we took him in, and came to An Island; as also a City in it so called, in the Aegean Sea. Some think the Island is called Lesbos, in which this Mitylene is. Mitylene.

15 And we sailed thence, and came the next day over against A noted Island betwixt Lesbos and Samos in the Aegean Sea. Chios; And the next day we arrived at In Ionia: for there are several other Islands of this Name. Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; And the next day we came A Sea-Town 〈…〉 Continent, or firm land of Ionia. to Miletus.
〈◊〉 Promontory not far from Samos:

16 For Paul had determined to sail Which was not so far from Miletus; but lest he should hinder his Journey, he would not go thither. Or by Ephesus, because he would not spend the time in Asia: For Chap. 21▪4 •
▪ 12. he hasted as Chap. 18.21. If the Lord would: for his endeavour should not be wanting., if it were possible for him, to be at Jerusalem Not that he placed any Religion in the observing this Feast, which was abrogated and done away by being fulfilled, Chap. 2. but because of the vast concourse of people at all those solemn Feasts, when his opportunities to magnifie Christ and his Truths, might be the greater. the day of Pentecost.

17 ¶ And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the The Governors and Pastors of it; Elders being here not a Title respecting their Age, but their Place; and they might be the Twelve spoken of, Chap. 19.7. elders of the church.

18 And when they were come to him, he said unto them, Ye know Chap. 19. •• 10., from the first day that I came into Strictly and properly so called; or that part of the lesser Asia, whose Metropolis was Ephesus. Asia, after A singular Form for a good man to use, if he must of necessity leave his Charge or Flock when his Conscience does not accuse him. St. Paul spake not this, as boasting of what he had done, or how he had been amongst them; but setting his example before them and others, to be imitated; and calling them for to witness the truth of it. what manner I have been with you at all seasons,

19 Serving the Lord with In his Apostleship or publick Ministry; of which, if any ever could, he might have gloried: yet in this Office he clothes himself with humility, as the most becoming garment for a Minister of Jesus Christ; tho so high, yet so low. We need not cry (as one did, tho Ironically), Fie St. Paul, but fie upon all such as pretend to succeed in his dignity, and do not at all imitate him in his humility. all humility of mind, and with many He shed tears of compassion over the ignorant and blind, hard and perverse. It grieved him to see how large a Dominion the God of this World had, and what a little part was left for his dear Lord and Master Christ Jesus. tears, and Afflictions and troubles which befell him for Christ • and the Gospel's sake; which are so called, Iames 1.2. 1 Pet. 1.6. temptations
which befell me by the lying in wait of the Jews:

20 And how I kept back nothing that was Useful in order to Eternal Life to be known or hoped for, or to be done; shunning no labour or danger; concealing nothing out of fear or hope of advantage. profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you In the publick Synagogues and Schools. publickly, and from Privately, as Chap. 2.46. from house to house; not only speaking publickly and in general, but secretly and particularly, as every ones condition did require, exhorting some, reproving others▪ And indeed a good shepherd will labour to understand the sta • e of his flock, and to supply them with what is necessary and suitable for them. Iacob says, Gen. 31.39. that he bare the loss, and was fain to answer for all the sheep unto Laban. And of how much more value are the souls of men, to be sure in God's sight, who will require an account of them? house to house,

21 Testifying both to the Jews, and To all sorts and conditions of men: for there is no difference with God. also to the GreeksMat. 3.2. Ma • k. 1.15. Luke 24.47. That Repentance would be accepted from them by God, and that he was ready to give Repentance unto them; as Chap. 11.18., repentance toward God, and And that Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, was the true saving Faith, there being no other Name given, whereby we may be saved. Upon these Two depends the whole Gospel, and our salvation by it. faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.

22 And now behold, I go As powerfully perswaded by a divine instinct, to undertake this Journey, as if I were led or drawn to it by forcible means; being bound to obey God in all things, whom I take to be my God and Guide, my Sun and Shield: And I do not desire so much to act, as to be acted by him. This St. Paul says, not as if that he was drawn unto this Journey against his will, but lest any should attempt to disswade him from it, or that he should seem to hav • slighted the predictions of the Prophets, mentioned, 〈…〉 11, 12. Nay, he might say this, as being as certain of his bonds as if he felt them already. Such things as are foretold to such as know the Veracity of God, they are as present. Howsoever, he was content to be bound, to suffer, nay, to die for Christ. And as he is poor in spirit who crucifies the World, and is willing to want, if God sees good; so he is bound in spirit, who is thus willing to be bound for the Name of Christ. Howsoever, these words speak his firm Resolution to take this Journey upon him. bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing the things What the event shall be, in what measure he should be bound, and how long, he left in unto God's good Will and Pleasure. that shall befall me there:

23 Save that the holy Ghost witnesseth 1. Those that were endued with the Spirit of Prophesie, in every City, foretold his sufferings; as Chap. 21.4.11. 2dly, He did suffer more or less in every City or place he came to; So great was the malice of the Iews against him. in every city, saying, that bonds and afflictions▪ Or, wait for me. abide me.

24 But Chap. 21.13. none of these things They cannot deter me from my duty. move me, neither count I my I am so far from fearing bonds, that I would not fear death its self. He is said to account his Life precious, or dear, that spares it; as 2 Kings 1.13, 14. life dear unto my self, so that I might finish His general course of Christianity, or the special course of his Ministry; in either of which there is a Race to be run, and a Prize to be got, 2 Tim. 4.7. It implies the great and constant labour that all Christians must take in their general calling, and especially Ministers in their particular calling, 1 Cor. 9.24. my course Which ariseth from the Testimony of a good Conscience, which only is true joy; the other is madness, Eccles. 2.2. with joy, and the His Apostleship so called, Chap. 1.25 and Chap. 6.4. ministery Gal. 1.1. Titus 1.3., which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testifie the Gospel So the Gospel is called, because bestowed upon any Nation or People by Gods meer Grace onely. And also it declares the Grace of God in Christ Jesus to repenting and believing sinners. of the grace of God.

25 And now behold This is thought to have been spoken by St. Paul, as his present purpose and resolution only; as Rom. 15 24., I know that ye all, among whom I have gone preaching The Gospel by which his Kingdom is set up in the minds and hearts of men. the kingdom of God, shall see my face no more.

26 Wherefore I take I testifie and affirm unto you; and I dare appeal unto your selves concerning it. you to record this day, that I am pure From the guilt of destroying their souls. None of them have perished through my default, having faithfully shewed unto them the way of Life, and earnestly perswaded them to walk in it. Thus according as the Lord told Ezekiel, Chap. 3.19. The Prophet that hath warned the wicked man, hath delivered his own soul. from the blood of all men.

27 For I have not shunned to declare unto you Gods Decree, to save all that believe in Christ; or the whole Doctrine of Christianity, as it directs to an holy Life; whatsoever God requires of any one in order to a blessed Eternity. This is that which the Pharisees rejected, Luke 7.30. And so do all wicked and ungodly men, who refuse to take Gods counsel, or to obey his command. all the Eph. 1.11. counsel of God.

28 ¶ 1 Tim. 4. • 6. 1 Peter 5.2. Take heed therefore unto your Be mindful of your own salvation: For he that neglects his own, will not be careful of the salvation of another. selves, and to all the flock, over the which the 1: By his choosing and nominating of them, which was then by a special Instinct, or immediate Warrant from the Spirit, Chap. 1.24. Chap. 13.2. Or 2 Because they were constituted by the Apostles, who were filled with the Spirit, enabling of them to the choice of such persons, Chap. 14.23. But also 3. Whosoever is set apart to this Office, according to the Will of God, is made an Overseer by the Holy Ghost; God owning his Institutions, and concurring with them. holy Ghost hath made you The same, who, ver. 17. are called Elders, they were certainly such as had the government and care of the Church committed unto them. overseers, to As a shepherd does (for the Apostle continues here the Metaphor): Ier. 23.4. Iohn 21.16, 17. feed the church Our Saviour is so called; for the word was God, John 1.1. of God Eph. 1.7. Col. 1.14. 1 Peter 1.19. Rev. 5▪9., which he Christ by his bloody Death hath redeemed his Church, and obtained power to gather it, to rule over it, to protect and preserve it, Isa. 53.10. Phil. 2.8, 9, 30. hath purchased with The blood of Christ, called truly the blood of God, there being in Christ Two Natures in one Person, and a communion of the properties of each Nature. If Christ had not been Man, he could have had no blood to shed: Had he not been God, the blood which he shed could not have been a sufficient price of Redemption. Oh the depth of the Riches of the Wisdom and Knowledg of God, who found out such a Ransom; and the breadth, and length, and depth, and height of the Love of Christ, who paid this Ransom for us! Rom. 11.33. Eph. 3.18, 19. his own blood.

29 For I know this, that after my Either out of this Countrey, or out of this Life. departing shall grievous So false Teachers and Persecutors are called, the one destroying the body, the other the soul. In this the Metaphor is persisted in, the Disciples of Christ being as Sheep or Lambs; their Enemies are by our Saviour himself called Wolves, Matth. 7.15. wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.

30 Also Whilst Paul yet lived, and was onely departed from that place. Several Seducers may be reckoned up, as Nicolas the Deacon (from whom 'tis thought the Sect of the Nicolaitans came, Revel. 2.6.) Hymenaeus, Alexander, Phygellus, and Hermogenes, 1 Tim. 1.20. 2 Tim. 1.15. of your own selves shall men arise, speaking Perverting Scripture, establishing their false Doctrines by Scripture, which they wrest to their purpose. perverse things, to As members are forcibly plucked from their body; which speak the cruelty and violence of these Hereticks, and the tenderness of the Church towards her Members, being loath to part from them. draw away disciples Thus false Teachers gain indeed Disciples to themselves, but not unto the Lord. after them.

31 Therefore Take your selves heed, and warn others to take heed. watch, and remember that by the space From St. Pauls first coming to Ephesus it was three years current, and now almost compleat, Chap. 19.8, 10 and 20.3. of three years, I ceased not to warn every one night and day a great, and no feigned 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 ; as Christ wept over Ierusalem, Luke 19.41. so St. Paul over the unbelieving Iews; it went to his heart to think that they could not be saved •
▪ See how St. Paul loved Souls, and pitied Souls. with tears.

32 And now brethren, I It being so hard a matter to escape so many snares and dangers, the Apostle prays to God for them, who is able to keep them by his power, through Faith, unto Salvation, 1 Pet. 1.5. and 'tis in vain to look after any meaner defence. commend you to God, and to the The Gospel, which leads us to the Rock upon which we must build, if we would not be moved when the Storm comes. word of his grace, which is able to Encreasing the number of Believers, and augmenting their Graces. God is said to build, and so is his Word, both concurring: The Gospel builds, as a means appointed by God; and God builds, who blesses that means. Hence he is called the God of all Grace, 1 Pet. 5▪10. build you up, and to give you Heaven is called an Inheritance, because we have it only by Adoption, and it is given only unto Children, Rom. 8.17. as also, because it is a firm and lasting possession, not for a term of years, or a certain time, but for ever and ever. an Eph. 1.14, 15. inheritance among all them which are For without holiness none shall see God, Heb. 12.14. sanctified.

33 1 Sam. 12.3. I have Having spoken of the heavenly Inheritance, he tells them how willing he was to have his reward hereafter, and to wave receiving his wages here. In this, St. Paul imitates Moses, Numb. 16.15 and Samuel, 1 Sam. 12.3, 5. coveted no mans silver, or gold, or apparel.

34 Yea, you your selves know, that St. Paul working hard (as they all knew) for a livelyhood, Chap. 18.3. 1 Cor. 4.12. 1 Thes. 2.9. which he gives an account of, 2 Thes. 3.8. to have been done only, that in such a juncture, they being poor, and the false Teachers watching all advantages against him, he might not then be chargeable to them. these hands have ministred unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.

35 I have shewed you As verse 27. all things, 1 Cor. 9.12. 2 Cor. 11.9. a • d 12.13. how that With more than ordinary pains and constancy. so labouring ye ought to That they do not fall, or being fallen, that they may rise again. The word imports the stretching out of the hand to retain any that are going away, or to hold up any that are falling. support In Knowledge, Faith, or any other Grace. the weak; and to remember the Paul might have these words by the relation of others who heard them spoken by our Saviour; for all things that he said or did, could not be written, Ioh. 20.30. words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to Not so much in that giving speaks abundance and affluence; but as it shews our Charity and Goodness, in which we resemble and imitate God. The substance of these words which are attributed to our Saviour, tho not the terms, may be found in divers places, as Luke 6.38. and 16.9. give than to receive.

36 ¶ And when he had thus spoken, he A posture of great humility, becoming Prayer, and frequently used in such occasions, especially in a time of great trouble and distress; altho bodily exercise alone do not profit, 1 Tim. 4.8. yet we may, and must on occasion in Prayer bow the Knee, lift up the hand and eye▪ because it is a reasonable thing to give our bodies in his service, to God that made them. 2. By this we may shew that we are not ashamed to serve and own God before men. And 3. These outward signs do sometimes stir up our own and others devotion. Chap. 21.5. kneeled down, and prayed with them all.
37 And they all wept sore, and fell on Pauls neck, and As they used to do their Friends when they took their leave of them, Gen. 45.14. kissed him.

38 Sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should The loss of a faithful and painful Minister is a publick loss, and many are concerned in it; besides, they had found great benefit by his Ministry, and could not but be sensible of their missing of it. Add to this, Pauls gracious and humble conversation, and the sense of many good Offices done by him, could not but have endeared him unto them. see his face no more. And they Enjoying him as long and as far as they could, and expressing their last and utmost kindness unto him. accompanied him unto the ship.

div.head: CHAP. XXI.
div.p: ANd it came to pass, that after we were Had parted with them, as dearest Friends and Relations do one from the other; with much difficulty and reluctance. gotten from them, and had lanched, we came with a straight course unto An Island in the Mediteranean Sea, nigh unto Crete; where Hippocrates and Apelles are said to have been born. Choos, and the day following unto Another Island in the same Sea, of great fame for the Colosse, or vast Image of Brass which was there, accounted one of the wonders of the world. Rhodes, and from thence unto An Haven Town of Lycia, and its Metropolis. Patara.

2 And finding a ship Whose Master and Mariners intended such a Voyage.
• a •• ng over unto A Country in Syria, scituate nigh the Sea (and bordering upon Palestine) whose chief City was Tyre. Phenicia, we went aboard, and set forth.

3 Now when we had discovered Another Island in the Mediterranean. Cyprus, we left it on the left hand, and sailed unto Syria, and landed at Tyre • : for there the ship was to For Goods and Merchandize which she had taken in at Ephesus. unlade her burden.

4 And finding disciples, we tarried there They tarried the rather so long, that they might worship and serve the Lord on his day together. seven days: Chap. 20.23. who said to Paul By the spirit of Prophecy they foretold his sufferings at Ierusalem, which afterward accordingly befel unto him; and they being ignorant of his undertaking that Journey at Gods command, out of commiseration and pity disswade St. Paul from going to such a place, where they foresaw that he should suffer so much: And this, 'tis said, they did through the spirit, because they had that foreknowledge of all his sufferings from the Spirit; and knowing but in part, being ignorant of that special command Paul had had to go to Ierusalem, they did, according to what they knew, disswade Paul from that Journey: But they knowing that their Prophecy about St. Paul's sufferings must be fulfilled, and the Spirit by which they spake could not err or be mistaken; How come they to disswade St. Paul from going to Ierusalem? It may be answered, That they might think this Prediction of his sufferings to be only conditional, in case he went to Ierusalem; as David was told, That the men of Keilah would deliver him to Saul, 1 Sam. 23.11.12. That is, in case he had trusted himself amongst them. through the Spirit, that he should not go up to Jerusalem.

5 And when we had accomplished those days, we departed, and went our way, and they To shew their greater respect unto him, being loath to part with him so long as it was possible for them to enjoy him; so that they did not despise his temptation that was in the flesh, Gal. 4.14. But it is truly strange what follows, That he was received by them as an Angel of God, even as Christ Iesus. all brought us on our way, with wives and children, till we were out of the city: and we kneeled down This the Iews on extraordinary occasions were wont to do, whilst the Temple it self were standing, viz. make every place a place of Prayer in such a case, Chap. 20.36. on the shore, and prayed.
6 And when we had taken As Chap. 20.1. embracing one another at their parting. our leave one of another, we took ship; and they returned home again.

7 And when we had So far forth as to finished our course from Tyre, we came Ptolemais, a City in Phaenicia, so called from one of the Ptolemies King of Egypt; and is thought to be the same with Accho, mentioned Iudges 1.31. which ancient name is yet retained in the Syriac Translation. to Ptolemais, and saluted the brethren, and abode with them one day.

8 And the next day we that were of Chap. 13.13. Pauls company
departed, and came unto That which was called Caesarea Stratonis, to distinguish it from Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Mount Libanus, as also from another City of that name in Cappadocia; they having been all so called in honour of Caesar, to flatter and perpetuate that Family. The Caesarea here spoken of, was in Palestine, and is mentioned Chap. 10 1. and 18.22. Cesarea; and we entred into the house of Philip the whose office and charge it was to publish the Gospel, which Timothy is exhorted to do, 2 Tim. 4.5. This Office is placed between that of an Apostle and of a Pastor and Teacher, Eph 4.11. and was not so confined to a certain place or people as the latter of these were. Evangelist, Chap. 8.26. which was Of the seven Deacons; of which, see Chap. 6.5. Which Office of a Deacon, Philip having well discharged, did purchase to himself this good Degree, as 1 Tim. 3.13. one
• f the seven and abode with him.

9 And the same man had four daughters, By their Fathers, and their own voluntary determination, as 1 Cor. 7.37. neither is it said whether they continued in that state; but they were so Prophesied; virgins which did not by expounding the Prophesies or Word of God, for 1 Cor. 14.34. 1 Tim. 2.12. no woman is suffered to Teach publickly, but rather foretelling things to come, which Gift God did not debar that Sex from; especially it having been promised, Ioel 2.28. and in part fulfilled before, Chap. 2.17. By which, God would shew the enlargement of his Mercies, and plenty of his Spirit, reserved for the times of the Gospel. prophesie.

10 And as we tarried there many days, there came down from Judea a certain prophet, named Of whom mention is made, Chap. 11.28. of whose Prophecy they could not be ignorant by reason of the great collection which, on that account, was made for the Poor at Ierusalem. Agabus.

11 And when he was come unto us, he It wes ordinary amongst the Prophets to confirm, or at least to exemplify their Prophesies by outward signs and symboles, as Isa. 20.2. Ier. 13.1. Ezek. 12.5. But that of Ier. 27.2. is a parallel unto this; where the Prophet is commanded to make Bonds and Yokes, and to put them upon his neck, to foreshew the subjection of all those Nations unto Nebuchadnezzar. took Pauls girdle, and bound his own hands and feet, and said, Thus None of all the sufferings foreshewn concerning St. Paul, or others of Gods Children and Servants, but are ordered by God, who knows them altogether; and they came not out of the dust, or by casualty, or chance, so as not to have been the matter of Gods foreknowledge and Counsel, Eph. 1.11. saith the holy Ghost, Chap. 20.23. Verse 13. So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that oweth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the The Roman Powers at Ierusalem, and afterwards at Rome. Gentiles.

12 And when we heard these things, both we, and The Converts or Believers that were in Cesarea, pitying him, and having a tender affection for him, see Verse 4. they of that place, with tears, so earnest were they, as 'ith' following verse. besought him not to go up to Jerusalem.

13 Then Paul answered, Chap. 20.24. What mean you to weep, A strange strife, who should overcome by loving most, as in that betwixt David and Ionatham, 1 Sam. 20.40, &c. This undaunted Champion, who did not seem to feel any of his own afflictions and miseries, yet grieves for the grief and sympathy of others, and bears a double weight in his burdens; one directly and immediately from them, as lying upon himself; the other mediately, as recoiling from others (who suffered with him) unto him again. and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but As Christs love for us was stronger than death, Cant. 8.6. so must our love be to him again, or it is not of the same nature with his, nor begotten by it. also to die at Jerusalem for the His Truth, and Glory. name of the Lord Jesus.

14 And when he would not be perswaded, As having done their utmost, and what became them. we ceased, saying▪ They commit the event unto God; thus we pray dayly, That Gods Will may be done, Matth. 6.10. Luke 11.2. and thus our Saviour, not only by his Precept, but by his Example, hath taught us, Matth. 26.42. Luke 22.42. and when Gods will is done, our will is done also, Phil. 2.5. if the Mind and Spirit be in us that was in Christ, and otherwise we are none of his, Rom. 8.9. The will of the Lord be done.

15 And after those days we As they do pack up, that are to remove to another house or place, not intending to come thither any more again; this also did shew their readiness of mind to endure and suffer all things, as loss of Relations and Friends, and all accommodations for Christ. took up o • r carriages, and vvent up to J • rus • l • m.

16 There went with us also certain of th • disciples of Cesarea, Either this Mnason was in their company, or rather they were brought by the Disciples of Cesarea to the House of this Mnason, who was and brought with them one Mnason of Cyprus, one of them that was converted when Paul and Barnabas was at Cyprus, Chap. 13.4. an old disciple, with whom and Lodgings being scarce at Ierusalem (when all the Males were to appear there in those three annual Solemnities) it was no small kindness to be provided for by him. we should lodge.

17 And when we were come to Jerusalem, It is thought that by Brethren in this place, and verse the seventh, they are meant, who being Believers, were formed into a Church with its several Officers, and that they are called Disciples only, verse 4. who living dispersed, and in smaller numbers, could not constitute such a Church; but surely whatsoever there is of priviledge and happiness in this spiritual fraternity, That truly Catholick Charity that was in the Apostles and other holy men, would not so confine it, as to exclude any from enjoying of it, who did not exclude themselves by greater crimes than their paucity in number, or the consequences of that could amount unto. the brethren received us gladly.

18 And the day following Paul went in with us One of the Apostles, tho some think that he was a Kinsman of our Saviours, and at this time Bishop of Ierusalem, unto Gal. 1.19. James, and all the elders were present.as Chap. 15.6, 13. not so called for their age, but dignity or place in the Church.

19 And when he had saluted them, he declared God had so done those marvellous works, that they ought to be had in remembrance; and this was said by the Apostle, that God might not lose the Glory, nor the Church the benefit of any of those great things which God had wrought: Otherwise, St. Paul acknowledges that he was the least of the Apostles, and not meet to be called an Apostle, 1 Cor. 15.9. and all his power was ministerial, he was only an Instrument in Gods hand, to be acted by him, as Chap. 20.24. particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles q by his ministry.

20 And when they heard it, they Acknowledging all in that great work of the conversion of the Gentiles, to have been from God; and that Paul that had planted, and Apollos that had watered, were nothing, 1 Cor. 3.6, 7. glorified the Lord, and said unto him, Thou seest, brother, how many Tens of thousands, as the word does usually signify; a definite, for an indefinite number, signifying very many: And considering out of what small beginnings, and by what despicable means, and all within the space of about five and twenty years that this grain of Mustardseed had spared its self; and add to this, that they were Iews, that obstinate and prejudiced generation who are here spoken of, and they were then so many, so wonderfully many, who believed. thousands of Jews there are which believe, and they are Of Ceremonies, and concerning forbidden Meats, &c. For the Decree of the Apostles, Chap. 15.29. concerning these things, did only respect such as were converted from Paganisme to the Faith of Christ. And the Iews that were converted before the dispersion by Adrian (the Roman Emperor) many years after this time, did not throughly understand their freedom from that Law, but were under the burden of it, as appears by several Ecclesiastical Writers. all Rom. 10.2. Gal. 1.14. ze • lous of the law.

21 And they are Instructed or Catechised concerning thee; the Zealots had made it their business to instil such aspersions and odious reflections against Paul, as if their Accusations had been the fundamental truths of their Religion. informed of thee that thou teachest all the Jews which are among the Gentiles to forsake The Ceremonial Law, given by his Ministry. Moses, saying, that they ought not to circumcise their children, neither to To live, to act in their course of life after walk after the customs of their Fathers, or the rituals of Moses. the customs.

22 It can't be otherwise; or what else remains to be done? What is it therefore? All the faithful must meet; for the Magistrate then being Pagan, and enemies both to the Church and the Gospel; in matters of great moment, especially when there was any fear of a Schism, the whole multitude of Believers were gathered together to consult about it. the multitude must needs come together: for they will hear that thou art come.

23 Do therefore this that we say to thee: We have four men which have a Vows were either such as men did make in gratitude for any deliverance they had received, as from Sickness, Storms, or any imminent dangers: Or Secondly, to enable them the better to serve God on any occasion; and then they were bound to keep themselves from all those things which were forbidden to the Nazarite, as Wine and strong drink, and to nourish their Hair as the Nazarites were bound to do. This Vow they made for a certain time, and not perpetual: The Law concerning it, you may see, Numb. 6.2, 3, 4, 5. vow on them;

24 Them take and They advise Paul to perform all those Rites required of a Nazarite, the observation of which did legally purify him. purifie thy self with them, and be These charges were about the threefold Sacrifice which were to be offered, Numb. 6.10. two Turtles or young Pigeons, a Lamb, unleavened Bread, and Cakes of fine Flower, as Numb. 6.11, 12. and the other four spoken of, verse 23. being poor, they require Paul here to bear their charges also, that so he might appear to be the chief amongst them, and the more zealous in their Law, to take away the scandal that was taken up by the Iews against him (these Ceremonies being as yet not deadly, or evil; tho they were dead and indifferent.) at charges with them, that they may Numb. 6.2, 13, 18. Chap. 18.18. shave their heads: and all may know that those things whereof they were informed concerning thee, are nothing, but that thou thy self also Livest according to the Law of Moses, contrary unto what they reported of thee. walkest orderly, and keepest the law.Which was done at the end of their separation, and was the accomplishment of all; and they burned the Hair which they shaved off, under their Sacrifices, to shew, that all their legal performances were only acceptable unto God through Jesus Christ, who was sacrificed for us, 1 Cor. 5.7. and Heb. 10.12.

25 As touching the Gentiles These Ceremonies (after their accomplishment in Christ) not being at all necessary, they were not imposed upon any that received the Faith of Christ from amongst the Gentiles, or other Nations; only suffered for a while unto the Iews that turned to Christ for the hardness of their hearts, and inveterate zeal for them. which believe, Chap. 15.20. we have written and concluded, that they observe no such thing, save only that they keep themselves from things Of these things; see Chap. 15.29. offered to idols, and from blood and from strangled▪ and from fornication.

26 Then Paul agrees to their advice, and follows it; and having set such a time for his Vow as might end with the other four mens, he, with the four mentioned, Paul took the men, and the next day purifying himself with them, Chap. 24.18. entred into the temple, signify to the Priest (that was concerned to know it, because of the Sacrifices that were to be offered for them) that the time of their separation was fulfilled, which is here called the days of Purification, for the reason intimated, verse 24. Numb. 6.13. to signifie the accomplishment of the days of purification, until that Intending to abide in the Temple until all those Rites were performed which were required of them. an offering should be offered for every one of them.

27 And when Either, 1. after his coming, to Ierusalem, or rather 2. of his Vow; for 'tis thought that his Vow of Separation was but for Seven days: Or, 3. The Seven days of that Feast of Pentecost which he came unto. the seven days were almost ended, the Jews which were of Who were implacably set against him wheresoever he went, as Ch. 14.19. and 17.5. These Iews dwelt at Ephesus, and elsewhere, but were come to observe the Feast at Ierusalem. Asia, when they saw him in the temple, stirred up all the people, and By violence, and against Law. laid hands on him,

28 Crying out, Minding them by this Compellation, of their being a peculiar people unto God, and that none might be admitted with them in his worship. Men of Israel, help: This is the man that teacheth all men every where A Charge is laid against St. Paul consisting of divers Articles, but all false; for he was a most zealous lover of that people, and taught them nothing but the true use and meaning of the Law: But thus they had done to our Saviour, Matth. 26.61. and to St. Stephen, Chap 6.13. against the people, and the law, and this place: and farther, Chap. • 4.6. hath brought Greeks also That is, into the Court of the Iews, which was so far unlawful, that they might have killed a Roman if he had come in there; and every one was warned by an Inscription upon the Pillars. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . That no Stranger or Foreigner might come into that holy place. into the temple, and hath polluted this holy place.

29 (The Iews of Asia, who could not but know Trophimus; and he following of Paul in this Journey, either ignorantly, or maliciously they accuse the Apostle for taking him into the Temple with him; which was only their surmise, and the issue of their enraged Jealousy. For they had seen before with him in the city, Chap. 20.4. Trophimus an Ephesian, whom they supposed that Paul had brought into the temple▪)

30 There was a general concourse from all parts, Tantum Religio poterat, no such heats as such are which are moved about Religion; whilst the Wisdom that is from above, is first pure, then peaceable, Iames 3.17. And Chap. 26.21. all the city was moved, and the people ran together: and they took Paul, and drew him Lest by their uproar they should occasion any of the Gentiles to come in there to quell them; or intending to kill Paul, that they drew him thence, that he might not pollute that holy place with his Blood: Thus they strain at a Gnat, being unwilling to pollute the Temple; but they would swallow a Camel, not sticking to shed the blood of the Innocent. out of the temple: And forthwith the Either by the Keeper of the doors, or by the Soldiers of the Temple. doors were shut.

31 And as they went about to kill him, tidings came unto the The Commander in chief over all the Soldiers there; or one that had the command over a Thousand. At the three great Feasts there was usually a considerable number of Soldiers at Ierusalem, the confluence from all parts being then so great, and the Iews so impatient of any Yoke or Government, the Romans durst not trust such multitudes without some check upon them. Thus at the Passover, when they took and crucified our Saviour, these Soldiers were made use of, Iohn 18.12. chief captain of the band, that all Jerusalem was in an uprore.

32 Who A wonderful Providence of God for Paul's preservation, that the chief Captain should be so near, as to be able to hinder the Massacring of Paul; and especially that he should be defended and preserved by one that was a stranger to him, and an enemy to his Religion; immediately took soldiers, and centurions, and ran down unto them: And when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, they lest they should have been set upon by the Soldiers, for breaking the Peace, &c. The fear of man caused them to forbear what the fear of God could not. left beating of Paul.

33 Then the chief captain cam • near and took him, and Verse 11▪ commanded him to be bound with two chains; and demanded who he was, and what he had done.Whether as Peter was, see Chap. 12.6. Or that he was bound with one upon his feet, and with the other upon his hands, it was exactly fulfilled what Agabus had prophesied concerning him, verse 11. So does God provide, that not one word of his Servants which they speak from him, shall fail; and that St. Paul should be heard before he was condemned.

34 And • ome As is usual in popular commotions, they agreed in doing mischief, but not in the reason of it. cried one thing, some another, among the multitude: and when he could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried Called Antonia, because it was built in honour of Mark Antony, on the North side of the Temple. into the castle.

35 And when he came In the ascent to the Castle; upon the stairs, so it was that he was born he was born of the Soldiers, either because the preass was so great, he being in the midst of them; or being taken up by them, to secure him from the fury of the enraged multitude. of the souldiers, for the violence of the people.

36 For the multitude of the people followed after, crying, That is, kill him; for that was indeed • o take him out of their way. The same speech they used against our Saviour, Luke 23.18. Iohn 19.15. when they desired his death. Chap. 22.22. Away with him.

37 And as Paul was to be led into the castle, he said un • o the chief captain A common expression in that Language, whereby he craves leave, and bespeaks attention. ▪ May I speak unto thee? Who said, Canst thou speak Greek?After the Grecian Empire, their Langugage became and continued to be very common in Asia and Egypt, and very well known amongst all the Romans of any Education or Quality.

38 Chap. 5.36. Art not thou A famous Ring-leader of a Rebellious Crew, as some think, in the Reign of Tiberius; but as others, in the Thirteenth Year of the Emperor Claudius, and continued till under Nero's Reign, and came from these Four Thousand mentioned here at his first setting up, to have Thirty Thousand Followers, pretending himself to be a Prophet; of whom Iosephus, Antiq. lib. 20. cap. 11. that Egyptian which before these days madest an uprore, and leddest out into the wilderness four thousand men that were Or Assassinates, that did wear Daggs or Stellatoes. murderers?

39 But Paul said, I Chap. 9.11. and 22.3. am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no It being the Metropolis, or chief City in Cilicia, built by Perseus, as some think; howsoever having the priviledg of the Roman Freedom; as Chap. 22.28. mean city: and St. Paul begs leave to speak unto the people, that he might not seem to affect popularity, or to be guilty of any Insurrection or Tumult. Thus he had leave also of Agrippa, before that he made that famous Apology, Chap. 26.1. I beseech thee, suffer me to speak unto the people.

40 And when he had given him licence, Paul stood As he was now about to be carried into the Castle, Antonia before mentioned; on the stairs, and signifying, that he craved their audience; as Chap. 12.17. and 13.16. beckned with the hand unto the people: And when there was m • de a great silence, he spake unto them The Hebrew Tongue being understood by all of them, and most grateful unto them. Yet this was not the pure and ancient Hebrew, which had been corrupted ever since their Captivity; but the Syriack Tongue, which they there learned, was called Hebrew, it having at first been derived from the Hebrew, and being then in use by those who were Hebrews. in the Hebrew tongue, saying,

div.head: CHAP. XXII.
div.p:
Altho ••• were wicked men, and cruel persecutors, St. Paul giveth them their titles of respect, which by the places God had put them in, are due unto them; see on, Chap. 7. • . MEn▪ brethren, and fathers, hear ye my de
••• ce, which I make now unto you.

2 ( • nd when they heard that he spake in the Th • ordinary Hebrew; that which was taken for Hebrew, and spoken by the Hebrews after their return from the Captivity, tho mixt with the Syriac; as Chap. 21.40. Hebr •• tongue to them, they It being more grateful unto them to hear Paul speak in their Mother Tongue; especially they having so great a prejudice against all other Nations and Languages. kept the more silence 〈◊〉 A • d he saith)

3 Chap. 21.39. 2 Cor. 11.22. I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city The Apostle alludes unto the posture that the Disciples of any Rabbi, o • Teacher, in those times did use; the Master sitting in some high or elevated place, did teach his Scholars, who sate at his feet on the ground; and as they grew in knowledg, were advanced to sit nearer to their Master▪ Deut. 33.3. And Abraham is thus said to be called to God's foot, Isaiah 41.2. And Mary sate at • ur Saviour's
〈◊〉 , Luke 10.39., at the feet of The same Gam • liel who made tha • moderating speech in the Apostle's 〈◊〉
Chap 5.34. This perfect manner of the Law is Ph ••• asaism, which the Ap •• tle was brought up in, and before his conversion made a profession of, Phil. 3.5. Not that the Apostle reckoned upon any perfection in this profe • sion; but because, as Chap. 26.5 it was the most strait sect of their Religion, observing a great deal of punctuality and accurateness, making, what they called, a Hedg about the Law. Gamaliel, and taught according to the s perfect manner of the law of the Not observing onely the Law, which was given by God to their Fathers by the hand of M • ses; but the Traditions of their Fathers he was exceeding zealous in; as Gal. 1.4. fathers, and was zealous Or as some Copies read, zealous towards the Law; both in the same sense. His zeal for the Law was sincere; not out of by-ends, but out of his love to God, tho it was not according to Knowledg, Rom. 10.2. It was truly according unto what he knew or believed; but it was not according to true Knowledg. towards God, as ye all are this day.

4 Chap. 8.3. And I persecuted The Doctrine and Practice of Christianity. this way unto As much as in him lies, being one of the most furious persecutors that hunted for the precious life, breathing out threatnings and slaughters with every breath, Chap. 9.1. the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.

5 As also the high priest doth bear me witness, and all the Their Sanhedrim, or great Council. estate of the elders: from whom also I received Commission or Orders. letters unto the The Iews of Damascus are called brethren, because descended from the Patriarchs as well as he. And still, as ver. 1. he would overcome that stubborn people with Civility, heaping up coals of fire on their heads, Rom. 12.20. that they might be melted, and then formed after a more excellent manner. brethren, and went to Damascus, to bring them which were there, bound unto Jerusalem, for to be punished.

6 And Chap 26.1 • . it came to pass, that as I made my journey, and was come nigh unto Damascus about noon, suddenly there As Lightning it suddenly encompassed him. But see Chap. 9. from the 3d verse; where this History is set down by St. Luke. And here little more can be taken notice of, than some small variety in the expressions. shone from heaven a great light round about me.

7 And I fell unto the ground, and heard a voice saying unto me As men that call another earnestly, repeat his Name; as when the Angel of the Lord called Abraham, Abraham, Gen. 22.11., S • ul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?

8 And I answered, Who art thou Lord? And he said unto me, I am Jesus of That contemned (tho not contemptible) Name is owned by Christ from Heaven; that they might not be ashamed when they were reproached by it on Earth. Of the rest, see Chap. 9.5. Nazareth whom thou persecutest.

9 And they that were with me, saw indeed the light, and were afraid; but they This may be added to what was formerly said, that the men who travelled with Paul, may be said not to have heard the voice of him that spake, because they did not understand it, or obey it: They were not converted, as Paul was, by it: the Hebrew Language putting hearing for obeying; as in many Scriptures: And both St. Paul, who here spake, and Luke, who penned this History, understood exactly the proprieties of that Tongue. heard not the voice of him that spake to me.Of this▪ see Chap. 9.7.

10 And I said, What shall I do, Lord? And the Lord said unto me, Arise, and go into Damascus, and there it shall be told thee of Such things as Ananias told him from Christ, were as if Christ himself had told him them: And by Ananias our Saviour satisfied St. Paul's question, What shall I do, Lord? all things which are appointed for thee to do.See Chap. 9.6.

11 And when I could not see for the glory of The Excellency of the Object over-powering hi • fight. It was a strange work of God that enabled St. Stephen to see Christ (who is now so glorious), Chap. 7.55. And it will be according to Gods wonderful power, when at the Resurrection we shall be enabled to look upon Christ in his greatest glory. that light, being Behold the goodness and severity of G • d upon Paul: Severity upon him in striking of him with blindness in his body; but goodness indeed to him, in enlightning, converting, and saving of his soul. led by the hand of them that were w th me, I came into Damascus.

12 And Chap. 9. one Ananias, a devout man This is added to distinguish him from a Proselyte, and to let them know that he had received the Gospel, not from a Convert out of Gentilism (who tho they admitted, yet they had a greater jealousie over, and less kindness for), but from one like unto themselves in all things. according
to t • e law, having a good report of all the Jew which dwelt there.

13 Came unto me That in this posture he might more conveniently put his hands upon Paul; which we read that he now did, Chap. 9.17. and was ordinarily done upon the miraculous curing of any., and stood, and said unto me, Brother Saul, receive thy sight. And the same Or, as Chap. 9.18. immediately. The suddenness of the Cures, spake the power from whence they came: None but God saves and delivers after this manner. hour I look • d up upon him.

14 And he said Nothing could please the people better than to hear God so stiled: For this they gloried in, above all things, that they and theirs had God to their Father, Iohn 8.41. And nothing could better suit St. Paul s purpose, who would not lie under that scandal of endeavouring an Apostacy from the Iewish Religion (for the Gospel which he preached, was but the substance and perfection of the Law); or that he served or worshipped any other God than the God of Abraham ▪ , The God of our fathers Chap. 26.16. hath He hath taken thee, as by the hand, and by his wonderful Providence brought thee into that condition in which thou art. chosen thee, that thou shouldest know his will, and see Chap 3.14. and 7.52. that just One, and shouldest hear the voice of his mouth.Christ is the Holy One, spotless and without blemish; God's righteous servant, Isa. 53.11. But this is here the rather spoken, that he might convince them of their sin, in putting our Lord to Death: For tho he sweetned his speech to them in what he might, he would not flatter them to their destruction; Like a skilful Chyrurgeon, he would not heal too fast. Now Paul saw Christ with the Eye of his mind, it being enlightned to believe in him: And he saw him in his Journey also with the Eyes of his body. Some read, 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , not 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . And then Ananias tells St. Paul, that he was sent to shew him that which was just and right in Gods sight; which he being blinded by his zeal for the Law, could not perceive.

15 For thou shalt be his The Apostles were in a more special manner Christs Witnesses; as Luke 24.48. Iohn 1.7. Chap. 1.8.
